metadata.title: What Happens After You Click Buy? | Inside 3PL with Radial
metadata.author: WorkflowLife
metadata.shortDescription:
What really happens after you click "Buy Now" on Shopify, Amazon, or an online store?

Behind every online order, there's an entire world of warehouses, inventory systems, integrations, fulfillment operations, and technology working together.

In this video, I'm taking you behind the scenes of the e-commerce industry through my conversation with Anthony Hockaday from Radial, a major third-party logistics (3PL) provider, now part of Paxon.

I met Anthony while attending the Pipe17 Customer Advisory Board in Seattle, where I had the opportunity to speak with professionals working across different areas of e-commerce technology and operations.

Before jumping into the interview, I'll explain what a 3PL company actually does from my perspective as an IT Manager working with ERP systems, Shopify, NetSuite, warehouse integrations, and automation.

In this video, we explore:

What a 3PL company does and why it matters

How online orders move from e-commerce platforms to warehouses

The technology connecting inventory, orders, and fulfillment

Challenges facing modern logistics providers

The potential role of AI and automation in fulfillment

My conversation with Anthony from Radial

About this channel

I share real experiences building AI tools, exploring new technology, working with enterprise systems, and learning from people across the tech industry.

This is the first interview I'm sharing from my Seattle trip, with more conversations coming soon!

🔔 Subscribe for more videos about AI, e-commerce technology, automation, and real-world tech projects.

💬 Question for you: Do you think AI will eventually manage warehouse operations and order fulfillment with minimal human involvement? Share your thoughts in the comments!

#Ecommerce #3PL #Radial #Logistics #AI #Automation #Pipe17

[music] Ask your 3PL for its peak season calendar in writing, the order cutoff dates, the receiving deadlines for new inventory, and any peak season surcharges, [music] and build your plan around those dates, not around hope. The third piece is the allocation problem and it is the piece that catches [music] sellers with more than one warehouse. When your inventory sits in two 3PL warehouses, one east, one west, [music] a stockout is not always a total stockout. It can be a regional stockout. The east warehouse is empty while the west warehouse still has 100 units and the eastern customers get slow shipping or a cancellation while the western stock sits unsold. The fix is a transfer rule. When one warehouse falls below its reorder point and the [music] other still holds a surplus, move a portion of the stock between warehouses or rebalance the next inbound shipment toward the warehouse that is running low. The 3PL [music] system should show the stock level at each warehouse separately, and your weekly review should look at the regional numbers, not just the total. One approach is the weekly 15-minute review. Every Monday, open the inventory dashboard, [music] check each product at each warehouse, place the reorder for anything at or below its reorder point, and confirm the inbound shipment dates for anything already on order. 15 minutes a week is the whole job, and it is the job that prevents the stock out. Remember, don't skip. The full benefit comes from watching it all. The fourth piece is the slow stock problem because forecasting is not only about having enough, [music] it is about not having too much. Inventory that does not sell is money sitting on a shelf paying storage fees every month, and the peak season is the worst time to discover it because the warehouse is full of your best sellers and your slow products are taking the space. The habit is the quarterly review. Every 3 months, list every product by [music] its turn rate, how many times its stock sells through in a year, and act on the slowest ones. A product that is not sold in 90 days gets a discount, a bundle with a best seller or a listing refresh. A product that is not sold in 6 months gets a decision. Clear it at a discount, return it, or accept that it is a loss and stop paying storage on it. [music] One more detail that matters for peak season. Never let a slow product storage fees eat the profit of your best sellers. The warehouse bill does not separate them, [music] but your spreadsheet should. Let me close this module with the peak season checklist because it turns the whole system into one page. Eight weeks before peak, confirm the forecast, place [music] the main inventory order, and confirm the 3PL's receiving deadline. Four weeks before [music] peak, confirm the stock has arrived and been received. Check the regional split and set the low stock alerts. Two weeks before peak, confirm the shipping cutoff dates, confirm the carrier capacity, and [music] confirm the returns process for the orders that will come back in January. During peak, run the Monday inventory review. Watch the reorder points daily [music] for your top three products and keep a small emergency reserve. A few dozen units of your best seller [music] held back from the normal allocation so a surprise spike never empties the shelf completely. And after peak, [music] count what sold, count what is left, and write down what the forecast got right and what it got wrong [music] because next year's forecast is this year's actual sales. And the sellers who improve their forecast every year [music] are the sellers who never run out of their best product twice. So here is the whole blueprint in one breath. Add up the full cost per order, pick and pack, storage, receiving, returns, [music] and the monthly minimum. And compare the total against packing it yourself, not the headline fee. And forecast like an owner. Set the reorder point, hold the safety stock, plan the peak season eight weeks out, and run the 15-minute Monday review so your best seller is never out of stock when customers want it most. Your first step this week is simple. Pull your last three months of orders, count the packing hours, and map where your customers live. Then request quotes from three 3PLs that operate in those regions and run the one order cost test on each. Every time you click "Buy Now," an enormous logistics network goes to work behind the scenes.

But how do products travel from overseas factories to American warehouses, and eventually reach your doorstep?

Welcome to the world of **3PL Logistics (Third-Party Logistics)** — the hidden infrastructure powering modern e-commerce and global trade.

In this MonopolyInsights documentary, we explore how third-party logistics companies operate, how they make money, and why businesses across the United States rely on them to manage their supply chains.

From warehouse operations and inventory management to international freight, automated fulfillment, and advanced logistics technology, discover how this multi-layered industry connects manufacturers, businesses, and customers.

🚢 How products travel from overseas factories to US warehouses.

📊 How Warehouse Management Systems (WMS), Transportation Management Systems (TMS), and Order Management Systems (OMS) work.
🤖 How AI, robotics, and warehouse automation are transforming logistics.
🌎 How distributed warehousing and international supply chains operate.
🏢 The difference between Amazon FBA, independent 3PLs, and 4PL.
💰 How logistics companies generate revenue and calculate fulfillment costs.
📈 How businesses evaluate and select the right logistics partners.

- Supply chain and logistics professionals
- Anyone interested in global trade and business infrastructure

What Is a 3PL? We Went Inside a Real Warehouse to Show You

We went inside a real warehouse and filmed how a 3PL actually works.
From the moment your inventory arrives to the moment it ships to your customer.

Made for Shopify brands trying to figure out if a 3PL is right for them.
Run a 3PL warehouse yourself? Stick around too — this shows exactly what brands look for in a partner.

⏱ Timestamps

3:55 How to Level Up Your 3PL Offer with Dates & Rates

What does 3PL mean?
Third-Party Logistics.
A company that stores, picks, packs, and ships your products for you.
So you don't have to.

How does a 3PL actually work? (This is what we filmed)
You ship your inventory to their warehouse.
A customer orders from your Shopify store.
They pick it, pack it, ship it out.
We walk through the whole process on the warehouse floor.

Do you need one?
Packing your own orders? Outgrowing your space?
A 3PL takes that off your plate.
Not just for huge stores — plenty of small and mid-size Shopify sellers use one too.

How to choose a provider
Know your supply chain first.
Where do your products come from? How do they arrive? How many orders do you ship per day?
Then compare shipping rates and carrier relationships.
Most importantly: can they actually promise accurate delivery dates?
Vague delivery windows are the top reason brands switch 3PLs.

Shopify Orders in NetSuite, Fulfilled by Your 3PL | Live Demo Webinar

Running Shopify with a 3PL and NetSuite shouldn’t mean manual exports, stock mismatches, and monthly finance clean-up.
Yet for many teams, that’s still the daily reality.

In this 40-minute webinar, Novutech and Celigo show what a clean, fully integrated Shopify → 3PL → NetSuite flow looks like in practice — with a live demo and real-life scenarios.

🔍 What you’ll learn:

✔️ End-to-end order flow from Shopify to 3PL and financial posting in NetSuite
✔️ Inventory and order status alignment across systems
✔️ How to handle edge cases: partial shipments, returns, backorders
✔️ Live demo of key integration flows
✔️ A scalable rollout approach across brands, warehouses, and regions

🎯 Who should watch:

• E-commerce Operations
• Supply Chain & Logistics
• Finance teams
• NetSuite Admins
• RevOps / IT

🔔 Subscribe for more content on NetSuite, integrations, and scaling operations

metadata.title: What Is High-Ticket Dropshipping?
metadata.author: Anton Kraly - Drop Ship Lifestyle
metadata.shortDescription:
If you've ever asked yourself, "What is high-ticket dropshipping?", this video is for you. Join eCommerce expert Anton Kraly from Drop Ship Lifestyle as he breaks down this powerful business model in simple, beginner-friendly terms.

Discover the world of high ticket dropshipping and learn how to start dropshipping with this beginner-friendly guide! Perfect for those looking to build a profitable online business through ecommerce, this dropshipping tutorial will provide the essential steps. Learn how to start dropshipping and create your own shopify dropshipping store today.

This isn't your average dropshipping guide. Anton explains how high-ticket dropshipping is a real, profitable business focused on selling premium products ($500-$5,000) with reliable suppliers to customers who are willing to invest in quality. Learn how it works, why it's better than low-ticket dropshipping, and why it's more relevant than ever in 2025.

The video covers:
* The High-Ticket Dropshipping Business Model (Step-by-Step Breakdown)
* High-Ticket vs. Low-Ticket Dropshipping
* The 5 Key Components of the Business Model (Niche, Suppliers, Store, Traffic, Customers)
* Why High-Ticket Dropshipping Still Works in 2025
* Common Dropshipping Myths Debunked
* Is High-Ticket Dropshipping Right for You?

Anton also debunks common myths about dropshipping, showing that you don't need a huge budget or thousands of visitors to be profitable. This business model is all about quality over quantity, offering a path to a location-independent lifestyle with higher profit margins per sale.

Ready to take the next step? Anton invites you to join his free high-ticket dropship training, where you'll get a two-hour training and a free ebook with 500 high-ticket niche ideas. Click the link in the description to get started!

---

Resources Mentioned:

Free High-Ticket Dropship Training & 500 Niche Ideas: https://www.dropshiplifestyle.com/watch/

---

high ticket drop shipping is this really
simple business model where you just
take expensive products from well-known
name brands and you put them on a
website and you market them online and
sell them. And then when you get a sale,
you send the purchase order to that
brand of which you have a agreement
with. That's known as an authorized
dealer agreement. And they're going to
invoice you for the dealer cost of the
product while you sold it at the MAP
price, which MAP means minimum
advertised price or you know other words
a sale price that they um you know agree
upon that you can sell it at. And uh you
keep the difference and usually the
margins are like 15 all the way up to
30% sometimes more. Sometimes it can be
less too. It really depends on shipping
costs and taxes and other things like
that. um you'll figure that stuff out as
you go into this, but high ticket drop
shipping is really simple um in the fact
that you can make more money per sale.
So the average order value instead of
being like a hundred or $200 like that
range, you're looking at a,000 to $2,000
maybe higher. Okay? So, high ticket drop
shipping, instead of making like 20 to
$40 per sale, you're going to be making
$200 to $400 per sale, which is a huge
difference because when you get a sale
and you make $300 in profit after
everything's said and done, and you get
points from using a a business credit
card to uh purchase cost of goods sold
and, you know, spend money on ads and
software and stuff like that, um, you
can have a really profitable business
with only maybe 10 or 20 30 orders per
month. And if you can scale it up past
that 50 to 100 orders per month, you can
have an insanely profitable business.
Um, now it does come with some caveats
and that is number one there is higher
risk involved because when there is an
order defect like let's say shipping
damage or the order is not delivered
correctly or the whatever the the
customer is not satisfied with the
order. Um, you're going to end up having
to deal with that. And sometimes, rarely
it happens, but sometimes there's
disputes, credit card chargebacks that
happen. And because there's such high
ticket orders, those huge disputes, um
it can take up to 30 to 60 days to
resolve. Um and sometimes the bank side
with the customer even though they
should side with you. So sometimes those
high ticket disputes can really eat away
at your margins and your cash flow. So
it does come with a little bit higher
risk. But that also means that as long
as you're responsible and you do your
work as a high ticket salesperson and
you handle customer service well, um you
go back and forth properly and
communicate between the customer and the
supplier and you also know the niche and
the products very well in the way so
that you can help the customer to uh you
know understand the products, you should
do just fine. Um, like a lot of the
time, um, little shipping damage issues
and product defect issues can just be
fixed by setting it up correctly or or
maybe making a little tweak here and

really well already and have a lot of
experience, um, you'll be able to offer
that advice to the customer so that
they're going to easily be able to fix
the issue on their end. Um, otherwise,
they'll have to take it to a service
center of some sort or get somebody to
come out to their house to fix the
product. A lot of times these high
ticket products, especially the really
high ticket ones, actually require
somebody to come to the customer's home
or business and actually install or set
up the product for them. And that's
what's known as white glove delivery.
Um, sometimes they they're so complex
these products that actually requires
that to happen. So you'll have to
coordinate between the white glove
delivery uh company if it's a third
party company um or the supplier might
even just work directly with them. Every
niche is different. Okay? So, you're
just going to be diving way more into
not just the sales side of it and the
marketing side of it, but also the
customer support side and the
fulfillment side of things. Um, the
supplier is going to help you a lot with

more money. So the biggest difference
between this business model and other

that authorized dealer agreement you

segments.text: Hi, I'm Stephen with LedgerGurus,
and in this video I'm gonna talk about contribution margin.
We will unpack everything you need to know to understand, calculate,
and use contribution margin to optimize your profitability.
Let's start with the basics of contribution margin.
Every sale you make brings in revenue,
but not all that money stays in your pocket.
To understand how much of that actually contributes to your operations and your
profit, let's dive into variable and fixed costs.
Variable costs increase as your sales increase. Fixed costs, on the other hand,
stay constant regardless of how much you sell. In the world of ecommerce,
variable costs include things like cost of goods sold,
fulfillment and shipping costs, payment processor fees, and advertising costs.
These costs can be categorized as cost of goods sold, or cost of sales,
or total cost of sales. Fixed costs would include things like payroll, software,
rent, non-advertising, marketing spend, and so on. In theory,
variable costs go up proportionately with sales and fixed costs stay constant.
In reality,
the variable costs vary and fixed costs do have to go up as your business gets
bigger. For example, you'll see different product costs by sku or product item.
Shipping costs can vary based on the product item, size, weight,
or bundle of products.
Payment processing fees can vary based on the credit card that the customer
uses. Finally, advertising costs can vary by the month, week, day,
and even time of day. Fixed costs can't stay fixed forever.
As your business grows, eventually you're going to have to increase those costs.
They typically increase in step functions.
Calculating your contribution margin is straightforward.
You simply subtract your variable costs from your revenue.
What you're left over with is used to pay your fixed costs and ultimately
generate a profit.
You can calculate contribution margin at the product item level,
at the sales channel level, and ultimately at the overall business level.
Let's do an example at the product item level.
Say that you're selling a product for $20 and the variable costs are $14.
You're left with $6 in contribution margin.
If you wanted to calculate a contribution margin ratio,
you divide the $6 of contribution margin by the $20 of revenue,
and that would give you a 30% contribution margin ratio.
There are a few key insights that take away from contribution margin. First,
your profitability will never exceed your contribution margin.
If your contribution margin is 30%,
your net operating income ratio or operating margin ratio is never gonna be
greater than that. Second takeaway.
If you have a contribution margin of 0% or less, you have a broken business.
Your fundamental pricing and variable costs must change.
You need to raise prices and or decrease your cost of goods and or decrease your
cost of sales. Act quickly if you find yourself in this situation.
Third takeaway is you can use your contribution margin ratio and your fixed cost
to determine a break even revenue point. For example,
if you had a contribution margin of 30% and fixed cost of $300,000 to determine
your break even revenue, you would simply divide your fixed cost of $300,000,
buy your 30% contribution margin, which gives you a million dollars,
add a million dollars in sales,
your break even anything above that should generate profit.
As I mentioned earlier, reality is a bit messier,
but this calculation will get you to the right target. Finally, there is great.
Benefit at tracking the contribution margin at the business level.
There is also benefit at tracking the contribution margin at the sales channel
level. This will allow you to determine if selling through Amazon or Shopify is
generating the margins that you expect.
Tracking contribution margin at the product item or SKU level can also be
beneficial, but very time consuming. Start at the top, work your way down.
Calculating contribution margin requires good accounting, and in particular,
accrual accounting.
There's some additional videos in the comments that will help you with a lot of
the concepts that I've discussed. If you want to go deeper on any of them,
if you need help determining your contribution margin,
help with your ecommerce accounting or just help with business advisory,
reach out to us in the link in the comments.
And if you found this video helpful, like it,
ask me a question in the comments and subscribe to our channel for more content
like this.

metadata.title: How to Work Out Landed Cost for a Shipment Into Dubai
metadata.author: Witners Shipping
metadata.shortDescription:
Your supplier's invoice is not what a shipment really costs. This guide shows how to work out landed cost for goods imported into Dubai: the customs value (CIF), customs duty, import VAT, and the clearance, port and delivery charges around them, with a simple order to build your own landed cost sheet.

Chapters:
00:00 Introduction
00:24 What is landed cost?
00:49 Step 1: Customs value
01:25 Step 2: Customs duty
01:56 Step 3: Import VAT
02:25 Who pays VAT, and when
02:56 The other charges
03:23 Your landed cost sheet
03:58 Plan your shipment with WITNERS

WITNERS has in-house, licensed UAE customs brokers handling imports, exports and free-zone movements, with air, ocean and road freight through one accountable team.
Plan your next shipment: https://witners.com/#contact

Customs Clearance in Dubai: Documents, Mirsal 2 and Duties: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d6H-s2lWydE

Sources checked on 17 Nov 2026:
- Dubai Customs, Customs Policy DCP7: Implementation of Agreement on Customs Valuation (customs value, additions to transaction value): https://www.dubaicustoms.gov.ae/en/PoliciesAndNotices/Policies/ImplementationofAgreementonCustomsValuationDCP7.pdf
- Dubai Customs, Customer Guide (v3.03), section 7 (Customs Duty, 5% of CIF value, tariff rates), section 8 (Customs Valuation), section 10 (Customs Service Charges) and section 13 (Duty Exemptions): https://www.dubaicustoms.gov.ae/en/OpenData/Publications/Customer_Guide_Booklet_EN.pdf
- Federal Tax Authority, Federal Decree-Law No. 8 of 2017 on VAT and amendments, Article 35 (Value of Import) and Article 48 (Reverse Charge): https://tax.gov.ae/datafolder/Files/Legislation/2025/Federal%20Decree-Law%20No.%208%20of%202017%20and%20amendments%20-%20publishing%2028%2011%202025.pdf
- Federal Tax Authority, VAT Import Declaration User Guide (import VAT calculated on the value inclusive of customs duty and excise tax): https://tax.gov.ae/datafolder/Files/Guides/VAT/VAT%20Guides/VAT%20Importers%20User%20Guide%20English_V6.0%2003%2001%202022.pdf
- Federal Tax Authority, FAQ: Will VAT be paid on imports?: https://tax.gov.ae/en/faq.aspx?keyword=Will+VAT+be+paid+on+imports
- Federal Tax Authority, E-Commerce VAT Guide, section 3.5 (VAT on import of goods): https://tax.gov.ae/DownloadOpenTextFile?fileUrl=en%2FVAT_VAT_Guides%2FE_Commerce%2FE_Commerce_VAT+Guide_EN_09_08_2020_EN.pdf
- Federal Tax Authority, Importation of goods by agents (VATP012): https://tax.gov.ae/DataFolder/Files/Pdf/VATP012%20-%20Importation%20of%20goods%20by%20agents.pdf

Importers should confirm current requirements with Dubai Customs and the relevant authorities, and rates, free time and terms with their providers before shipping.

segments.text: Landed cost is what a shipment really
costs you by the time it is cleared in
Dubai, not just the price on the
supplier's invoice.
This guide shows how the main pieces fit
together, the customs value, customs
duty, import VAT, and the other charges
around clearance. It uses official Dubai
customs and federal tax authority
sources checked on the 17th of November
Landed cost is the total cost of getting
goods to your door. It starts with the
product cost,
then it adds international freight and
insurance, customs duty, import VAT, and
the handling, [snorts] clearance, and
delivery charges quoted by your
providers.
Dubai customs and the FTA define the
first parts. The rest depends on your
shipment, so those figures should always
come from real quotations.
Customs duty starts from the customs
value.
Under Dubai customs valuation policy,
that is the transaction value, meaning
the price actually paid or payable for
the goods plus certain additions if they
are not already in the price. These
include transport to the borders of the
GCC states, loading, unloading,
handling, and insurance charges to those
borders, packing, containers, and
commissions other than buying
commissions. In practice, this is the
CIF value, cost, insurance, and freight.
Charges after the goods reach the border
are not among those additions.
Dubai customs customer guide says the
common customs tariff of the GCC Customs
Union is 5% of the CIF value for foreign
goods imported from outside the Customs
Union. Ad valorem duty is simply a
percentage of the CIF value, but rates
are determined by the goods
classification, so your HS code matters.
Some goods carry other rates. For
example, the guide lists 100% on tobacco
products and 50% on alcoholic products.
It also lists duty exemptions such as
for diplomatic goods and returned goods.
Import VAT is 5% unless the goods would
be rated or exempt if supplied in the
UAE. The Federal Tax Authority says the
import value is the customs value,
including the value of insurance,
freight, and any customs fees and excise
tax paid on the import.
Its importer guide says import VAT is
calculated on the value of the goods
inclusive of any customs duty and excise
tax. So VAT is charged on the CIF value
plus duty, not on the invoice price
alone.
How import VAT is paid depends on
registration.
If the importer is registered for VAT
with the Federal Tax Authority, VAT is
due on the import under a reverse charge
mechanism. If the importer is not
registered, VAT must be paid before the
goods are released.
The FTA explains that a registered owner
of imported goods can recover import VAT
under its normal recovery position. So a
registered business should ask its tax
advisor whether recoverable VAT belongs
in its landed cost.
Beyond duty and VAT, landed cost
includes the charges around the
shipment.
Dubai Customs levies a processing charge
on most customs transactions set out in
its fee structure.
Port, terminal, delivery order,
clearance and delivery charges come from
your carrier, terminal and broker, so
ask each for a written quotation. Unlike
customs value, these are not set by one
tariff and they vary by shipment and
provider.
Put it all in order. One, product
[clears throat] cost from the invoice.
Two, international freight and
insurance, which together with product
cost give the CIF value plus any packing
or commission additions. Three, customs
duty at the rate set by your HS code on
the CIF value.
Four, [snorts]
import VAT at 5% on the CIF value plus
duty unless zero rated or exempt. Five,
clearance, port, terminal and delivery
charges from your quotations. Add them
up, then divide by the number of units
to get a landed cost per unit.
W I T E E R S has in-house licensed UAE
customs brokers handling imports,
exports, and free zone movements with
air, ocean, and road freight through one
accountable team. Tell us about your
shipment using the contact link on
screen. This is general information.
Confirm current requirements with Dubai
Customs and the Federal Tax Authority
before shipping.

metadata.title: A Message On New Tariffs And De Minimis (Section 321)
metadata.author: Stord
metadata.shortDescription:
Today we enter into a new world for e-commerce and retail. This is not a political post, but a reflection on what this means for brands and their supply chains.

As of April 2nd, the White House made sweeping changes to global trade through executive action - eliminating De Minimis (Section 321) exemption for imports from China and Hong Kong and implementing a universal 10% tariff on nearly all imported goods, with specific higher "reciprocal" tariffs on countries perceived to have trade imbalances and barriers.

These changes will have huge impacts on both legacy retail giants and disruptive e-commerce brands alike. Disruptions, price changes, delays, and more impacts will occur over  the coming weeks.

However, these changes, while massive, were not unpredictable nor unprecedented. The seeds of these new regulations were planted back in 2016 during President Trump’s first presidential campaign and have been a clear priority for his second term.

But as we've seen, the status quo has rapidly changed in recent months and years - from COVID pandemic restrictions, to war, to changes in USPS parcel services, changes to IMMEX, collapsing fulfillment and parcel providers, and more - it is clear that change is the new constant.

At Stord, we prepared.

Since our founding, we have been laser focused on building a resilient and flexible fulfillment and commerce enablement platform that can endure the tumultuous environment of rapid-growth e-commerce business. We have the ability to rapidly launch nationwide fulfillment for brands in days when providers or tariffs change, reduce parcel costs when carriers levy new GRIs, and drive additional customer loyalty with cutting-edge pre and post-purchase tooling

This has meant conscious investment poured into our technologies and fulfillment network to level the playing field for brands of all sizes.

This means:
Strategically placed fulfillment centers across the United States and Canada with an integrated partner network for improved reach
A diversified mesh of national and local carriers for accelerated delivery times at the cheapest cost possible
Proactive import strategies to reduce fees and drayage costs 
Close collaboration with government officials to stay informed and prepared on changes

These operational advantages have taken nearly a decade to build, and have prepared us to meet this moment of upheaval. Not only is Stord ready, but so are our customers.

Customers like True Classic and CANN. Both recently came to Stord under pressure from mounting costs. Both were implemented in record time - enjoying our integrated systems, network scale, and dedicated partnership. This work has shielded their end consumers from experiencing delays. 

Here is what we did for True Classic, getting them live in 19 days.

Embed True Classic announcement video

We will continue to monitor and adapt as the realities of this executive order are felt throughout the broader market.

To our customers, thank you for your trust and confidence in Stord - know that we have your back and are ready to support. To those struggling and uncertain how to navigate these changes, please reach out, we would be happy to help.

Throughout it all, our priority is unchanged - to redefine the commerce journey, empowering merchants to deliver experiences that delight consumers at scale.

If you need help overcoming these new challenges, the Stord team is standing by.  https://www.stord.com/getstord/changes-to-de-minimis-tariff

Thank you,
Sean Henry

segments.text: Tariffs are in the spotlight—and they can swing your margins fast. If you don’t know
exactly what you’ll owe before you quote your customer, you’re gambling with profitability.
I’m Kari Crane, editor of Shipping Solutions International Trade Blog Passages.
In a few minutes, you’ll have a clear, working grasp of duties,
tariffs and taxes—how they differ, how they’re calculated,
and how to roll everything into a reliable landed cost so you can price with confidence.
But before we dive in, make sure you subscribe to our channel! We publish Basics of Exporting
and Importing videos twice a week to help you simplify international trade.
Let’s start simple. Taxes fund public services. In cross-border trade, you’ll most often see
VAT or GST. Even if your product qualifies for duty-free treatment under a free trade agreement,
VAT or GST may still apply at import. “Duties” is the broader umbrella for
charges on goods crossing borders—what many call customs duties. Your rate hinges on two things:
the product’s HTS code and its country of origin. Why do countries levy duties? Two main reasons:
revenue and industry protection. You’ll see two basic duty types:
a fixed amount per unit, weight, or quantity; or a percentage of value.
Most countries charge import duties; export duties are less common, but resource-rich
nations sometimes use them on commodities. “Tariffs” are a specific kind of duty—targeted
taxes on certain products or origins, often tied to policy decisions. They change with negotiations
and disputes. For example, trade agreements like USMCA eliminate tariffs on most products
among the U.S., Canada and Mexico, while the U.S. also imposes tariffs on certain goods from China,
with rates that vary by product. Depending on your shipment and route,
some of the add-ons you may encounter include anti-dumping and countervailing duties; customs
clearance fees; an Import Processing Fee (called the Merchandise Processing Fee in the U.S.);
excise taxes on things like alcohol, tobacco or fuel; inspection fees for safety checks; dangerous
goods surcharges; and a fee if your containers sit too long. None of these are exotic; they’re just
easy to overlook if you’re estimating on the fly. To calculate the total cost of getting your
product from supplier to the customer’s doorstep, start by getting the HTS code right,
because that determines the duty rate you’ll pay. Then build the full landed cost—that means rolling
in the purchase price, transportation, insurance, customs duties, taxes, import processing charges,
and any add-ons like anti-dumping duties. Miss even one, and a quote that looked great
on paper can fall apart when the invoices land. This is where our compliance software makes life
easier. Our Product Classification Software helps you lock in the correct HS code fast.
It includes an HS Mapping tool for equivalent 10-digit HTS codes in other countries and shows
default duty rates so you can see if an FTA actually helps—before you commit.
Then the Landed Cost Calculator pulls everything together. It estimates import
duties, VAT and excise taxes, adds government fees, transportation and insurance, and lets
you compare sourcing options side-by-side—local versus China, Mexico, or wherever you’re buying.
You can sign up for a free trial of both by clicking here.
And if Incoterms ever trip you up—because remember,
they determine who pays for what— there are links to several articles below that can help,
and you’ll find dozens more on our blog. Thanks for watching and I’ll see you back here soon.

segments.text: Landed cost calculation explained, the
one video that actually makes it click.
No fluff, no filler, straight from Candy
Mentor.
Before a product reaches your warehouse,
its price can change dramatically.
This chapter builds the foundation for
understanding what landed cost really
measures.
Landed cost goes beyond the supplier's
invoice price. It captures the spending
required to purchase, transport, clear,
and receive the inventory.
The purchase price is only the starting
point. Freight, insurance, customs
charges, and receiving expenses can all
increase what each unit truly costs you.
Purchase price tells you what the
supplier charges. Landed cost tells you
what the product costs after it has
traveled through the entire inbound
supply chain.
The basic formula adds the product value
to every cost needed to bring it into
your facility.
In practice, companies may expand this
formula with storage, inspection, or
financing costs. The process starts with
a purchase order and continues through
transportation and customs.
Once the goods arrive, the total
spending is assigned to the inventory
received. Direct product costs are tied
closely to the goods themselves.
The invoice is usually the largest item,
but packaging and customization can also
belong in the product cost base.
Logistics and import costs are where
many estimates go wrong. A shipment may
involve several carriers, brokers,
ports, and government charges before it
reaches the warehouse.
To price or analyze individual products,
divide the shipment's total landed cost
by the number of units received. The
result gives you a more realistic cost
per sellable unit. Some costs stay
broadly the same whether you import 100
or 1,000 units.
Others increase with volume, so
separating these categories helps you
allocate costs accurately. Now, let's
focus on the international trade details
that can make landed cost confusing.
Customs valuation and shipping terms
often determine who pays which bill.
Customs value is not always identical to
your total landed cost. It is the
valuation basis used by authorities,
often centered on the goods transaction
value plus specific additions. Import
duty is calculated by applying the
relevant tariff rate to the customs
value. The rate can vary by product
classification, origin country, and
trade agreement. Incoterms clarify who
arranges transportation, who pays for
it, and when risk transfers. They are
essential because the same product can
have very different buyer costs under
different terms. With FOB, the buyer
typically takes responsibility for the
main international movement and import
process. With DDP, the seller handles
much more of the journey, so the buyer's
invoice may look higher, but be more
complete. First, classify the product
correctly and establish its customs
value. Then apply the duty rate, add
applicable taxes and fees, and record
the costs using your accounting policy.
A useful mental shortcut is to think in
three layers: the product itself,
international trade costs, and delivery
into your operation. This framework
helps you spot missing cost categories
quickly. Taxes and fees can be easy to
overlook because they arrive on separate
documents. Check broker statements,
customs entries, and carrier invoices
instead of relying only on the supplier
bill. Import tax depends on the taxable
base and the applicable rate. The
taxable base may differ from customs
value because local rules can include
duties or freight in the calculation. A
shipment often contains multiple
products, but freight and fees arrive as
shared totals.
This chapter shows how to distribute
those costs fairly across the units
received. A value-based method assigns
more shared cost to higher value product
lines. It is simple and useful when
freight consumption broadly follows the
value of the goods. Allocating by value
is convenient, but it may not reflect
how the carrier charges you.
Weight or volume can be more appropriate
when large, heavy, or bulky products
consume most of the transport capacity.
Start by listing every product line and
collecting the shipment level charges.
Choose an allocation basis, assign the
shared costs, and then divide each
product line's total by its received
quantity.
International purchases often involve
more than one currency.
Use a documented exchange rate policy,
keep the conversion assumptions visible,
and separate later foreign exchange
movements from the original landed cost
when required. Demurrage is a
delay-related cost that can appear when
containers remain at a terminal too
long.
It is a good example of an avoidable
charge that should be investigated
rather than automatically treated as
normal freight. Picture the receiving
dock. Cartons are counted, damage is
checked, and paperwork is matched to the
shipment. This is where the theoretical
calculation meets the physical
inventory, and missing costs often
surface.
In an interview, the goal is not just to
recite a formula.
You need to show that you can define the
scope, choose sensible assumptions, and
explain how the result supports a
business decision.
A strong answer begins by clarifying
whether the question asks for total
shipment cost or cost per unit.
Then identify the cost components,
confirm the trade terms, explain your
allocation method, and perform a
reasonableness check.
Here is a compact example with a $10,000
product purchase, $1,200 of freight, 500
in duty, and 300 in fees.
Since the shipment contains 1,000 units,
we can turn the total into a unit cost.
Adding the four cost categories produces
a $12,000 landed cost.
Divide that by 1,000 units, and the true
cost becomes $12 per unit instead of the
$10 supplier price.
The biggest mistakes come from using the
invoice price alone, or treating shared
charges inconsistently.
Best practice is to define the scope,
document assumptions, apply one method
consistently, and reconcile estimates to
actual bills.
Before finalizing the calculation,
confirm every charge, verify the customs
classification, and check the agreed
shipping terms.
Finish by comparing the estimate with
actual invoices, so the model improves
over time.
And that's a complete breakdown of this
topic from start to finish. If it helped
you understand things more clearly,
share it with someone who's learning,
too.
Like, share, and subscribe to Candy
Mentor for more videos like this.

ICT Landed Cost Calculator — free, world-class, and built for buyers who need the real number. Most offshore quotes show only the unit price, but the true cost of a part is everything it takes to get it to your dock and pay for it. Indiana Consulting and Trade’s free Landed Cost Calculator adds up every one of those costs, line by line:

the supplier’s price converted to U.S. dollars from 160+ currencies
Section 232 metal tariffs and the base duty for the part’s HTS code (2,682 codes in the built-in library)
Section 301 and other country-specific tariffs
ocean or truck freight, with 20-ft vs. 40-ft container sizing
customs fees: Merchandise Processing Fee, Harbor Maintenance Fee and broker charges
the risk of inventory going obsolete in the pipeline
the cost of cash tied up in deposits and inventory
a three-year currency-risk premium

It then puts that total side by side with a U.S. source, shows the days your cash is tied up both ways, and calculates how many months the tooling takes to pay back. You enter only your part details. The auto-update fields, shown in green, fill in on their own from the built-in library: exchange rates, tariff and duty rates, transit times and customs fees. Each data source shows its as-of date and is flagged OK or STALE, so you always know how current the number is. Clients and licensed users get these fields kept up to date automatically. Get the real number before you sign the PO.

The last line repeats the tagline from your flyer. If “auto-update field” meant something else, such as the Assumptions overrides recalculating everything, tell me and I’ll rework that part.

metadata.title: Jewelry Landed Cost: Duty, Sets and True Margin, from PO to Sale
metadata.author: SKUio
metadata.shortDescription:
How does an import jewelry brand know what a piece really costs? We follow one gold necklace from its tariff code to a sale, on a demo brand we made up for this video.

You will see:
- Duty estimated on the purchase order, line by line, from each product's tariff code
- The estimate going into stock cost at receipt, held in Accrued Customs Duty
- The customs broker's bill replacing the estimate, with only the difference moving
- True cost of goods and margin on a web order
- Gold and silver sets as bundles that never sell a piece you do not have
- One stock count shared by Shopify, boutiques and department stores
- A late supplier on the scorecard (on-time, lead time, fill rate)
- A short shipment, received in part and closed short
- Asking an AI assistant which pieces are about to run out, through the SKU.io MCP server

The brand, products, orders and costs are invented for this demo. Duty rates are illustrative, so confirm real rates with your customs broker.

Narrated with an AI voice.

See it with your own products: https://meet.sku.io

Chapters:
0:00 The scenario
0:59 One necklace, from purchase order to sale
4:46 Gold and silver sets
5:29 One stock count for every channel
6:26 A late supplier
7:23 A short shipment
7:46 Ask an AI assistant

#landedcost #jewelrybusiness #inventorymanagement #shopify #ecommerce

segments.text: Meet Wrenmere Jewelry, a brand we made up for this demo.
It designs gold and silver pieces, and overseas factories make them.
It sells on its own online store, and wholesale to boutiques and department stores.
Every order, cost and customer you will see is invented.
The duty rates are illustrative too, so confirm real rates with your customs broker.
Brands like this often price a piece on its factory cost.
The duty shows up weeks later, on the customs broker's bill.
Until then, every margin report looks better than the truth.
So let's see how the full cost of one piece is built, and kept honest.
We will follow one piece, this Marin paperclip necklace in gold, from purchase order to sale.
Then gold and silver sets, one stock count for every channel, a late supplier, a short shipment, and an AI assistant.
Start with the tariff code, set on the product.
The landed cost card does the math: fourteen dollars and fifty cents a unit.
That is twelve twenty-four from the factory, plus two twenty-six of duty.
The duty rate is eleven percent base, plus seven and a half percent under Section three oh one.
Here is the next order for it, purchase order twelve sixteen, in production at the China factory.
Every line already carries its estimated duty.
For this necklace, eleven hundred thirteen units bring two thousand five hundred sixty-seven dollars of duty.
Across the whole order, the estimate is seventeen thousand eight hundred thirty-four dollars.
The card says what happens next.
At receipt, the estimate goes into inventory cost, and it is trued up when the customs duty bill arrives.
The order before it, twelve fifteen, landed yesterday.
At receipt, the estimated duty went straight into the cost of the stock.
So necklaces sold this week already carry their duty.
Until the broker bills, the duty is held as an accrual: two thousand five hundred sixty-seven dollars on this line.
Accounting sees every open accrual in one report.
Twenty thousand five hundred sixty dollars is still waiting for a bill, across eighteen lines.
It sits in Accrued Customs Duty until the bills arrive.
Now the last step, the broker's bill.
Here is an order where the broker's bill came in, purchase order twelve thirteen.
The estimate was seven thousand five hundred eighty dollars and eighty-seven cents.
The broker's bill replaced it, and nothing is left in the accrual.
Only the difference moved, a few dollars a line, like a three dollar and twenty-seven cent variance.
Back on the necklace, its average cost is fifteen dollars and thirty cents.
The base product is twelve dollars and twenty-four cents.
Then come two kinds of duty.
One dollar sixteen is estimated, on the stock that landed yesterday.
One dollar fifteen is already billed, on older stock.
Packaging and freight make up the rest.
The landed cost card checks the estimate against the broker.
The estimate is two dollars and twenty-six cents a unit, and the last duty actually paid was two dollars and thirty-two.
Each receipt is its own cost layer.
Yesterday's eleven hundred thirteen necklaces carry fourteen dollars and fifty-five cents each, with the duty estimate inside.
October's layer is sixteen dollars and ten cents, with freight, packaging and the billed duty.
Sales draw from the oldest layer first, so cost of goods follows the real cost of what shipped.
Now a sale.
This web order sold one necklace for sixty-two dollars.
Its cost of goods is sixteen dollars and five cents, with the duty, freight and packaging on that stock.
That leaves forty-five dollars and ninety-five cents of profit, a seventy-four percent margin.
That was one necklace.
For the whole catalog, the Landed Cost Breakdown report does the same math.
Pick the last three hundred sixty-five days, and group by product.
Then generate the report, built from every sale in that window.
Over the year, fifty-six thousand twenty-nine units sold.
They landed at eleven dollars and ninety-three cents a unit.
Customs duty is a dollar sixty-five of that, close to fourteen percent.
Freight and packaging are smaller, but every unit carries them.
Sets are built as bundles.
The Marin Set of two in gold is the gold necklace plus the gold bracelet.
A set holds no stock of its own, so its stock line reads zero.
It is only as available as its pieces.
Silver sets have their own recipes, all silver.
This Marin Set of three in silver is the necklace, the hoops and the bracelet.
A department store ordered four hundred ninety-six of these sets by EDI.
On the order, the silver necklaces and bracelets are allocated.
The silver hoops ran short, so twenty-four are backordered.
The shortage shows up on the order, instead of an oversold set.
Back to the gold necklace, and the orders holding stock of it.

metadata.title: Calculating Landed Cost for Exported and Imported Goods
metadata.author: New York SBDC
metadata.shortDescription:
Landed cost is the total cost of getting a product from the factory to the customer’s door. It includes all expenses incurred from origin to final destination—such as shipping fees, insurance, and any customs duties or taxes applied when goods cross international borders.

In this webinar, participants will learn how to determine the true total price of products exported from the United States and how to accurately calculate the cost of foreign-imported merchandise. The session will also provide guidance on how to interpret and account for new US tariffs on imports that may affect overall pricing.

This webinar will help you better understand how to price your goods, manage expenses, and avoid unexpected charges.

Presenters:

- John Tracy, Senior International Trade Specialist with the US Commercial Service, US Department of Commerce Syracuse Associate Office
- Dr. Mercedes Sanchez-Moore, Director of the NYSBDC International Trade Initiative

Funded in part through a Cooperative Agreement with the U.S. Small Business Administration. All opinions, conclusions, and/or recommendations expressed herein are those of the speaker(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of the SBA or the SBDC. Full funding disclosures are available at https://nysbdc.org/funding-disclosures.

segments.text: Your supplier's invoice is only the starting point.
To know what your goods really cost, you need a landed cost estimate.
Here is how to build one.
Landed cost is the total cost of getting the goods into your warehouse:
the goods themselves, freight, insurance, customs brokerage, any duties and taxes,
and delivery.
Start with the supplier invoice and the agreed Incoterms rule.
Then add the freight, and any origin or destination charges the rule leaves with
you.
Here is a fictional worksheet.
Each line is a placeholder, marked as an estimate.
Your real numbers come from your invoice, your forwarder's quote and your customs
broker.
Next, insurance. If the risk in transit is yours under the Incoterms rule, decide
whether to buy cargo insurance, and add its cost.
Duties and taxes depend on the tariff classification, the origin and the value of
the goods. Have them estimated by a customs broker.
RRA Group works with in-house customs brokers within our group.
Then add the service fees: customs brokerage, terminal and handling charges, and the
final delivery to your door.
Mark every estimate as an estimate, note what you do not know yet, and update the
sheet when real quotes arrive.
Rates change, so date your estimate.
A fictional example. A Calgary importer adds up the goods, freight, fees, duties and
delivery, then divides by the number of units.
That landed cost per unit is what to compare with the selling price.
So: start with the invoice, add freight, insurance and fees, get duties and taxes
estimated by a customs broker, and mark your estimates.
Next: why freight quotes expire.

partner agents, then handles the freight booking, in-house customs brokers within

way. One team. Every step.

or email info@rragroup.ca.
One team. Every step.

metadata.title: How to Handle Shopify Dropshipping Returns, Refunds, and Return Policies.
metadata.author: Shopify Mastery
metadata.shortDescription:
🟢 BEST Current Deal - Get a 3-day Shopify trial + $1/month for first 3 months:
https://shopify.pxf.io/5k7ga3
 
🎨 Best Shopify Themes – High-converting themes to boost sales:
https://shopify.pxf.io/best-shopify-themes
 
📲 Must-Have Shopify Apps – Essential apps to grow your store:
https://shopify.pxf.io/best-free-shopify-apps
 
In this video, I’ll go over how to handle Shopify dropshipping returns without losing money on every refund, replacement, or return request. I’ll walk through how dropshipping returns work, why most suppliers do not accept returns, and how to write a clear Shopify return policy before the first sale. You’ll also learn how to set up a refund policy in Shopify, use the photo evidence method for damaged goods, and protect profit margins with a simple return reserve.

Be sure to watch this video all the way as I cover when to refund without requiring a return, when to request the item back, and how to process returns inside Shopify admin. I’ll show how to manage refunds, exchanges, return labels, supplier issues, chargebacks, defective products, damaged items, customer complaints, partial refunds, and replacement orders. You’ll also see how to handle low-value products, high-value products, return shipping costs, original shipping refunds, restocking settings, and customer service without making dropshipping returns harder than needed.

Shopify dropshipping returns work better when a store has a clear system, a simple refund policy, and real pricing margins that include return costs. A strong process helps protect e-commerce profit, reduce chargeback risk, improve customer trust, and keep a Shopify store running smoothly when products arrive damaged, customers change their mind, or suppliers refuse returns. By planning refunds, exchanges, return rules, Shopify policies, supplier messages, photo proof, and profit buffers ahead of time, dropshipping returns become a normal part of running an online store instead of a surprise that hurts cash flow.
 
If you want to know more about Shopify, watch our other videos:
 
How to Add Legal Pages to Your Shopify Store (Privacy, Terms & Refund)
https://youtu.be/Cpz7HFblWgo
 
How to Build a Shopify Bundle Landing Page That Increases AOV with Replo
https://youtu.be/Gk-Nt4LWsFo
 
Subscribe to our channel to learn more about everything related to e-commerce. Our channel is dedicated to helping you learn and master e-commerce, dropshipping, and making money online.
 
Thank you for watching, and have a great day!
 
– Eric
 
#ShopifyDropshipping #ShopifyTips #EcommerceTips
 
Timeline:
0:00 - Introduction
0:30 - The Reality of Dropshipping Returns
1:27 - Writing a Return Policy That Protects You
2:48 - Adding Your Policy to Shopify
3:25 - When to Refund Without Requiring a Return
4:49 - How to Process a Return in Shopify Admin
6:32 - Handling a Return When the Supplier Won't Take It Back
7:37 - The Photo Evidence Method for Damaged Goods
8:24 - Exchanges in Shopify
8:57 - Building a Return Reserve into Your Margins
9:36 - Getting Your Store Set Up
9:52 - Wrapping Up

The commission is paid by the retailers at no cost to you, and this helps to support our channel and keep our videos free. Thank you! Trying to decide between Avalara, TaxJar and TaxCloud?

In this video, we compare three of the most popular sales tax software platforms for ecommerce brands and answer the questions business owners, CFOs, accountants, and ecommerce operators ask most often. We break down pricing, sales tax filing costs, customer support, SST eligibility, integrations, and the total cost of compliance as your business grows.

You'll learn how Avalara, TaxJar, and TaxCloud compare for Shopify, Shopify Plus, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, Amazon, Etsy, and multi-channel ecommerce businesses.

Questions answered in this video:

• Is Avalara worth the price?
• Has TaxJar become too expensive after the latest pricing changes?
• Which platform offers the best value for growing ecommerce brands?
• Which sales tax provider offers audit support?
• How does the SST (Streamlined Sales Tax) program impact filing costs?
• What is the best sales tax solution for mid-market ecommerce businesses?

In this comparison, you'll learn which platform is the best fit for your business:

✅ Avalara — Best for large enterprises with global tax requirements and ERP integrations
✅ TaxJar — Best for small ecommerce sellers and marketplace businesses
✅ TaxCloud — Best for growing mid-market ecommerce brands looking for full compliance support and transparent pricing

plan at $99 a month. And since the acquisition, customers say that even the basic tasks like
adding a new state have gotten harder. One review simply reads, "I cannot get anyone to respond to

offers hands on audit defense. So the moment a state audit begins, you are on your own. If

order volume and filing starts as low as $39 per return and can go down to $20 per return with

Provider, which means free registration and filing in all 24 SST states as soon as you meet the
eligibility criteria. So that is a structural cost advantage that compounds as you expand into more

metadata.title: Tax 101: Does my online marketplace collect sales tax for me?
metadata.author: Avalara
metadata.shortDescription:
It’s easy to sell your products or services to anyone in the country, and even the world, thanks to online marketplaces. It’s also important to remember that the more places you sell to, the more places you may be obligated to collect and remit sales tax. Learn more about how sales tax works with online marketplaces and how it may affect you.

In most cases, you must make sure you’re charging sales tax for all goods you sell, even on an online marketplace. The good news is that, in cases where your marketplace is counted as a marketplace facilitator, the marketplace collects and remits sales tax for you.

segments.text: Does my online marketplace collect sales tax for me?
Thanks to the internet, the whole world has become one giant marketplace,
and it's more than the big online marketplaces like Amazon,
Walmart, Etsy, eBay and the other e-commerce giants.
Selling on an online marketplace can feel like
getting their product on the shelves of one of the biggest stores in the country.

to sell online.
But that doesn't mean
you can just start a store on Amazon Marketplace and call it a day.
First, you need to know if your marketplace is collecting sales
tax for you.
Some marketplaces, including Amazon, Walmart and Etsy,
are required to collect sales tax on your behalf.
This is because of marketplace facilitator laws.
But let's start at the beginning.
What is a marketplace facilitator?
A marketplace facilitator is defined as anyone that provides a platform
to list or advertise taxable items for sale by marketplace sellers
and directly or indirectly collects payments from customers and remits it
back to the seller.
Online marketplaces are subject to marketplace facilitator laws.
These laws require the marketplace to collect and pay sales tax for its sellers.
That’s you.
That means a major marketplace like Amazon is already
taking care of sales tax for you.
But keep in mind that not all marketplaces and e-commerce platforms work the same.
While big names like eBay, Etsy and Amazon are classified
as marketplace facilitators, other platforms like Shopify are not.
That means you're still responsible for collecting sales tax on these platforms.

Free QuickBooks Online Audit: sandgbookkeeping.com

Ecommerce owners: sales tax doesn’t have to be chaos. In this video, I show you exactly how to set up TaxJar in minutes so you stay compliant and protect margins.

What you’ll learn:
1. Nexus 101: when you actually owe sales tax (economic vs. physical)

3. TaxJar basics.
4. How to autofile your sales tax returns.

metadata.title: Online Sales Tax: A Guide to Economic Nexus & Ecommerce
metadata.author: Tyler
metadata.shortDescription:
There’s a common accounting mistake that many ecommerce businesses unknowingly make that can cost millions of dollars and even lead to bankruptcy.

If your ecommerce business sells to customers all over the United States and is in hyper-growth mode, you’re going to want to keep reading … or you might face an unexpected lawsuit.

The South Dakota v. Wayfair decision overturned a 1992 ruling, known as Quill, that prohibited states from charging sales taxes to companies that don’t have a physical presence within the state.

Because of this new ruling, your business is now on the hook for tracking and paying sales tax in every state in which you meet the threshold for economic nexus. If that isn’t stressful enough, each state has its own set of rules for sales tax.

Worse: in some states, counties and cities also have this power — meaning that businesses will need to understand and continually stay up to date as laws change across over 12,000 jurisdictions in the U.S.

Keeping track of each individual state’s specific sales tax laws and economic nexus thresholds — and ensuring that your business doesn’t get sued — can be an expensive, ongoing challenge.

Welcome to our deep dive into the often-overlooked yet crucial world of ecommerce taxes. In this video, we unravel the complexities of economic nexus and the implications of internet sales tax that could be lurking behind your online transactions. Learn how the landmark Wayfair case reshaped the landscape of ecommerce sales nexus, establishing a new precedent for sales tax nexus across the states. Whether you're a budding entrepreneur or an established e-commerce veteran, understanding the nuances of tax nexus is vital to safeguarding your business against unexpected financial pitfalls. Stay tuned as we guide you through the maze of sales tax laws and show you how to stay compliant in the ever-evolving digital marketplace.


What is ecommerce sales nexus?
Ecommerce sales nexus is determined by your business's economic activity in a state, impacting when and where you are required to collect sales tax. Discover the critical factors that define nexus and how they affect your online store.

Why isn't my Shopify charging sales tax
If your Shopify store isn't charging sales tax, it could be due to the settings not being configured to handle tax calculations. Learn how to activate and set up accurate tax collection tailored to your business's locations.

How to set up sales tax Shopify dropshipping
Setting up sales tax for Shopify dropshipping involves understanding the nexus and tax obligations in the regions you operate. We’ll guide you through configuring your Shopify settings to handle these taxes seamlessly.

How to collect sales tax in the US on Shopify
Collecting sales tax in the US on Shopify requires you to determine if you have a sales tax nexus in any state and set up your Shopify store to apply taxes accordingly. This video explains the step-by-step process to ensure compliance.

Do you have to collect sales tax on Shopify
Whether you need to collect sales tax on Shopify depends on your economic nexus in various states. We break down the essentials of sales tax compliance and how Shopify can automate much of this process for you.

How to set up sales tax on Shopify nexus
To set up sales tax on Shopify considering the nexus, you need to first identify the states where you have tax obligations. Follow our straightforward guide to configure your tax settings accurately on Shopify.

Do i have to collect sales tax on all internet sales I make?
The requirement to collect sales tax on internet sales depends on whether your business meets the criteria for an economic nexus in different states. Find out how to determine your tax responsibilities and avoid penalties.

South Dakota vs Wayfair: What happened?
In the landmark case of South Dakota vs Wayfair, the Supreme Court ruled that states can require ecommerce businesses to collect and remit sales tax, even if they don't have a physical presence in the state. This decision has significant implications for all online retailers.

Google Shopping Feed Optimization is one of the most overlooked growth levers in eCommerce - and most brands get it completely wrong.

In this video, I break down why most stores don’t struggle because of campaign structure, bidding, or the latest “hack” - they struggle because the foundation is weak. And in Google Shopping, that foundation starts with your product feed.

You’ll learn:

✅ Why feed optimization matters more than most campaign “hacks”
✅ How poor product data leads to higher CPCs, lower CTR, and worse ROAS
✅ Why title optimization is the first and most important pillar
✅ How to write product descriptions that help both Google and the shopper
✅ What makes a strong Shopping image and why bad visuals kill performance
✅ How Google product categories improve targeting and matching
✅ Why pricing plays a huge role in Shopping success
✅ How bad feed data silently destroys performance
✅ Why ongoing feed management is not optional if you want to scale

I also walk through the 7 pillars of Google Shopping Feed Optimization and the 4-phase rollout process you can use to clean up your feed, improve traffic quality, and become more competitive in the auction.

If your Google Shopping campaigns are underperforming, there’s a good chance the issue is not your campaign structure - it’s your feed. This video will show you what actually matters, what to fix first, and how to build a product feed that gives your campaigns a real shot at scaling profitably.

metadata.shortDescription:
Join the fastest-growing Google Ads eCom community on Skool: https://www.skool.com/google-ads-ecom/about Get the full scaling system, weekly live calls, and PMAX teardowns alongside 1.7k+ eCom operators, backed by $200M+ in tracked sales.

DM me on IG: https://www.instagram.com/ecomchrisx/

In this video, I break down the core strategies for Google Shopping feed optimization and show you how to boost your eCommerce performance without overcomplicating things. If your Google Merchant Center (GMC) feed isn't optimized properly, you risk wasting ad spend, losing visibility, and hurting your ROI.

I explain the step-by-step process to ensure your feed is error-free, relevant, and optimized for better targeting, higher click-through rates (CTR), and more conversions. Whether you're optimizing top sellers or fixing underperforming products, I’ll show you how to improve your product listings and get better results from your Google Ads campaigns.

You’ll learn:
✅ How to avoid common feed errors and disapprovals
✅ The importance of feed health scans for better targeting
✅ Why feed consistency is key to avoiding account suspensions
✅ The best practices for optimizing titles, descriptions, and images
✅ How to use real data to build keyword-rich listings without overstuffing
✅ Why relevance and clarity should always be your top priority
✅ How to optimize product pricing to stay competitive in the Google Ads auction
✅ Why you should focus on high spend products with low performance
✅ How to use Google Ads data to find and implement the best keywords

If you want your Google Shopping feed to work as hard as your ads, this video will teach you how to make it happen.

Free Resource: https://swamp-hose-3ee.notion.site/Feed-Optimization-Mastery-External-2ca4f41b74f88055a705d93b1c0f2321?pvs=143

metadata.shortDescription:
Walmart Automation is the new hotness, replacing Amazon as the new grift for online scammers... But is it truly as good as they say? 
► Twitter: https://twitter.com/coffeebreak_YT
► Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/coffeebreak_yt/
🎶 Music: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nMSQ1yoPT2c&list=PL4qw3AkxFDSNhEgawXD1j6r0iN1072XIB&index=1
This video is an opinion and in no way should be construed as statements of fact. Scams, bad business opportunities, and fake gurus are subjective terms that mean different things to different people. I think someone who promises $100K/month for an upfront fee of $2K is a scam. Others would call it a Napolean Hill pitch.

metadata.title: Done-For-You AI Store: We Read the FTC Files
metadata.author: NET not GROSS
metadata.shortDescription:
"Your own AI-powered store. We build it, we run it, risk free." We read the FTC court files on four "done-for-you" e-commerce programs that sold AI-powered stores — Automators AI, Passive Scaling / FBA Machine, Ascend Ecom and Ecommerce Empire Builders. What they promised, what the stores actually sold, what happened to the "guarantee", and where the money went. Everything here is what the FTC alleged or what a court ordered; all four cases ended in settlements without admission of the allegations.

Chapters:
0:00 The pitch
0:22 The paperwork
1:07 Same pitch, four times
2:42 What "AI" meant
3:31 The client's receipt
4:50 The results
6:02 The guarantee
7:15 Where the money went
7:51 The pattern
8:25 The verdict
9:04 What's next

Sources:
• FTC — Automators AI: complaint press release (Aug 22 2023): https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2023/08/ftc-action-stops-business-opportunity-scheme-promised-its-ai-boosted-tools-would-power-high-earnings · settlement (Feb 27 2024, $21,765,902.65 judgment, partially suspended): https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/02/ftc-action-leads-ban-owners-automators-ai-e-commerce-money-making-scheme
• FTC v. FBA Machine / Passive Scaling (D.N.J. 2:24-cv-06635) — second amended complaint (Oct 2024): https://ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/83-SecondAmendedComplaint.pdf · settlement (Jul 30 2025, $15.7M judgment, partially suspended): https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/07/ftc-obtains-permanent-ban-e-commerce-business-opportunity-scheme-operator
• FTC v. Ascend Ecom (C.D. Cal. 2:24-cv-07660) — complaint (Sep 2024): https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/2423023ascendecomcomplaint.pdf · settlement (Jun 23 2025, $25M judgment, partially suspended): https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/06/ftc-case-leads-order-banning-ascend-ecom-its-owners-business-opportunity-marketing
• FTC v. Empire Holdings Group (Ecommerce Empire Builders) (E.D. Pa. 2:24-cv-04949) — complaint (Sep 2024): https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/2423027ecommercebuilderscomplaint.pdf
• FTC — "Operation AI Comply" (Sep 25 2024): https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/09/ftc-announces-crackdown-deceptive-ai-claims-schemes

Our calculations: the $77M total is the sum of the four amounts the FTC alleged ($22M + $15.9M + $25M + $14.3M). Narrated with an AI voice.

This video is for education only and is not financial or legal advice. It describes allegations in public FTC court filings and the terms of court-approved settlements; the defendants did not admit the allegations.
