"We build it. We run it. You just collect."
"And it's risk free. Guaranteed."
That's the pitch. And people paid for it — often tens of thousands of dollars each.
Remember the word "guaranteed". Later we'll see what happened when people actually tried to use it.
In the last episode we promised to read the court files. So we did.
Four federal cases brought by the US Federal Trade Commission between 2023 and 2024. Automators AI. Passive Scaling, later renamed FBA Machine. Ascend Ecom. And Ecommerce Empire Builders.
Add up what the FTC alleges these four operations took from consumers, and you get about seventy-seven million dollars.

One word matters here: alleged. All four cases ended in settlements. That's normal for these cases — and it means the companies didn't admit the claims. So everything in this video is what the FTC alleged, or what a court ordered.
We're naming the companies because it's all in public court records. We're not naming any of the people behind them.
Here's what jumped out when we laid the four files side by side.
They're four different companies, in different states, with different names. But they sold almost the same thing. Nineteen of these twenty boxes are ticked.
One: artificial intelligence. Every one of them pitched its stores as AI-powered.
Two: it's done for you. You don't run the store. You're the "investor". They do the work.

And the income they promised wasn't small. Ten thousand dollars a month, at one company. Five figures a month in passive income, at another. One sales pitch, the FTC says, told people they could passively make a hundred thousand dollars a month. And one website claimed most clients hit six-figure monthly revenues within twelve to sixteen months.

Another company advertised that it had already built fifty-seven ten-thousand-a-month stores, thirty-four fifty-thousand-a-month stores, and six million-dollar stores. The FTC says it had no evidence to back up claims like these.

Three: a big fee, paid up front. Ten to thirty-five thousand dollars at one company. Thirty to eighty thousand at another. Up to a hundred twenty-five thousand at a third. And at one, the FTC says the fee ranged up to five hundred thousand dollars.

Four: it's "risk free". At two companies there was a written guarantee: if the store doesn't earn your money back, you get a refund, or they buy the store back. A third simply called it risk-free. The fourth is the one exception — its fine print said it could not guarantee results.
And five — the one nobody puts in the ad: a clause in the contract about what you're allowed to say afterwards. We'll come back to that one.
So what was the artificial intelligence?
In one complaint, the FTC put it plainly: since about 2023, the sales pitch said the business was powered by AI. Not the business. The pitch.
The model underneath was the same old one: someone runs a store on Amazon or Walmart with your money. The AI was what changed in the advertising.
In another file, the AI the company described was a repricing tool — software that adjusts prices. Plenty of ordinary sellers use repricing software. It doesn't turn a store into passive income.

And in a third, the FTC describes the method shown in the company's own ad: find hobbies listed on Wikipedia, look at bestsellers on Amazon, then sell similar products from overseas dropshipping suppliers like AliExpress. If that sounds familiar, it's the business we took apart two episodes ago.
Now let's print the receipt. We'll use the numbers from one file, because it lists them in detail.
This is the promise. A profit projection shown to prospective buyers: about two hundred thirty thousand dollars of profit over two years, from a single Amazon store.

Here's the deal underneath it. Thirty-five thousand dollars up front. A ninety-nine-dollar software fee every month. And the company keeps thirty-five percent of any profit the store makes. Automators, by the way, took the same thirty-five percent.
And on top of that, buyers were told to have forty to fifty thousand dollars available for inventory. That's not a fee — it's your money, sitting in the store, at risk.

So what did the stores actually sell? Of the forty-two known clients whose stores this company ran, the FTC says about eighty-six percent had total sales of fifteen thousand dollars or less. Not profit. Sales — before the cost of the products, before Amazon's fees, before refunds.

Let's be generous and pretend every dollar of those sales was pure profit, and the company took none of it. Fifteen thousand in, thirty-seven thousand three hundred seventy-six out. Net: minus twenty-two thousand dollars. That's the best case.
The real number is worse, because sales aren't profit. The products, the platform fees and the refunds all come out of that fifteen thousand.
And that wasn't one bad company. The other files tell the same story.

At Ascend, of seventy-four known clients, the FTC says nineteen percent of the stores had no sales at all. Another twenty-three percent sold something, but less than five thousand dollars. That's four in ten clients under five thousand dollars in sales — after start-up fees of thirty to eighty thousand.

At Passive Scaling, the earlier name of the same operation, about seventy-six percent of four hundred sixty-one known clients made sixty thousand dollars or less in gross sales — on fees that started at thirty thousand.
And at Automators AI, the FTC said Amazon and Walmart routinely suspended or terminated the stores. A store that gets shut down by the platform doesn't make passive income. It makes nothing.
The FTC's summary of that case: the vast majority of clients didn't make the promised earnings — or even get their investment back.

And at two of these companies, clients also had to open bank accounts, credit cards or loans with access to at least fifteen thousand dollars for inventory. When the store didn't sell, that debt was still theirs. Both complaints use the same words: consumers left with "depleted bank accounts and hefty credit card bills."
Which brings us back to the word from the start: guaranteed.
The pitch said you couldn't lose, because if the store didn't pay back your fee, you'd get a refund — or the company would buy the store back.
At Passive Scaling, the promise was simple: if you didn't earn back your fee within eighteen months, you could ask for a refund. At Ascend, the buyback came after twenty-four or thirty-six months.
Here's what the FTC alleges happened when people tried to use it. In one case: refunds were often made conditional on the customer removing their complaints about the company.

In another: customers who posted negative reviews were told they'd broken the contract — and could lose the buyback guarantee. The FTC also describes threats of legal action against people who wouldn't take their reviews down, and one case of a threatening message sent to a reviewer's family.
And in a third, people who asked for refunds were offered something else instead: a new store, on a different platform.
That clause about what you're allowed to say? In standard consumer contracts in the US, clauses that punish honest reviews have been illegal since 2016. The settlements we read ban them.
And that's the part that should change how you read the reviews. If unhappy customers are pressured to stay quiet, the reviews you can still see are the happy ones.
So did people get their money back?
The settlements came with big monetary judgments: about twenty-two million, fifteen point seven million, twenty-five million.

But read the next line in each press release: the judgments are partially suspended, based on the defendants' inability to pay the full amount. In plain words: much of the money is already gone. The FTC said one operation appears to have dissipated more than twenty-five million dollars.
What the courts could order was a ban. Most of the people behind these operations are now banned from selling business opportunities. That stops the next customer. It doesn't refund the last one.
So, without naming any company that isn't in a court file — what does the pattern look like?

These are the five things that run through these files — four of them in every single case. On their own, any one of them can be innocent. AI tools are real. Done-for-you services exist. But when all five show up in the same sales call, you've heard this pitch before. Four federal cases' worth of it.
One more thing from the files: under US rules, a seller of a business opportunity has to hand over a disclosure document, and back up any earnings claim. The FTC alleges these companies didn't.
Time to close the receipt.

The pitch: an AI-powered store that pays you while you do nothing, with no risk. The files: a large fee, stores that mostly sold very little, guarantees that came with conditions, and money that mostly can't be recovered.

"Done-for-you AI store, passive income, risk free"? Myth. Not because AI is fake, or because online stores can't make money. But in all four cases the FTC took to court, the guaranteed income was the product — and the store was just the packaging.
If you take one thing from these files, it's this: the FTC's case pages are public. A company name plus the letters F-T-C is a search anyone can do.
Next: the question behind this whole series. In "make money online", who actually makes the money? Often, it's the person selling the course. We'll follow the money.
What should go on the receipt after that? Tell us in the comments.

metadata.title: Inventory Estimates and the Cash Conversion Cycle | ACC 300 Lecture 20
metadata.author: Understanding Accounting
metadata.shortDescription:
Inventory estimates depend on the relationship between cost and selling price. This ACC 300 lecture explains gross profit and retail estimates, then connects inventory, customer collection, and supplier payment.

Follow Sound Decision through gross profit margin and markup, retail cost layers, and markdowns. Then calculate collection days, inventory days, payment days, and the cash conversion cycle using matched credit flows and unrounded intermediate amounts.

Pause at the five questions and practice cases before watching the explanations. All company amounts are fictional teaching inputs.

Course schedule and resources:
https://understandingaccounting.org/acc300/schedule/

Chapters
0:00 Opening
1:44 Gross profit method
7:34 Retail
16:15 Flows
17:24 Collection
19:32 Payment
23:49 Synthesis
28:15 Evaluation
29:48 Next meeting

segments.text: This is Lecture 20 for November 10.
We will estimate inventory and analyze the cash conversion cycle.
Sound Decision supplies fictional examples that are separate from the
reading's Second Helping cases.
All company amounts are teaching inputs in United States dollars.
Keep a calculator nearby and pause at each independent attempt before
continuing to its explanation.
The company buys goods, holds them, sells them, and collects cash.
We need two different kinds of information along that sequence.
An inventory estimate supplies a cost amount when a count is unavailable.
Operating analysis estimates the time between paying suppliers and collecting
from customers.
An amount reported as inventory does not, by itself, tell us that financing
interval.
A full count takes employee time and may interrupt operations.
Managers can need an interim balance or a preliminary purchasing estimate
before the next scheduled count.
A loss can destroy goods that employees can no longer count.
The purpose matters when selecting an estimation method.
An estimate also needs reliable purchase and sales records; it cannot repair
missing inputs automatically.
Both methods estimate ending inventory at cost, but they start with different
records.
The gross profit method applies an assumed gross profit margin or markup to
sales.
The retail method uses cost and retail selling-price records for the same
goods.
Retail value here includes goods still on hand; it does not mean revenue
already earned.
We will first estimate the cost assigned to sales, then subtract it from goods
available at cost.
The gross profit method supplies that expense estimate when we cannot yet
finish the inventory count.
Beginning inventory plus net purchases supplies the cost available for sale.
Part goes to cost of goods sold, and the remainder stays in ending inventory.
Estimate gross profit by applying a supported margin to net sales.
Subtract that estimated profit from sales to obtain estimated cost of goods
sold.
Then subtract the expense estimate from available cost.
Check ownership, cutoff, purchases, and sales before using the result.
Gross profit equals net sales minus cost of goods sold.
We cannot calculate the current actual margin without the ending inventory
amount we are trying to estimate.
Use a prior-period margin only when it fits current prices,
costs, and product mix, or use other supporting information.
Margin uses sales as its denominator.
Applying that percentage to current sales estimates profit, not inventory
directly.
Sound Decision needs an internal inventory estimate for February 2026 before
its quarterly count.
Beginning inventory costs 27,100 dollars, net purchases cost 98,600 dollars,
and net sales are 142,000 dollars.
Management supports a 35 percent gross profit margin.
Assume goods were either sold or remain on hand.
Estimate cost of goods sold, then the cost remaining in inventory.
Multiply 142,000 dollars of sales by 35 percent to estimate gross profit of
49,700 dollars.
Subtract that profit from sales for estimated cost of goods sold of 92,300
dollars.
Beginning inventory plus purchases gives 125,700 dollars available at cost.
Subtract the 92,300-dollar expense estimate.
Ending inventory is estimated at 33,400 dollars.
Pause for a separate July case.
Beginning inventory is 24,000 dollars, purchases are 76,000 dollars, and sales
are 120,000 dollars.
The supported gross profit margin is 30 percent.
Assume no goods are missing.
Calculate estimated cost of goods sold, goods available at cost, and ending
inventory.
Work before moving to the poll.
Submit the July ending inventory estimate.
A is 64,000 dollars, B is 84,000 dollars, C is 16,000 dollars, and D is
negative 8,000 dollars.
Use the same July records: beginning inventory of 24,000 dollars, purchases of
76,000 dollars, and sales of 120,000 dollars at a 30 percent margin.
Pause and select the cost remaining.
C is correct.
The company estimates 16,000 dollars of ending inventory.
A uses the profit share as though it were the cost share.
B gives estimated cost of goods sold instead of the ending asset.
D omits beginning inventory from available cost.
Keep the amount assigned to sales separate from the amount still held.
July gross profit is 30 percent of 120,000 dollars, or 36,000 dollars.
Estimated cost of goods sold is the remaining 84,000 dollars.
Beginning inventory of 24,000 dollars plus purchases of 76,000 dollars gives
100,000 dollars available at cost.
Subtract the 84,000-dollar expense estimate for 16,000 dollars of ending
inventory.
The asset and expense amounts reconcile to available cost.
This separate product costs 100 dollars and sells for 125 dollars.
Its gross profit is 25 dollars.
Divide profit by cost for a 25 percent markup.
Divide the same profit by selling price for a 20 percent gross profit margin.
To convert decimal markup to margin, divide markup by one plus markup.
The denominator must include the cost and profit portions of the selling
price.
Evaluate whether prices,
acquisition costs, and product mix still support the assumed margin.
Check purchase and sales records before interpreting an unexpected estimate.
Missing goods can reduce quantities, while damage can reduce recoverable
value.
When the later physical count occurs,
adjust for intervening purchases and sales, compare the estimated balance with
the count, and investigate differences.
Return to February's 125,700 dollars available at cost and 142,000 dollars of
sales.
A 30 percent margin gives 99,400 dollars of estimated expense and 26,300
dollars of ending inventory.
At 35 percent, ending inventory is 33,400 dollars.
At 40 percent, estimated expense falls to 85,200 dollars and ending inventory
rises to 40,500 dollars.
The assumed margin materially changes the estimate.
The retail method estimates the cost of unsold goods from their retail selling
prices.
Keep the cost records and retail records tied to the same pool.
A retail pool groups goods with suitable cost-to-retail relationships.
The cost column records acquisition cost.
The retail column records selling prices for those same goods, including
unsold inventory.
Add beginning goods and purchases in each column.
Available retail value is an amount assigned to goods, not revenue already
recognized.
A shared ratio works only when it fits the goods remaining.
Use a new April pool for Sound Decision.
Beginning inventory costs 18,200 dollars and has a retail value of 28,000
dollars.
Purchases cost 72,800 dollars and have a retail value of 112,000 dollars.
Available cost is 91,000 dollars, and available retail value is 140,000
dollars.
Net sales are 106,000 dollars.
Assume no price changes,
returns, transfers, or shrinkage.
Divide available cost of 91,000 dollars by available retail value of 140,000
dollars.
The ratio is 65 percent.
Those goods cost 65 percent of their recorded retail selling prices.
Apply that cost share to the retail amount still unsold,
assuming the same relationship fits the remaining pool.
Do not apply the ratio to a different group of products.
Subtract April sales of 106,000 dollars from 140,000 dollars available at
retail.
Ending inventory has a retail value of 34,000 dollars.
Multiply that amount by 65 percent to estimate ending cost of 22,100 dollars.
Subtract the ending cost from 91,000 dollars available at cost.
Estimated cost of goods sold is 68,900 dollars.
Pause for a separate August pool.
Beginning goods cost 18,000 dollars and have a retail value of 30,000 dollars.
Purchases cost 72,000 dollars and have a retail value of 120,000 dollars.
Sales are 110,000 dollars.
Use average-cost retail with no price changes or missing goods.
Calculate the ratio, ending retail value, and ending cost before answering the
next poll.
For August, which amount estimates ending inventory at cost?
A is 24,000 dollars, B is 66,000 dollars, C is 40,000 dollars, and D is 50,000
dollars.
Use the pool from the preceding practice: 90,000 dollars available at cost,
150,000 dollars available at retail, and sales of 110,000 dollars.
Pause and convert the remaining retail value to cost.
A is correct.
Ending inventory is estimated at 24,000 dollars of cost.
B estimates cost of goods sold by applying the ratio to sales.
C leaves the remaining goods at their retail selling prices.
D subtracts a retail amount from available cost.
Subtract and compare amounts on the same measurement basis.
Available cost is 18,000 plus 72,000 dollars, or 90,000 dollars.
Available retail value is 30,000 plus 120,000 dollars, or 150,000 dollars.
Their ratio is 60 percent.
Subtract 110,000 dollars of sales from available retail value.
The remaining 40,000 dollars at retail, multiplied by 60 percent, gives
estimated ending cost of 24,000 dollars.
Use a different May pool with periodic cost assignments.
Opening inventory costs 24,000 dollars and has a retail value of 40,000
dollars, giving a 60 percent ratio.
Purchases cost 60,000 dollars and have a retail value of 80,000 dollars,
giving a 75 percent ratio.
The combined ratio is 70 percent.
Sales of 60,000 dollars leave 60,000 dollars of inventory at retail.
Keep prices unchanged and assume no missing goods.
Average-cost retail applies the combined 70 percent ratio to the remaining
60,000 dollars at retail.
Ending cost is 42,000 dollars.
First in, first out assigns opening costs to sales first.
The remaining retail value fits inside May's purchases, so use their 75
percent ratio.
Ending cost is 45,000 dollars.
These methods assign costs; they do not establish which physical goods
customers selected.
Last in, first out assigns current costs to sales first.
The entire opening layer remains at its 24,000-dollar recorded cost.
Ending retail value is 60,000 dollars, including the opening layer's 40,000
dollars.
The remaining 20,000-dollar retail increment uses May's 75 percent ratio,
giving 15,000 dollars of cost.
Total ending inventory is 39,000 dollars.
Subtract it from 84,000 dollars available at cost for 45,000 dollars of
expense.
A markdown reduces a retail selling price while acquisition cost stays
unchanged.
Both methods subtract markdowns and sales when finding ending inventory at
retail. Average-cost retail also subtracts markdowns in the ratio denominator.
Conventional retail excludes them from that denominator, producing a lower
ratio in this example and approximating lower of cost or market.
Apply an appropriate method consistently; a voluntary change requires
justification that the new method is preferable.
Pause for the separate June pool.
Available cost is 48,000 dollars, original retail value is 80,000 dollars,
markdowns are 16,000 dollars, and sales are 32,000 dollars.
Only those markdowns change prices, and no goods are missing.
Calculate the common ending retail value, each cost-to-retail ratio, and each
ending inventory amount.
Explain why the results differ.
Ending retail value is 80,000 less 16,000 less 32,000 dollars, or 32,000
dollars.
Average-cost retail divides 48,000 dollars by 64,000 dollars after markdowns,
giving 75 percent.
Ending cost is 24,000 dollars.
Conventional retail divides 48,000 dollars by the original 80,000-dollar
retail amount, giving 60 percent.
Apply it to the same 32,000-dollar ending retail value for 19,200 dollars.
The denominator difference causes the lower conventional estimate.
A markdown changes the selling price; a write-down reduces the recorded
inventory amount.
Under United States guidance, retail-method inventory uses lower of cost or
market, including first-in, first-out retail.
A cost estimate still needs that measurement check.
Conventional retail can approximate the required result when adequate
markdowns reflect damage, obsolescence, and reduced selling prices.
Inadequate markdowns can leave inventory overstated.
Record price changes and missing goods before trusting the retail balance.
Group goods with suitable cost-to-retail relationships;
the remaining products may have a different cost share from those sold.
Identify whether the ratio follows average-cost or conventional retail.
Reconcile quantities and assess lower of cost or market.
A mathematically correct ratio cannot establish that every item still exists
or retains its value.
We will now connect inventory with customer collection and supplier payment.
These measures estimate timing from balances and matching activity.
Acquiring inventory begins the operating cycle.
Selling on credit transfers the wait from inventory to receivables, and
collection ends that cycle.
Supplier credit covers purchase to supplier payment.
Subtract payment days to find the remaining financing interval.
The diagram places payment before sale for illustration.
Actual supplier payment may occur before or after the sale.
Match each average balance with the flow that created or used it.
Compare net receivables with net credit sales per day.
Compare inventory cost with cost of goods sold per day.
Compare related payables with net credit inventory purchases per day.
Average beginning and ending balances, then divide annual activity by 365 for
daily activity.
Compatible inputs make the resulting days interpretable.
Receivable turnover divides annual net credit sales by average net trade
receivables.
It expresses how often annual sales cover the average unpaid balance.
Collection days divides the same balance by daily credit sales.
Equivalently, divide 365 by annual turnover.
Higher turnover gives fewer days, but neither average shows the age of a
particular unpaid invoice.
This is a new company-wide annual case for Sound Decision.
Net credit sales are 657,000 dollars, cash sales are 109,500 dollars, and cost
of goods sold is 401,500 dollars.
The table supplies beginning and ending inventory, net receivables, and
related payables.
All inventory purchases are on credit, the credit-loss allowance is unchanged,
and no other inventory movement applies.
We will calculate each timing component separately.
Average net receivables of 61,000 and 83,000 dollars to obtain 72,000 dollars.
Divide annual credit sales of 657,000 dollars by that balance for turnover of
about 9.13 times.
Daily credit sales are 1,800 dollars.
Divide the average balance of 72,000 dollars by 1,800 dollars for 40
collection days.
Investigate customer aging and terms before attributing longer days to slower
payment.
Cash sales do not create trade receivables.
Using net credit sales gives 1,800 dollars per day and 40 collection days.
Adding 109,500 dollars of cash sales increases the daily denominator,
reducing the computed result to about 34.29 days.
That change does not establish faster collections.
When credit sales are unavailable and total sales are used, label the result
as a proxy.
Next match inventory and supplier balances with their own cost flows.
Supplier payment days require credit purchases rather than customer sales.
Keep the matching rule visible as we change components.
Inventory days compare average inventory cost with daily cost of goods sold.
Collection days use credit sales, while payment days use related credit
purchases.
The same averaging procedure applies, but the underlying flows differ.
A common denominator would mix different transactions.
Average beginning inventory of 48,000 dollars and ending inventory of 62,000
dollars.
Average inventory is 55,000 dollars.
Divide 401,500 dollars of annual expense by that balance for turnover of 7.30
times.
Daily cost of goods sold is 1,100 dollars.
Divide 55,000 dollars by 1,100 dollars for 50 inventory days.
Use cost amounts on both sides rather than comparing inventory cost with
selling prices.
Reconcile purchases using beginning and ending inventory net of any valuation
allowance.
Add losses excluded from reported cost of goods sold, but do not add a loss
already included there.
For a manufacturer, include changes in raw materials, work in process, and
finished goods.
Subtract production labor and overhead added to inventory to isolate materials
purchases.
Those production costs are not purchases of materials from suppliers.
Return to the supplier balance.
Average related trade payables and divide by net credit inventory purchases
per day.
Use purchases for the same goods and period as the payables.
The daily denominator is annual credit purchases divided by the number of
days.

Sound Decision supplies fictional examples that are separate from the reading's Second Helping cases. All company amounts are teaching inputs in United States dollars. Keep a calculator nearby and pause at each independent attempt before continuing to its explanation. The company buys goods, holds them, sells them, and collects cash. We need two different kinds of information along that sequence. An inventory estimate supplies a cost amount when a count is unavailable. Operating analysis estimates the time between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. An amount reported as inventory does not, by itself, tell us that financing interval. A full count takes employee time and may interrupt operations. Managers can need an interim balance or a preliminary purchasing estimate before the next scheduled count. A loss can destroy goods that employees can no longer count. The purpose matters when selecting an estimation method. An estimate also needs reliable purchase and sales records; it cannot repair missing inputs automatically. Both methods estimate ending inventory at cost, but they start with different records. The gross profit method applies an assumed gross profit margin or markup to sales. The retail method uses cost and retail selling-price records for the same goods. Retail value here includes goods still on hand; it does not mean revenue already earned. We will first estimate the cost assigned to sales, then subtract it from goods available at cost. The gross profit method supplies that expense estimate when we cannot yet finish the inventory count. Beginning inventory plus net purchases supplies the cost available for sale. Part goes to cost of goods sold, and the remainder stays in ending inventory. Estimate gross profit by applying a supported margin to net sales. Subtract that estimated profit from sales to obtain estimated cost of goods sold. Then subtract the expense estimate from available cost. Check ownership, cutoff, purchases, and sales before using the result. Gross profit equals net sales minus cost of goods sold. We cannot calculate the current actual margin without the ending inventory amount we are trying to estimate. Use a prior-period margin only when it fits current prices, costs, and product mix, or use other supporting information. Margin uses sales as its denominator. Applying that percentage to current sales estimates profit, not inventory directly. Sound Decision needs an internal inventory estimate for February 2026 before its quarterly count. Beginning inventory costs 27,100 dollars, net purchases cost 98,600 dollars, and net sales are 142,000 dollars. Management supports a 35 percent gross profit margin. Assume goods were either sold or remain on hand. Estimate cost of goods sold, then the cost remaining in inventory. Multiply 142,000 dollars of sales by 35 percent to estimate gross profit of 49,700 dollars. Subtract that profit from sales for estimated cost of goods sold of 92,300 dollars. Beginning inventory plus purchases gives 125,700 dollars available at cost. Subtract the 92,300-dollar expense estimate. Ending inventory is estimated at 33,400 dollars. Pause for a separate July case. Beginning inventory is 24,000 dollars, purchases are 76,000 dollars, and sales are 120,000 dollars. The supported gross profit margin is 30 percent. Assume no goods are missing. Calculate estimated cost of goods sold, goods available at cost, and ending inventory. Work before moving to the poll. Submit the July ending inventory estimate. A is 64,000 dollars, B is 84,000 dollars, C is 16,000 dollars, and D is negative 8,000 dollars. Use the same July records: beginning inventory of 24,000 dollars, purchases of 76,000 dollars, and sales of 120,000 dollars at a 30 percent margin. Pause and select the cost remaining. C is correct. The company estimates 16,000 dollars of ending inventory. A uses the profit share as though it were the cost share. B gives estimated cost of goods sold instead of the ending asset. D omits beginning inventory from available cost. Keep the amount assigned to sales separate from the amount still held. July gross profit is 30 percent of 120,000 dollars, or 36,000 dollars. Estimated cost of goods sold is the remaining 84,000 dollars. Beginning inventory of 24,000 dollars plus purchases of 76,000 dollars gives 100,000 dollars available at cost. Subtract the 84,000-dollar expense estimate for 16,000 dollars of ending inventory. The asset and expense amounts reconcile to available cost. This separate product costs 100 dollars and sells for 125 dollars. Its gross profit is 25 dollars. Divide profit by cost for a 25 percent markup. Divide the same profit by selling price for a 20 percent gross profit margin. To convert decimal markup to margin, divide markup by one plus markup. The denominator must include the cost and profit portions of the selling price. Evaluate whether prices, acquisition costs, and product mix still support the assumed margin. When the later physical count occurs, adjust for intervening purchases and sales, compare the estimated balance with the count, and investigate differences. the average time the business was without its cash from paying suppliers to getting paid by customers a short cash conversion cycle is best it's an indication of an efficient supply chain efficient operations and good overall cash flow management so let's take a quick look at each of the terms that make up the cash conversion cycle calculation days sales outstanding DSO is a measure of how quickly a business is paid by its customers if all customers paid immediately known as a cash sale just like you or I do when buying something from a shop then the DSO would be zero but in business to business sales that's not always the case so DSO considers how much money a businesses waiting to be paid from credit sales rather than cash sales relative to the quantity of sales made for cash flow we want our Day sales outstanding to be as small small as possible day's inventory outstanding Dio is the average time the inventory spends in the ownership of the business it describes the average metadata.author: Understanding Accounting
metadata.shortDescription:
Inventory estimates depend on cost and selling-price relationships. This narrated Chapter 18 explains gross profit and retail estimates, then connects inventory, customer collection, and supplier payment.

Follow Second Helping through gross profit margin and markup, retail cost layers, markdowns, and inventory losses. Calculate collection days, inventory days, payment days, and the cash conversion cycle. Compare annual results and consider the limits of ratios drawn from published financial statements.

Pause at the questions and worked calculations before hearing the explanations. The separate practice uses Confetti Party Supply. All company amounts are fictional teaching inputs.

Course schedule and reading resources:
https://understandingaccounting.org/acc300/schedule/

segments.text: You are listening to Chapter 18 of the A C C 300 course reading.
Second Helping supplies fictional kitchenware examples of inventory estimates
and operating analysis.
We will use gross profit and retail records to estimate inventory, then
connect inventory,
customer collection, and supplier payment.
Pause at each question before hearing its answer.
All company amounts are fictional teaching inputs in United States dollars.
A company's inventory records may show what it purchased and sold without
establishing exactly what remains on hand.
When a physical count is unavailable,
information about sales,
costs, and selling prices can provide an estimate.
But the result is only as reliable as the relationships used to calculate it.
A change in selling prices or the mix of products sold, for example, can make
a mathematically correct calculation misleading.
Inventory also affects how long a company must finance its operations.
Cash may be tied up in goods awaiting sale and in receivables awaiting
collection, while credit from suppliers delays the need to pay for purchases.
The cash conversion cycle combines these periods to help explain how operating
decisions affect the timing of cash flows.
When an inventory estimate is useful.
A company may need to determine its inventory balance before it can complete a
physical count.
In other situations, such as a fire, some goods may no longer be available to
count.
Even when a physical count is possible, it establishes quantities, not
necessarily ownership or cost.
Inventory estimates offer another way to approximate the cost of goods on hand
using available accounting information.
Two common approaches are the gross-profit method, which uses sales and an
assumed gross profit margin, and the retail inventory method, which uses
records maintained at both cost and retail selling prices.
Neither requires the company to identify and cost every individual item
remaining in inventory.
Management may use an estimate to monitor monthly operations,
prepare interim financial statements, or assess inventory destroyed in a fire.
The reporting rules differ between the two methods.
A S C Topic 270, Subtopic 10, Section 45, paragraph 6(a) allows companies to
use the gross-profit method for interim reports, such as quarterly statements,
even when they use another method at year-end.
Companies must disclose the interim method and any significant adjustments
from reconciling the estimates with the annual physical inventory.
The gross-profit method is not a regular year-end inventory valuation method.
The retail inventory method can be used for both interim and annual reports
under A S C Topic 330, Subtopic 10, Section 30, paragraph 13.
It works best for goods with similar gross profit margins and requires
reliable cost and selling-price records.
The later retail-method section explains how those records support the
estimate.
Check your understanding.
Which inventory estimation method can a company use for regular annual
reporting: gross-profit or retail?
Pause to answer.
Answer.
The retail inventory method, when appropriate.
The gross-profit method can support interim reports but is not a regular
year-end inventory valuation method.
The gross-profit method.
Refresher:
gross profit
Review gross profit and gross profit margin in Chapter 6.
Chapter 6 introduced gross profit and the gross profit margin when comparing
income statements.
For a retailer, gross profit is net sales less cost of goods sold.
The gross profit margin expresses that profit as a percentage of net sales.
Without a reliable ending inventory amount, the company cannot finish
calculating current cost of goods sold or gross profit.
It therefore estimates the gross profit margin from prior periods, comparable
products, or other supporting information.
Part of each sales dollar covers the cost of the goods, and the remainder
represents gross profit.
An assumed profit share lets the company estimate the cost share and then the
inventory remaining.
Gross profit margin equals gross profit divided by net sales, multiplied by
100 percent.
Suppose management estimates gross profit at 32 percent of sales.
For each dollar of sales, 32 cents represents gross profit and 68 cents
represents the cost of goods sold.
If that relationship holds for the current period, the retailer can estimate
cost of goods sold from its sales.
Estimated cost of goods sold equals net sales multiplied by one minus the
assumed gross profit margin.
Express the margin as a decimal.
The company can then use the inventory relationship from earlier chapters.
Goods available for sale must either have been sold or remain in ending
inventory, assuming no other inventory movements.
Subtracting estimated cost of goods sold from goods available at cost gives
estimated ending inventory.
Estimated ending inventory equals beginning inventory plus net purchases,
minus estimated cost of goods sold.
Net sales and net purchases must reflect applicable returns,
allowances, and discounts, with qualifying freight included in purchase cost.
Inventory costs and transactions must also be recorded in the correct periods.
A monthly inventory estimate.
Assume that Second Helping begins March 2026 with inventory of 38,600 dollars
and net purchases of 115,400 dollars.
Net sales are 168,000 dollars.
Based on comparable products and recent selling prices, management supports an
estimated gross profit margin of 32.00 percent of sales.
No other inventory movements apply.
For the March estimate,
beginning inventory is 38,600 dollars and net purchases are 115,400 dollars.
Together they supply 154,000 dollars of goods available at cost.
Net sales are 168,000 dollars.
Multiply sales by the 32 percent gross profit margin to estimate profit of
53,760 dollars.
Subtract that profit from sales.
Estimated cost of goods sold is one hundred fourteen thousand two hundred
forty dollars.
Subtract that expense from available cost for ending inventory of 39,760
dollars.
Check your understanding.
Why would multiplying goods available for sale by the 32 percent gross profit
margin give an incorrect estimate of ending inventory?
Pause to answer.
Answer.
The 32 percent gross profit margin describes gross profit relative to sales,
not ending inventory relative to goods available for sale.
Apply the gross profit margin to sales to estimate gross profit, then
determine cost of goods sold.
Subtract estimated cost of goods sold from goods available for sale to
estimate ending inventory.
Markup on cost versus gross profit margin.
A retailer may set a selling price by adding a percentage to an item's cost.
This percentage is the markup on cost.
The amount added becomes gross profit when the item sells at that price.
An item costing 100 dollars with a 25 percent markup sells for 125 dollars.
Of that selling price, 100 dollars covers cost and 25 dollars is gross profit.
To express gross profit as a percentage of sales, divide the 25 dollars profit
by the 125 dollars selling price:
The item costs 100 dollars and sells for 125 dollars, producing 25 dollars of
gross profit.
For gross profit margin,
divide 25 dollars by the selling price of 125 dollars.
The margin is 20 percent.
For markup on cost, divide the same 25 dollars by the cost of 100 dollars.
The markup is 25 percent.
The profit amount is unchanged; the denominator changes.
Gross profit accounts for 20 percent of sales, leaving 80 percent as cost.
We can use those percentages to estimate cost of goods sold from sales.
To convert a markup on cost to a gross profit margin,
enter the markup as a decimal.
For a 25 percent markup, use 0.25.
The result is also a decimal; multiply it by 100 to express the gross profit
margin as a percentage.
To convert markup on cost to gross profit margin,
divide the decimal markup by one plus that markup.
For the item above, the selling price is cost plus a 25 percent markup, or
1.25 times cost.
Divide the markup by that selling-price factor to express the profit as a
share of sales:
Divide zero point two five by one plus zero point two five.
The denominator is one point two five.
Dividing zero point two five by one point two five gives zero point two zero.
That is a 20 percent gross profit margin.
The denominator includes both cost and markup because the gross profit margin
uses the full selling price as its base.
When the markup is known, cost can also be estimated directly from sales.
Enter net sales in dollars and the markup as a decimal.
The result is estimated cost of goods sold in dollars.
When the stated percentage is markup on cost,
estimate cost of goods sold by dividing net sales by one plus the decimal
markup.
Apply this 25 percent markup to Second Helping's March net sales of 168,000
dollars.
Goods available for sale at cost remain 154,000 dollars: beginning inventory
of 38,600 dollars plus net purchases of 115,400 dollars.
For markup on cost,
divide net sales by one plus the decimal markup.
Divide $168,000 by 1.25 to estimate cost of goods sold of $134,400.
Subtract that expense from $154,000 of goods available at cost.
Estimated ending inventory is $19,600.
Check your understanding.
An item sells for 150 dollars after a 50 percent markup on cost.
What are its cost and gross profit margin?
Pause to answer.
Answer.
Selling price is 1.50 times cost.
Divide 150 dollars by 1.50 to obtain a cost of 100 dollars.
Gross profit is 50 dollars.
Divide 50 dollars by 150 dollars for a gross profit margin of approximately
33.33 percent.
Limits of the gross-profit method.
The gross-profit method assumes that the relationship between sales and cost
of goods sold is reasonably predictable.
But purchase prices, selling prices,
discounts, and product mix can change that relationship.
An estimate based on an earlier gross profit margin may therefore misstate
both cost of goods sold and ending inventory.
The markup calculation likewise assumes that the stated markup represents the
goods actually sold, including the effects of discounts.
A posted markup may not represent the relationship between actual net sales
and cost.
Return to Second Helping's March estimate and change the assumed gross profit
margin:
Assumed gross profit margin, 28.00 percent; Estimated cost of goods sold,
120,960 dollars; Estimated ending inventory, 33,040 dollars.
Assumed gross profit margin, 32.00 percent; Estimated cost of goods sold,
114,240 dollars; Estimated ending inventory, 39,760 dollars.
Assumed gross profit margin, 36.00 percent; Estimated cost of goods sold,
107,520 dollars; Estimated ending inventory, 46,480 dollars.
A lower gross profit margin means that a larger share of sales represents the
cost of the goods sold.
With goods available for sale unchanged,
more cost assigned to goods sold leaves less in ending inventory.
A higher gross profit margin has the opposite effect.
For example,
reducing the assumed gross profit margin from 32 percent to 28 percent reduces
estimated ending inventory by 6,720 dollars.
That difference measures the estimate's sensitivity to the assumed gross
profit margin.
It does not establish that either gross profit margin is correct or that the
resulting inventory amounts form a statistical confidence interval.
When products have substantially different gross profit margins,
changes in the mix of goods sold can affect the overall gross profit margin
even if sales remain stable.
Estimating separate product groups may produce a more reasonable result when
reliable records support the distinction.
Estimating inventory losses.
Refresher: inventory write-downs Review inventory measurement and write-downs
in Chapter 17.
When goods are lost or destroyed, the company may be unable to count them.
A fire,
flood, or earthquake can leave only part of the inventory available for
inspection.
The gross-profit method can estimate the cost of inventory that should have
been on hand before the event.
To estimate the cost of missing goods,
subtract the original cost of goods still present from the estimated inventory
cost before the event.
Both amounts must cover the same inventory and date, with any intervening
movements accounted for.
Estimated cost of missing inventory equals estimated inventory cost before the
event, minus the cost of inventory still present.
The difference estimates missing inventory; it does not establish why the
goods are missing.
Management must investigate earlier losses and recording errors before
attributing the entire difference to a particular event.
Goods still present but damaged require a separate evaluation for a
write-down.
In the monthly inventory estimate above, we calculated Second Helping's March
ending inventory as 39,760 dollars using a 32 percent gross profit margin.
Now suppose a fire occurs immediately after March ends, before any additional
inventory movements.
That earlier estimate is therefore the estimated inventory immediately before
the fire.
Investigators establish that the surviving goods have a cost of 5,600 dollars.
Applying the missing-inventory calculation gives:
Subtract 5,600 dollars of inventory still present from estimated cost before
the event of 39,760 dollars.
The estimated cost of missing inventory is 34,160 dollars.
Management may use a gross-profit estimate to assess a potential loss or
prepare an insurance claim, including at year-end.
That use differs from using the method to establish the regular annual
inventory balance.
The insurer determines any reimbursement from the policy and other relevant
facts, not this estimate alone.
Missing inventory and inventory destroyed in the fire are not necessarily the
same thing.
If goods had already disappeared through theft or unrecorded removals, the
34,160 dollars difference could include losses unrelated to the fire.
An unsuitable gross profit margin could also make the estimated inventory
before the fire too high or too low.
The company must evaluate those possibilities before attributing the entire
difference to the fire or recording an adjustment.
Assume management completes that investigation and supports the estimated
34,160 dollars fire loss.
Before recording the loss, the Inventory account has a debit balance of 39,760
dollars.
The surviving goods remain usable and require no write-down.
Second Helping records the loss by debiting an expense and crediting
Inventory:
On the date of the fire,
debit Inventory Loss from Fire and credit Inventory for 34,160 dollars.
The debit records expense, and the credit reduces the inventory asset.
The entry reduces current income by 34,160 dollars and leaves Inventory at
5,600 dollars, the cost of the surviving goods.
Any insurance recovery requires a separate assessment; this entry records only
the inventory loss.
The retail inventory method estimates inventory cost using records of the same
goods at two amounts: their acquisition cost and their retail selling prices.
Merchandise that cost 60 dollars may have a retail selling price of 100
dollars.
The retail inventory method uses that relationship to estimate how much of the
selling-price value of unsold goods represents cost.
The retailer obtains retail value from its inventory quantities and
selling-price records.
For each product, it multiplies the quantity by the recorded selling price,
then adds those amounts across products.
It records beginning inventory and purchases at both cost and retail value.
The retail amount for a purchase is what the retailer plans to charge
customers, not what it paid the supplier.
A retailer may track the selling-price value of merchandise remaining without
identifying the cost of every individual item.
If selling prices have not changed and sales are the only reduction in
inventory, subtracting sales from goods available at retail gives the retail
value of goods remaining.
The company cannot report the retail selling-price value of its unsold goods
as inventory cost.
It includes an anticipated gross profit that the company has not yet earned.
The company must estimate how much of the remaining retail value represents
cost.
The cost-to-retail ratio expresses the recorded cost of merchandise as a
percentage of its retail value.
For merchandise costing 60 dollars with a retail value of 100 dollars, the
ratio is 60 percent.
Applying that percentage to the retail value of unsold merchandise estimates
its cost.
Chapter 16 distinguished the costs assigned under average cost, first in,
first out, and last in, first out.
Retail estimation also requires a cost-flow assumption.
Under average-cost retail, we combine beginning inventory and purchases into
one cost-to-retail ratio.
first in, first out and last in, first out retail calculations keep those
amounts separate.
We first work through average-cost retail, then compare the layer
calculations.
A pool is the group of goods included in that calculation.
Cost-to-retail ratio equals goods available at cost divided by goods available
at retail.
Ending inventory at retail equals goods available at retail minus net sales.
Estimated ending inventory at cost equals ending inventory at retail
multiplied by the cost-to-retail ratio.
The ratio gives a reasonable estimate only if the unsold goods have a similar
cost-to-retail relationship to the goods in the full pool.
Check your understanding.
Unsold goods have a retail value of 40,000 dollars and a cost-to-retail ratio
of 60 percent.
What is their estimated cost?
Pause to answer.
Answer.
Multiply the 40,000 dollars retail value by 60 percent.
Estimated ending inventory cost is 24,000 dollars.
From retail value to estimated cost.
For the retail-method example, instead assume that Second Helping has the
following April 2026 kitchenware inventory.
Its records include beginning inventory and purchases at both cost and retail
selling prices.
Net sales are 143,000 dollars.
There are no price changes, sales returns,
inventory losses, or other movements.
The recorded retail prices reflect the prices at which goods were sold.
April inventory pool, Beginning inventory;
Cost, 22,800 dollars; Retail, 38,000 dollars.
April inventory pool,
Net purchases;
Cost, 91,200 dollars; Retail, 152,000 dollars.
April inventory pool,
Goods available; Cost, 114,000 dollars; Retail, 190,000 dollars.
Both columns describe the same merchandise.
The cost column records what the goods cost Second Helping;
the retail column records their selling-price value.
The calculation has three steps.
First, determine the cost represented by each dollar of retail value.
Next, subtract sales to find the retail value remaining.
Finally, apply the ratio to estimate the cost of those unsold goods.
First calculate the whole pool's cost share.
Divide 114,000 dollars of available cost by 190,000 dollars at retail to
obtain 60 percent.
Then subtract 143,000 dollars of sales from the 190,000 dollars available
retail value.
Unsold goods have a retail value of 47,000 dollars.
Multiply 47,000 dollars by 60 percent to estimate ending cost of 28,200
dollars.
The ratio relates cost and retail value for the same pool.
Each dollar of recorded retail value represents 60 cents of cost and 40 cents
of anticipated gross profit, on average.
Applying the ratio removes that estimated profit portion from the unsold
goods.
After estimating ending inventory,
calculate cost of goods sold:
Formula, Goods available at cost minus Estimated ending inventory at cost;
Calculation, 114,000 dollars minus 28,200 dollars; Estimated cost of goods
sold, 85,800 dollars.
first in, first out and last in, first out retail estimates.
Refresher:
cost layers
Review the cost-flow methods in Chapter 16.
first in, first out assigns older costs to sales first;
last in, first out assigns newer costs first.
The retail calculation begins the same way under each cost-flow assumption:
subtract sales from goods available at retail to find ending inventory at
retail.
The difference is which cost-to-retail ratio applies to the remaining goods.
Under average-cost retail, we use a combined ratio.
Under first in, first out retail, ending inventory comes from the newer
purchases when those purchases cover the ending balance.
Under last in, first out retail, older layers remain, and an increase adds a
new layer at the current period's ratio.
Different ratios for beginning inventory and purchases.
Instead, assume that Second Helping has the following April records.
Selling prices remain unchanged, but purchase costs have increased.
All current purchases have the same cost-to-retail ratio.
Beginning inventory is one opening layer; there are no markdowns, losses,
returns, or other inventory movements.
These are periodic estimates made at the end of April.
Beginning inventory costs 20,000 dollars and has a retail value of 40,000
dollars, giving a 50 percent ratio.
April purchases cost 112,000 dollars and have a retail value of 160,000
dollars, giving a 70 percent ratio.
Combined available cost is 132,000 dollars, and available retail value is
200,000 dollars.
Their combined ratio is 66 percent.
There are two layer ratios:
50 percent for beginning inventory and 70 percent for April purchases.
The opening ratio relates the opening goods' retail value to their recorded
cost.
The purchases ratio relates April's retail value to April's purchase cost.
first in, first out and last in, first out keep these relationships separate;
the 66 percent combined ratio is used only for the average-cost comparison.
Net sales are 140,000 dollars.
The unsold retail value is the same under all three cost-flow assumptions:
Subtract 140,000 dollars of net sales from 200,000 dollars of goods available
at retail.
Ending inventory at retail is 60,000 dollars.
The layer diagrams use the same older-at-bottom, newer-at-top arrangement as
Chapter 16.
Start with the same goods under each method,
assign the sales, and calculate the cost of the remaining layers.
Retail amounts identify the portions assigned to sales and to ending
inventory.
Both cost of goods sold and ending inventory are measured at cost.
The applicable ratio converts a retail amount to cost; an opening layer
retains its recorded cost.
The diagrams represent cost assignments, not the physical order in which goods
sell.
first in, first out retail:
apply the purchases ratio to remaining goods.
first in, first out assigns the opening layer to sales first at its recorded
cost,
which corresponds to the 50 percent opening ratio.
Sales then use part of April's purchases at their 70 percent ratio.
Only April purchases remain, so the ending inventory estimate uses the
purchases ratio.
Under first in, first out, assign opening inventory to sales first.
The opening layer has 40,000 dollars of retail value and carries 20,000
dollars of cost.
The remaining 100,000 dollars of sales uses April's 70 percent ratio,
assigning another 70,000 dollars of cost to sales.
Total cost of goods sold is 90,000 dollars.
The remaining April goods have 60,000 dollars of retail value.
Multiply that amount by 70 percent for 42,000 dollars of ending inventory
cost.
Cost of goods sold plus ending inventory equals the available cost of 132,000
dollars.
last in, first out retail:
retain the opening layer and cost the increase.
last in, first out assigns sales to April's purchases first, using their 70
percent ratio to estimate cost of goods sold.
The remaining April purchases use that same ratio.
The entire opening layer also remains at its recorded cost, which corresponds
to its 50 percent ratio.
Ending inventory therefore contains costs from both layers; the purchases
ratio does not replace the opening ratio.
Under last in, first out, assign the 140,000 dollars of sales to April's
purchases at the 70 percent ratio.
Cost of goods sold is 98,000 dollars.
April's purchases originally had 160,000 dollars of retail value, so 20,000
dollars of that retail layer remains.
Its cost is 14,000 dollars.
Opening inventory retains its recorded cost of 20,000 dollars.
The two remaining layers total 34,000 dollars.
Adding 98,000 dollars of cost of goods sold reconciles to 132,000 dollars of
available cost.
With several opening last in, first out layers, an inventory decrease removes
the newest of those layers first.
When retail prices change, dollar-value last in, first out retail requires
price indexes to distinguish price changes from changes in the inventory pool.
The unchanged-price illustration above does not require that adjustment.
Compare the cost assignments.
Average-cost retail combines the two sources before costing the unsold goods.
Under first in, first out, all remaining goods come from April purchases, so
their cost uses April's 70 percent cost-to-retail ratio.
last in, first out retail retains the opening cost and adds the cost of the
new layer.
For average-cost retail,
multiply 60,000 dollars of ending retail value by 66 percent.
Ending cost is 39,600 dollars.
For first-in, first-out retail,
multiply 60,000 dollars by 70 percent to obtain 42,000 dollars.
For last-in, first-out retail, add the opening cost of 20,000 dollars to the
current layer's 14,000 dollars.
Ending cost is 34,000 dollars.
Purchase costs increased while selling prices stayed unchanged.
first in, first out therefore leaves the higher current costs in inventory,
last in, first out retains older lower costs, and average cost falls between
them, as in Chapter 16.
Check your understanding.
Under last in, first out retail, which ratio applies to beginning inventory
that remains unsold:
its original ratio or the current purchases ratio?
Pause to answer.
Answer.
Its original ratio.
The company retains the beginning inventory at its recorded cost and uses the
current purchases ratio for a new layer.
Apply the inventory measurement rule after estimating cost.
Refresher:
retail inventory measurement
Review Chapter 17's lower-of-cost-or-market rule for inventory measured using
last in, first out or the retail method.
The amounts above estimate cost before any required write-down.
Under United States generally accepted accounting principles, retail-method
inventory remains subject to lower of cost or market under A S C Topic 330,
Subtopic 10, Section 35, paragraphs 1 C and 7.
That includes average-cost retail and first in, first out retail.
The lower-of-cost-and-net-realizable-value rule for ordinary first in, first
out or average-cost inventory does not apply merely because a retail
calculation uses that cost-flow assumption.
The retail method remains part of the company's measurement basis.
Limits of the retail inventory method.
The April calculation assumes unchanged selling prices and that recorded sales
account for all merchandise no longer on hand.
Actual retail operations can include price changes and inventory losses.
Price changes affect retail value without necessarily changing cost.
Suppose Second Helping reduces an item's price from 100 dollars to 80 dollars.
Its recorded retail value falls by 20 dollars, even though its original cost
has not changed.
Ignoring the price reduction would overstate the retail value still available
for sale.
A markdown is a reduction from a previously established retail price.
Retailers record permanent markdowns as reductions in inventory's retail value
when they reduce the prices.
The acquisition cost of those goods has not changed.
Markdowns in the retail calculation.
A retailer can use average-cost retail or conventional retail to determine the
inventory amount it reports in its financial statements.
Average-cost retail estimates cost first, followed by any required write-down.
Conventional retail approximates lower of cost or market within the
calculation.
The company selects an appropriate method for the inventory being measured and
applies it consistently.
It does not calculate both each period and choose the preferred result.
Chapter 17 established that inventory measured using the retail method is
subject to lower of cost or market.
That requirement applies to both methods.
A markdown reduces a selling price; it does not directly measure the
replacement cost,
ceiling, and floor used to determine market in Chapter 17.
However, a permanent price reduction can indicate that merchandise has lost
value.
Conventional retail uses that reduction to approximate the decline.
The company must still evaluate whether the result reasonably reflects lower
of cost or market.
In the formulas below, original retail value means the retail value of all
goods available before markdowns.
Under average-cost retail,
subtract markdowns from goods available at retail before calculating the
cost-to-retail ratio.
The smaller retail denominator produces a higher ratio:
each dollar of the reduced selling price now represents more cost.
Under average-cost retail,
divide goods available at cost by original retail value minus markdowns.
Markdowns reduce the ratio's retail denominator.
Under conventional retail,
exclude markdowns from the ratio calculation but subtract them when
determining ending inventory at retail.
The ratio therefore does not rise to offset the lower retail prices.
Applying that ratio to the reduced retail value produces a lower inventory
amount, which is how the method approximates a decline in value.
Under conventional retail,
divide goods available at cost by original retail value.
Exclude markdowns from the ratio denominator.
For both methods,
subtract markdowns and net sales to determine the retail value remaining.
Use the cost-to-retail ratio for the selected method.
These formulas assume no other price changes or inventory movements.
For either method,
ending inventory at retail equals original retail value minus markdowns and
net sales.
Then multiply that ending retail amount by the selected cost-to-retail ratio.
Suppose Second Helping has goods available costing 60,000 dollars, with
original retail prices totaling 100,000 dollars.
It records permanent markdowns of 20,000 dollars and net sales of 40,000

videos.full_text: You are listening to Chapter 18 of the A C C 300 course reading. Second Helping supplies fictional kitchenware examples of inventory estimates and operating analysis. We will use gross profit and retail records to estimate inventory, then connect inventory, customer collection, and supplier payment. Pause at each question before hearing its answer. All company amounts are fictional teaching inputs in United States dollars. A company's inventory records may show what it purchased and sold without establishing exactly what remains on hand. When a physical count is unavailable, information about sales, costs, and selling prices can provide an estimate. But the result is only as reliable as the relationships used to calculate it. A change in selling prices or the mix of products sold, for example, can make a mathematically correct calculation misleading. Inventory also affects how long a company must finance its operations. Cash may be tied up in goods awaiting sale and in receivables awaiting collection, while credit from suppliers delays the need to pay for purchases. The cash conversion cycle combines these periods to help explain how operating decisions affect the timing of cash flows. When an inventory estimate is useful. A company may need to determine its inventory balance before it can complete a physical count. In other situations, such as a fire, some goods may no longer be available to count. Even when a physical count is possible, it establishes quantities, not necessarily ownership or cost. Inventory estimates offer another way to approximate the cost of goods on hand using available accounting information. Two common approaches are the gross-profit method, which uses sales and an assumed gross profit margin, and the retail inventory method, which uses records maintained at both cost and retail selling prices. Neither requires the company to identify and cost every individual item remaining in inventory. Management may use an estimate to monitor monthly operations, prepare interim financial statements, or assess inventory destroyed in a fire. The reporting rules differ between the two methods. A S C Topic 270, Subtopic 10, Section 45, paragraph 6(a) allows companies to use the gross-profit method for interim reports, such as quarterly statements, even when they use another method at year-end. Companies must disclose the interim method and any significant adjustments from reconciling the estimates with the annual physical inventory. The gross-profit method is not a regular year-end inventory valuation method. The retail inventory method can be used for both interim and annual reports under A S C Topic 330, Subtopic 10, Section 30, paragraph 13. It works best for goods with similar gross profit margins and requires reliable cost and selling-price records. The later retail-method section explains how those records support the estimate. Check your understanding. Which inventory estimation method can a company use for regular annual reporting: gross-profit or retail? Pause to answer. Answer. The retail inventory method, when appropriate. The gross-profit method can support interim reports but is not a regular year-end inventory valuation method. The gross-profit method. Refresher: gross profit Review gross profit and gross profit margin in Chapter 6. Chapter 6 introduced gross profit and the gross profit margin when comparing income statements. For a retailer, gross profit is net sales less cost of goods sold. The gross profit margin expresses that profit as a percentage of net sales. Without a reliable ending inventory amount, the company cannot finish calculating current cost of goods sold or gross profit. It therefore estimates the gross profit margin from prior periods, comparable products, or other supporting information. Part of each sales dollar covers the cost of the goods, and the remainder represents gross profit. An assumed profit share lets the company estimate the cost share and then the inventory remaining. Gross profit margin equals gross profit divided by net sales, multiplied by 100 percent. Suppose management estimates gross profit at 32 percent of sales. For each dollar of sales, 32 cents represents gross profit and 68 cents represents the cost of goods sold. If that relationship holds for the current period, the retailer can estimate cost of goods sold from its sales. Estimated cost of goods sold equals net sales multiplied by one minus the assumed gross profit margin. Express the margin as a decimal. The company can then use the inventory relationship from earlier chapters. Goods available for sale must either have been sold or remain in ending inventory, assuming no other inventory movements. Subtracting estimated cost of goods sold from goods available at cost gives estimated ending inventory. Estimated ending inventory equals beginning inventory plus net purchases, minus estimated cost of goods sold. Net sales and net purchases must reflect applicable returns, allowances, and discounts, with qualifying freight included in purchase cost. Inventory costs and transactions must also be recorded in the correct periods. A monthly inventory estimate. Assume that Second Helping begins March 2026 with inventory of 38,600 dollars and net purchases of 115,400 dollars. Net sales are 168,000 dollars. Based on comparable products and recent selling prices, management supports an estimated gross profit margin of 32.00 percent of sales. No other inventory movements apply. For the March estimate, beginning inventory is 38,600 dollars and net purchases are 115,400 dollars. Together they supply 154,000 dollars of goods available at cost. Net sales are 168,000 dollars. Multiply sales by the 32 percent gross profit margin to estimate profit of 53,760 dollars. Subtract that profit from sales. Estimated cost of goods sold is one hundred fourteen thousand two hundred forty dollars. Subtract that expense from available cost for ending inventory of 39,760 dollars. Check your understanding. Why would multiplying goods available for sale by the 32 percent gross profit margin give an incorrect estimate of ending inventory? Pause to answer. Answer. The 32 percent gross profit margin describes gross profit relative to sales, not ending inventory relative to goods available for sale. metadata.title: The Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) Explained | Formula, Working Capital & Cash Flow Mastery
metadata.author: One Minute Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to Lecture 14, where we break down one of the most powerful financial and operational metrics in business: The Cash Conversion Cycle, widely known as the CCC. Understanding how many days it takes for every dollar invested in inventory and daily operations to convert back into cash in your bank account is essential for founders, financial analysts, accountants, and business operators. In this comprehensive session, we explain the exact mechanics of the #CashConversionCycle and why mastering #WorkingCapital is the key to scaling a business sustainably without running into liquidity crunches. Even a business that looks profitable on paper can struggle to survive if its cash is tied up in slow-moving inventory or overdue customer invoices, making #CashFlowManagement a vital skill across every industry.

Throughout this lecture, we walk step by step through the three core pillars of the CCC formula: Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO), Days Sales Outstanding (DSO), and Days Payable Outstanding (DPO). You will learn how to calculate each component accurately, interpret what a shortening or lengthening cycle signals about a company's financial health, and pinpoint exactly where cash bottlenecks are hiding. Building on our comparison of modern business models, we also explore how top-performing #ECommerce brands and #SaaS companies optimize their customer billing, inventory turnover, and vendor payment terms to achieve a negative cash conversion cycle—effectively using customer payments to finance their own growth. By applying these proven frameworks in #FinancialAnalysis, #BusinessFinance, and #UnitEconomics, you can unlock trapped cash and strengthen operational efficiency.

Make sure to watch this entire lesson and take notes on the actionable levers you can pull to speed up collections, streamline inventory, and negotiate better supplier terms. If you gained value from #Lecture14, hit the like button, subscribe to the channel, and turn on notifications so you never miss an upcoming lesson in our complete course series. Share your biggest takeaway or drop any questions about the CCC formula in the comments below, and pass this video along to anyone learning #AccountingAndFinance and #BusinessStrategy.

Plenty of ecommerce businesses are profitable on paper but still stressed about cash. The cash conversion cycle explains why, and what you can do about it.

🔗 Inventory Reality Check Diagnostic (find the cash stuck in your inventory): https://ledgergurus.com/resources/assessment/inventory-reality-check/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cash-conversion-cycle

In this video, we break down the cash conversion cycle as a cash survival tool, not just an accounting concept. You'll learn how long your cash gets stuck before it comes back to you, why fast growth can make cash worse, and how real ecommerce businesses shorten the cycle without chasing more sales.

- Why profit does not equal cash in ecommerce
- What the cash conversion cycle actually measures, in plain English
- How inventory, payouts, and supplier terms trap cash
- The three parts of the cycle: inventory time, payout time, and payment timing
- Why wholesale and Amazon change your cash picture fast
- Real examples of brands growing revenue while cash shrinks
- How companies like Dell and Costco use cash speed to their advantage
- Simple ways to improve cash flow without increasing sales

metadata.title: Cash Conversion Cycle - Meaning, Formula, Calculation & Interpretations
metadata.author: WallStreetMojo
metadata.shortDescription:
Download Ratio Analysis Template - https://tinyurl.com/ratio-analysis-template-wsm

In this cash conversion cycle tutorial, we'll go over the finer details of what it means,  its formula and step-by-step calculations. Following that, we will calculate the cash conversion cycle using the Colgate Case Study and interpret the findings. 

What is Cash Conversion Cycle?
--------------------------------------------
The cash conversion cycle measures the time it takes for a company to turn its inventory and other inputs into cash. It takes into account how much time the company needs to sell inventory, collect receivables, and pay its bills. 

Formula
--------------------------------------------
Cash Conversion Cycle Formula = Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) – Days Payable Outstanding (DPO)

 Interpretation of Cash Conversion Cycle 
--------------------------------------------
- A shorter cash conversion cycle is beneficial to a company since it allows it to buy, sell, and receive cash from customers more quickly and vice versa.
For more details, you can refer to our article - https://www.wallstreetmojo.com/cash-conversion-cycle/

metadata.title: What is the Cash Conversion Cycle?
metadata.author: Marketing Business Network
metadata.shortDescription:
The cash conversion cycle measures the time a business's money is tied up between paying for inventory and collecting customer cash. An imagined lamp batch spends 40 days in stock, takes another 20 days to collect, and comes with 30 days to pay the supplier.

Follow the 30-day funding gap and the formula: inventory days plus collection days minus supplier payment days. The video covers company averages, agreed payment terms and negative cycles, while keeping cash timing separate from profit and the ability to pay every bill.

Sources:
BDC: the cash conversion cycle
https://www.bdc.ca/en/articles-tools/money-finance/manage-finances/how-boost-cash-flow
Export Development Canada: cash conversion cycles
https://www.edc.ca/content/dam/edc/en/non-premium/ungated/guide/cash-conversion-cycles-edc-report.pdf
RBC: working capital management
https://www.rbcroyalbank.com/business/paying-and-receiving/my-payments-playbook/working-capital-management.html

Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCI8Xs2oPTMb9DkuYsEqCnnQ/join

#CashConversionCycle #WorkingCapital #CashFlow

segments.text: What is the cash conversion cycle?
The cash conversion cycle measures how many days a
business's money is tied up between paying for inventory
and collecting cash from selling it.
It tracks the waiting time behind a sale.
A business may hold products before selling them, then
wait for customers to pay.
Suppliers may also give it time to pay their
bills. The cycle combines those three pieces of timing.
Imagine a small company buying a batch of lamps
for resale. The lamps arrive on day zero, but
its supplier allows thirty days before payment is due.
Cash has not left yet.
The lamps stay in stock for forty days before
the company sells and delivers them.
That is forty days of inventory holding time, measured
from receiving the batch to making the sale.
The customer then takes another twenty days to pay.
The company receives the money on day sixty.
Selling the lamps on day forty did not immediately
put cash into its account.
Meanwhile, the company paid its supplier on day thirty,
as agreed. It had to fund the period from
day thirty until day sixty, when the customer money
finally arrived in its account.
That gap is thirty days.
You can calculate it by adding forty days of
inventory time and twenty days waiting for customer payment,
then subtracting the supplier's thirty days of payment time.
The supplier's allowance is subtracted because the company did
not have to pay immediately when the lamps arrived.
Part of the holding and collection period was financed
by the agreed supplier terms.
For a whole company, the calculation normally uses average
days for inventory, customer collection, and supplier payment.
Our single batch makes the timing visible, but real
businesses have many overlapping orders.
A shorter cycle can free cash sooner.
The lamp company could sell stock faster or collect
customer payments earlier.
Longer supplier terms can also help, if the supplier
agrees to them.
Simply paying late is different from negotiating more time.
Missed deadlines may damage relationships or bring charges.
Likewise, keeping too little stock can leave customers waiting
and cost the company sales.
Some businesses collect customer money before they pay suppliers,
producing a negative cash conversion cycle.
That describes payment timing, not a loss.
The business may have cash arriving before its related
inventory bill falls due.
The cycle does not measure profit or guarantee that
every bill can be paid.
The lamp company still needs a cash forecast covering
wages, rent, taxes, and other commitments while its sales
are turning into cash.
Thanks for watching Marketing Business Network.

metadata.title: You’re Not Broke, Your Cash Is Just Stuck (Cash Conversion Cycle Explained)
metadata.author: Kurtis Hanni
metadata.shortDescription:
Most businesses don’t fail because they aren’t profitable.
They fail because they run out of cash.

In this video, I break down the Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) — one of the most important, and most misunderstood, metrics in business.

You’ll learn:
- What the cash conversion cycle actually is (in plain English)
- How cash moves through your business in a loop
- Why long cash cycles choke growth
- How one company reduced their CCC from 230 days to 45 days
- How that change freed up over $168,000 in cash without increasing profit

I’m opening enrollment for my next cohort where we work hands-on to increase your profits and put more cash in your pocket.
