metadata.title: AI for "where is my order" tickets in Gorgias
metadata.author: Macha
metadata.shortDescription:
An AI agent can answer "where is my order" tickets inside Gorgias from your Shopify store. It reads the ticket, looks up
the order in Shopify, checks the email on the order matches the person asking, and replies with what the order shows.
This video walks through each case on an invented store.

What Gorgias does on its own (gorgias.com and docs.gorgias.com, checked 13 November 2026):
- Shopify integration, on every helpdesk plan: the shopper's orders in the ticket sidebar with fulfilment status.
- Intents and rules: order questions get the Order::Status intent; a rule can tag them and send them to a view.
- Macros: fill in Shopify details, but read the customer's most recent order.
- Gorgias AI Agent: resolves order tracking questions on email, chat, SMS and social. $0.90 per automated interaction on
  annual plans, $1.00 on monthly, $1.50 above the plan allowance; each one also counts as a helpdesk ticket. If you want
  one vendor across every channel, it's the simpler route.

How the AI agent handles each case:
1. Finding the order: by the order number in the ticket (Shopify Get order), or by the customer's email and their recent
   orders. It checks the email matches before sharing anything.
2. Shipped: replies with the carrier, tracking number and tracking link saved in Shopify, for the order asked about. It
   can follow the wording of your Gorgias macros, and tags the ticket so you can build a view. It doesn't guess a
   delivery date; for live carrier status, our team connects your tracking app during setup.
3. Not shipped yet: checks your shipping window in the knowledge base and says when the order should leave.
4. Fulfilled with no tracking: says it has shipped, raises the priority and tags it for a teammate.
5. Late: past your limit, it apologises and assigns the ticket to your fulfilment team with a note.
6. Different email: shares no order details and asks for the checkout email. Several orders: lists each open one.

When a person takes over: delivered but not received, damaged or wrong items, address changes, cancelled or refunded
orders, angry customers and chargeback mentions. The agent leaves a note and assigns the ticket to the right team.

Cost: Macha's team sets it up (20-minute call, help desk analysis, knowledge base from your help centre, website,
documents and past replies, Gorgias and Shopify, your rules, testing on past order tickets, safe mode with internal notes
until about 9 in 10 drafts are approved, a bar agreed with your team). Setup is included in every plan, no setup fee. From $299 a
month for 750 tickets, about $0.40 a ticket; one ticket is one charge however many replies it takes. 1,500 $599 · 3,000
$1,199 · 5,000 $1,999 · 7,500 $2,999 · 10,000 $3,999. Free trial: $50 of usage, no card. Most teams have their first
category live within a week.

Full written guide: https://www.getmacha.com/blog/auto-resolve-wismo-in-gorgias-with-ai
Done-for-you setup: https://www.getmacha.com/done-for-you

segments.text: Gorgias AI is the AI Agent built into the Gorgias help desk for Shopify stores.
It answers support questions and helps shoppers buy.
Gorgias charges for each automated interaction: a dollar each on monthly billing,
90 cents on annual, and a dollar 50 past your plan's allowance.
You set it up yourself.
If you'd rather keep Gorgias, pay per ticket and have it set up for you,
the better option is Macha, an AI agent that runs inside your Gorgias help desk.
Our team builds it for you.
Setup is included on every plan with no setup fee,
from $299 a month for 750 tickets.
Prefer to build it yourself?
Start the free trial, and we'll help if you get stuck.
Gorgias prices checked on the 20th of November 2026.
Gorgias calls its current version AI Agent 3.0.
It has two jobs.
As a support agent, it answers questions like "where's my order" and "can I return
this", and it can take actions in Shopify, such as cancelling an order or applying a
discount.
As a Shopping Assistant, it answers questions before a sale,
recommends products and adds items to the cart.
It replies on email, live chat, SMS, Instagram,
Facebook Messenger and WhatsApp.
You need a Shopify store connected to Gorgias to use it.
Gorgias says it automates up to 60% of customer conversations.
Gorgias automation is the scripted side, with no AI writing the reply.
Rules run inside the help desk: when a ticket matches a condition,
they tag it, assign it or send a reply.
Flows are scripted, step-by-step answers a shopper clicks through,
mostly in chat.
Order Management lets shoppers track, return or cancel an order themselves.
Quick Responses used to be a separate feature.
In 2024 Gorgias turned them into one-step Flows.
The billing ties them together.
When a Flow or Order Management resolves a request with no person involved,
it counts as an automated interaction, the same as an AI Agent resolution,
and it comes out of the same allowance.
A message sent by a rule counts as a help desk ticket.
Your team builds it in Gorgias, in seven steps.
Give it access to your Shopify data.
Add knowledge: guidance you write, your help centre articles,
your website, public pages and documents.
Create skills, which decide which conversations it handles.
Add actions if you want it to do things in Shopify,
though you can go live without them.
Set the tone and the handover rules.
Test it in the Playground, where test conversations aren't billed.
Then switch it on for each channel.
Gorgias says you can be live in under an hour.
That first hour gets it running.
Writing the guidance, adding skills for each topic and testing them is ongoing work
for your team.
Past tickets aren't a knowledge source, so it learns your policies from what you
write.
A dedicated success manager depends on your annual Shopify sales.
Gorgias sells the help desk and AI Agent together,
priced by tickets, never per seat.
Billed monthly, Starter is $40 with 50 tickets and 30 automated interactions.
Basic is 90, with 300 tickets and 30 interactions.
Pro is 550, with 2,000 tickets and 190 interactions.
Advanced is 1,430, with 5,000 tickets and 530 interactions.
On Pro, 190 of the $550 is the AI Agent part,
which works out at a dollar an interaction.
Past the allowance, each one costs a dollar 50.
When AI Agent resolves a ticket on its own,
you pay the automation fee, and the ticket also counts toward your help desk plan.
If one of your agents replies within 72 hours,
it's charged only as a ticket.
The trial is seven days, with no card, and no setup fee is listed.
Here's our maths for two invented stores, assuming AI Agent resolves 30% of tickets.
A store with 1,000 tickets a month is on Pro.
300 resolutions is 110 past the allowance, which adds $165.
The month comes to 715.
A store with 5,000 tickets is on Advanced.
1,500 resolutions is 970 past the allowance,
which adds 1,455.
The month comes to 2,885.
The AI part of the bill grows with every resolution.
At 50%, the larger store's AI part goes from about $2,000 to 3,485.
For most Gorgias stores, it's Macha.
Macha is ours.
It runs inside the Gorgias help desk you already have,
so you keep your Gorgias plan and your inbox.
It reads each ticket, looks up the order in Shopify,
and replies or leaves an internal note.
The work around the AI is the main difference.
Our team builds the knowledge from your help centre,
website, documents and your past replies.
Then we run a Simulation on your past tickets.
It shows what the agent would have replied and done,
and posts nothing to your help desk.
It goes live in safe mode, as internal notes your team approves,
until it reaches the bar you agree with us,
about nine in 10 drafts approved.
After launch, a success manager tunes it and adds the next topic.
Macha charges about 40 cents for each ticket it works,
and one ticket is one charge however many replies it takes.
Using the same Gorgias plan, at 5,000 tickets Macha is $1,999,
level with Gorgias's AI part at 30% resolved,
and lower above it.
At 1,000 tickets, Gorgias's AI part costs less unless it resolves close to half.
Gorgias suits you if you want one vendor and one bill,
a Shopping Assistant that sells in chat, or to pay only when the AI resolves.
Our team builds it for you.
Book a 20-minute call.
We analyse your help desk, build the knowledge,
connect Shopify and the other systems the agent needs,
run a Simulation on your past tickets and go live in safe mode.
Setup is included on every plan with no setup fee,
from $299 a month for 750 tickets.
We reply within 24 hours and work to resolve your issue as fast as we can,
on email, a shared Slack channel or WhatsApp.
Prefer to build it yourself?
Start the free trial at getmacha.com, and we'll help if you get stuck.

metadata.shortDescription:
❓ What is it: Customer Service Platform

🏅 Differentiator: Gorgias is a customer service platform that allows you to automate frequent tickets, drive sales through the chat functionality, and unify all customer communications. With the many Shopify app integrations available, it allows for a 360-degree view of the customer needing support.

💰 Starting Price: $60/month

🚀 How we use it: For Customer Service
1️⃣ Live chat on site
2️⃣ All customer service interactions (Facebook/Instagram, emails, SMS messages, etc.)
3️⃣ Set up rules to automate the customer service process
4️⃣ Create premade macros to streamline customer service responses

You can learn more about and download the app here: https://gorgias.grsm.io/brandon

Sign-up for my weekly newsletter here! https://brandonamoroso.com/pages/weekly-newsletter-sign-up

My proven e-commerce strategies focus on increasing customer lifetime value and cultivating best-in-class consumer experiences. This model has successfully scaled early-stage start-ups, Fortune 1000 companies, and everything in between. 💸

As a Gen Z entrepreneur, my business approach focuses on creating empowered and thriving teams as a key driver of business success. My entrepreneurial endeavors work to break the mold and create innovation for clients and their customers. 🎆

I continue to serve the marketplace as an advisor for business growth and how to build direct access to customers for long-term business success in an uncertain environment. 💡

metadata.title: Helping an E-Commerce Brand Doing $5M/Year Scale
metadata.author: MoreMozi
metadata.shortDescription:
Download your free scaling roadmap here: https://www.acquisition.com/roadmap?el=yt-alex-highlights-oldcat-roadmap-202610&htrafficsource=youtube&utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=moremozi&utm_campaign=oldcatalog-202610&utm_content=scaling-roadmap

Business owners: Want to scale faster? We provide in-person advisory for companies doing at least $1M per year: https://www.acquisition.com/workshop-yt-d?el=yt-alex-highlights-oldcat-workshop-202610&htrafficsource=youtube&utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=moremozi&utm_campaign=oldcatalog-202610&utm_content=scaling-workshop

If you're new to my channel, my name is Alex Hormozi. I'm the founder and managing partner of Acquisition.com. It's a family office, which is just a formal way of saying we invest our own money into companies. Our 10 portfolio companies bring in over $250,000,000+ per year. Our ownership stake varies between 20% and 100% of them. Given this is a YT channel, and anyone can claim anything, I'll give you some stuff you can google to verify below.

How I got here…

21: Graduated Vanderbilt in 3 years Magna Cum Laude, and took a fancy consulting job.
23 yrs old: Left my fancy consulting job to start a business (a gym).
24 yrs old: Open 5 gym locations.
26 yrs old: Closed down 6th gym. Lost everything.
26 yrs old: Got back to launching gyms (launched 33). Then, lost everything for a 2nd time.
26 yrs old: In desperation, started licensing model as a hail mary. It worked.
27 yrs old: "Gym Launch" does $3M profit the next 6 months. Then $17M profit next 12 months.
28 yrs old: Started Prestige Labs. $20M the first year.
29 yrs old: Launched ALAN, a software company for agencies to work leads for customers. Scaled to $1.7mmo within 6 months.
31 yrs old: Sold 75% of UseAlan to a strategic buyer in an all stock deal.
31 yrs old: Sold 66% of Gym Launch & Prestige Labs at $46.2M valuation in all-cash deal to American Pacific Group. (you can google it)
31 yrs old: Started our family office Acquisition.com. We invest and scale companies using the $42M in distributions we had taken + the cash from the $46.2M exit.
32 yrs old: Started making free content showing how we grow companies to make real business education accessible to everyone (and) to attract business owners to invest or scale their businesses.
34 yrs old: I became co-owner of https://Skool.com to help the many people who want to start a business online do so.

Today: Our portfolio now does $200M/yr between 10 companies. The largest doing $100M/yr the smallest doing $5M per year. Our ownership varies between 20% and 100% ownership of the companies. Many of them we invested in early and helped grow (which is how we make our money - not youtube videos).

To all the gladiators in the arena, we're all in the middle of writing our own stories. The worse the monsters, the more epic the story.

You either get an epic outcome or an epic story. Both mean you win.

Keep crushing. May your desires be greater than your obstacles.

Never quit,

Alex

DISCLOSURE
Information shared here is for educational purposes only. Individuals and business owners should evaluate their own business strategies, and identify any potential risks. The information shared here is not a guarantee of success. Your results may vary.
Copyright © 2026.

Learn how successful e-commerce entrepreneurs think about growth, customer acquisition, offers, operations, and long-term business success. Alex breaks down practical insights that can help store owners avoid common mistakes and focus on what actually drives results.

metadata.author: Nick Theriot
metadata.shortDescription:
🏆 Have Nick Theriot Run Your Ads: https://www.theriotsolutions.com

💰 Have Nick Theriot Mentor You: https://theriotsolutions.com/innercircle


Every Level of Scaling an ECOM Brand ($0, $30k, $100k, $1m, $10m)

In this video, I walk you through every level of scaling Facebook ads for ecommerce brands, from zero to ten million dollars a month in revenue.

I explain how to move from offer validation at 0 to 30k a month, to channel expansion at 60k, and effort expansion at 100k to 200k, including budgets, creatives, landing pages, and the exact Facebook ads structure I use.

You’ll see how I think about CAC, LTV, and first-time customer ROAS as we scale to 500k to 1 million a month with product expansion, then 1 to 2 million a month with geo expansion using multi-store Shopify setups across countries like the USA, UK, Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, and the Netherlands.

I also show what it takes to become a true market leader at 5 to 10 million a month with multi-channel ads, Google Ads, paid influencers, retail expansion, and how this positions you for a big exit while building a long-term, scalable ecommerce brand.


💬 Nick’s Free Community Chat: https://t.me/+xGoAtUWhC7hlMWMx

📸 Follow Me On Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/nicktheriot_/

***

Hey! If you’re new to the channel, my name is Nick Theriot

I’ve been running Facebook ads since 2015 and have done over $50m in revenue for our clients. We work with a variety of brands, but the majority are e-commerce! 


#Facebookads #facebookadvertising #facebookmarketing

***

-Nick Theriot

Most ecommerce brands are looking at the wrong numbers.

ROAS alone won’t tell you if your business is actually healthy, scalable or profitable.

In this video, I break down the 5 financial metrics we look at before scaling any ecommerce brand:

• Contribution Margin
• Blended CAC
• CAC Payback Period
• 60-90 Day LTV
• MER (Marketing Efficiency Ratio)

These are the numbers that determine:

* how profitable your growth really is
* how quickly you recover cash
* how aggressive you can scale
* how efficient your acquisition system is
* whether your business model actually works at scale

Across the brands we work with at Leading Social, we manage over nine figures a year in ecommerce revenue and these are the metrics we consistently use to make scaling decisions.

If you run a Shopify or ecommerce brand and want to scale with more clarity, this video will help you understand the financial side of growth far beyond platform ROAS.

Topics covered:
Meta Ads
Google Ads
Ecommerce scaling
CAC & LTV
Contribution Margin
MER
Financial forecasting
Profit-first growth
Shopify growth strategy

With this in mind, we built the 'E-Commerce Growth Checklist' to help brands find their hidden bottlenecks. It's a list of 44 questions across Creative, Acquisition, Retention, and Data that reveal exactly where you're leaking growth.

metadata.title: Scaling Creative Brands Through Operations
metadata.author: Frankly eCommerce
metadata.shortDescription:
How does a bedroom art passion project scale into a full warehouse and a 40-convention schedule without losing its creative spark?   

Host Patrick sits down with Emlynn Jones and her dad Randy Jones of Milky Tomato to explore how creative vision and operational discipline come together. From daily content and new product drops to four-character inventory codes, pick-and-pack accuracy, conventions, and wholesale, they share how they stay aligned as a family and grow through steady, incremental improvements.   

Are you putting systems in place to support your creative momentum, or letting operational friction slow down your growth?   


Join the discussion on Frankly E-commerce.

In this episode you'll find: 
00:00 – From Bedroom Art to Warehouse Ops: Welcome to Milky Tomato   
04:55 – Manufacturer Timelines, Four-Character Codes & Pick-and-Pack Accuracy   
09:22 – Running 40+ Conventions a Year & Booth Sizes   
15:07 – Program Sponsor Ad Break: Alia
17:39 – Live Customer Feedback at Conventions   
19:14 – Retail Dreams, Wholesale Growth & Measuring Fulfillment Efficiency   
25:23 – Family Dynamics, Protecting Creative Focus & Choosing Not to Outsource to a 3PL   
33:01 – AI vs. Systems Thinking, Incremental Progress & Wrapping Up

It's just again, it's one of those things where we just have to be patient with ourselves and keep reminding ourselves, hey, we're we're crazy busy doing all these inventory or all these conventions and and such and so some of the products are are our solutions are growing slower than we'd like ideally, but it's just the reality of where we're at. We got to keep keep moving the machine forward. We can't stop, take a break and say, okay, for a couple of months, we're not going to do any conventions or fulfill any orders so we can build this great system. We don't have that luxury and we just have to keep incrementally improving and like I said, being patient with ourselves. I guess that's I have to be patient with myself. It's it's very hard sometimes we're getting going. I'm not getting this done fast enough and it's like, well, it it's progressing. Things are progressing. >> And then would you add anything to what he said or how do you we're we're wrapping up here in our last bit of the conversation. What I've heard Randy describe is this incremental approach, acknowledging progress, but not striving for perfection and knowing that you can come back and iterate again and again. At the same time, you're being, you know, practical because you got to get sales now and you can't wait until it's perfect. Anything you would speak to or add to that as you or maybe if you've observed over the last several years? >> Um yeah, I mean from from the very start of my business, I didn't fully know what I was doing, but I knew that I that the sooner I started, the sooner I could learn and improve it. Um I and like similarly, there have been things like that in the past where I had like delayed it or been like, okay, I need to learn every aspect of this so that I can do it correctly the first time. Um but with the business, um it started in in an imperfect way and we've learned so much and while we still make mistakes, it's just just as um my dad said, it's something that we're always striving to improve instead of um letting it delay us. We of course have um you know, we have a threshold that that we are we're not going to just be like, you know what, let's make listings and sell like 50 products that I haven't even created yet and then we'll just figure it out. Like we we definitely have um like a good balance between a system that we know works and um when we don't fully know how we're going to do things, we still keep it moving forward without using it as an excuse to just not do it. Um and yeah, that's something that's just always been part of our small business and as I talk to other people with small business businesses, it's the exact same way. So that's definitely been a core part of running a small business from from my perspective. It's just like seeing where we mess up and seeing how we can improve it um just over time. >> Well, that's a universal bit of wisdom for any business owner. Find incremental ways to get better and know that you're kind of making it up as you go along. You couldn't do any more than what you already already learning as you go. metadata.title: Scaling an Ecommerce Brand Is Hard Until You Understand These 3 Systems
metadata.author: Noah Haynes
metadata.shortDescription:
Get a free retention audit for your brand: https://yt.duhretention.com/how-to-scale

Grab The Welcome Series Guide: https://go.duhretention.com/welcome-flow-masterclass/

Our Website: https://www.duhretention.com/

Scaling an ecommerce brand can be hard, and it's usually for a reason nobody talks about. 

In this video, I'm breaking down the three systems sitting underneath every ecom brand that grows quickly, and why scaling an ecommerce brand gets a lot simpler once all three are actually running.

I've watched brands with incredible products hit the same revenue ceiling over and over, and I've watched others blow straight through it. 

The product was never the difference. It came down to these three growth pillars, and how each one changes the way you approach scaling an ecommerce brand and where you spend your time.

If you're running a Shopify store, building a DTC brand, or you're an ecommerce marketer trying to figure out why growth went flat, this is the ecommerce growth strategy breakdown for you. 

Scaling an ecommerce brand is really about knowing which systems actually move the number and that’s what this video is about. 

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If you're new to the channel, my name's Noah. I'm the founder of Duh Retention, a retention and lifecycle marketing agency that works with DTC Shopify brands doing $10M–$150M/year in revenue.

Here's how I got here…

18 yrs old: Sold my first brand for $22K. Nothing crazy, but it paid off college tuition + got me hooked on marketing.

19–22 yrs old: Launched 15+ brands. Every single one failed at some level. Some broke even, most lost money. Burned through roughly $150K figuring out what didn't work. While freelancing in growth marketing, CRO, and funnel building, I stumbled on retention marketing. It's the first thing that truly clicked. 

I build email marketing out as a service for an Inc 500 marketing agency, then made the leap to build my own agency.

22–25 yrs old: Went all-in. Turned the hard lessons from my own failed brands into a valuable skill set for growing brands. 

Built Duh Retention into a boutique agency working with 12 DTC brands doing $10M–$150M/year...Helping them retain customers, grow repeat revenue, and build out truly valuable lifecycle programs.

A few things worth knowing about me:

I built this agency without outside funding, a large following, or a famous last name. Just a lot of failed brands, a lot of client work, and a genuine obsession with what makes customers stay hooked onto a brand for life.

segments.text: What do we commerce brands like this,
this, and this have [music] in common?
Well, for one, they've all scaled to
over 100 million in revenue. But more
importantly, they all followed the same
three-step playbook to get there. See,
after studying hundreds, if not
thousands of D2C brands, I've realized
[music]
every single one nails these three
steps, while the losers usually don't
even know what they are. That's why in
this video, I'm going to break down each
one, because the brands that are scaling
the fastest aren't necessarily just
running more ads or converting more
traffic. They're using a playbook that
makes it almost impossible to lose. Now,
the first thing they nail is the market
The market you choose to play in is the
single biggest determiner of how high
you can peak once you succeed. You can
be the best operator alive with the best
product and the best ads in the game.
But if you niche down too hard, you're
going to hit a ceiling of who you can
sell to. That ceiling is known as your
TAM, or your total addressable market.
Basically, the total amount of people
who would ever realistically buy from
you. And the reason I'm talking about
this in the first place is because TAM
can be pretty deceptive when you're just
getting off the ground. At first, it
feels great because you're converting
people left and right because your
content, messaging, and product are all
honed in to one avatar. But once a year
or two passes, and you've already
reached everybody you could hit within
your budget, things start to go
sideways. Suddenly, you have to pay a
lot more and work a lot harder to find
new people to sell your core product to,
which ultimately slows your growth.
That's why you need to choose a market
that's big enough to let you find unique
pools of customers without having to
create one-off products that don't truly
scale. Take Hold Socks for example. They
sell compression socks. That's a
multi-billion-dollar market, which
obviously, the TAM there is big enough.
They just needed a way to break into it.
And they did it with a pack of fur. They
chose a premium quality material that is
just niche enough to be unique, but
doesn't affect the core market or core
audience. Then, instead of focusing on
the biggest segment of the market, socks
for medical purposes, they targeted
hikers first. Then they moved on to
runners. They sold the exact same
product. All that changed was the
marketing and the angle of who they
decided to speak to. Now, most people
would have looked at the compression
sock market and thought it was saturated
with competition. But most of the time,
having a lot of brands in a market is
actually a good signal. Think about all
the tumbler brands out there. Stanley,
Hydro Flask, Simple Modern, even all the
Target knockoffs. Every single dollar
each of these brands spends convincing
people they need an indestructible,
BPA-free tumbler benefits every single
water bottle brand in the world. So, if
the market is active and growing, even
your competitors ads can boost your
sales in the long run. That's why it's
vital to check for market growth before
you ever even think about product. And
there are three levels to it. At a high
level, you look at broad industry
trends. Is this category as a whole
growing, flatlining, or worse,
declining? Mid-level is where you pull
Google Trends, keyword volume, Ahrefs,
and Shopify spy tools to see whether
demand and search interest has been
climbing over the last few years and is
sustaining. And then at the bottom
level, it's good to do a lightweight gut
check by looking at the ads and websites
of brands that have been around for the
last 12 to 24 months. Because if you
find 50 brands are running ads for
Alaskan cod collagen gummies, at least
you know the market's active. All you
have to do to break through is find a
single niche to target first and slowly
expand over time. So, let's say you
found a big growing market. That brings
us to the second system, your business
model. And this is where you need to
understand unit economics. The first is
your AOV, or average order value, which
is how much your average customer spends
per order. This is the metric that
brands use running regular sales models
to see how much they can actually spend
to acquire new customers and spend on
ads. So, the perceived value of your
core offer has to be high enough to
where the math works out. The second is
your COGS, or your cost of goods. This
is every little thing you spend money on
before the customer ever receives the
product. Your ingredients, your
materials, your pick pack fees, and most
importantly, your shipping costs all
need to bake into your final COGS.
Shipping alone costs brands 20 to 40% of
their total cost depending on their
product size. So, knocking off a few
ounces or pounds will directly impact
your bottom line. If you're not obsessed
with COGS, no amount of clever marketing
will ever get your P&L in a place to
where your brand can actually scale. And
lastly, there's product complexity. This
one's a bit of a double-edged sword,
because on one hand, a simple product,
like a protein or vitamin powder, is
something you can scale in your sleep.
While on the other hand, something like
a Ninja Blender with a hundred tiny
parts can become a manufacturing
nightmare as you grow. More parts means
more suppliers, and more suppliers means
more bottlenecks. However, even though
too much complexity can make your
business model a lot riskier, the right
amount of complexity can become your
killer edge, the thing that makes your
product impossible to copy. Because if
your formula has 20 plus ingredients
that are hyper specific, no copycat can
just go to a contract manufacturer and
copy you overnight. The key is finding a
balance where you can still grow in
profit while being just hard enough to
copy so that you don't lose your
business to the first competitor that
pops up. So, how do you come up with a
product that does both? Simple. Ask
yourself, what's the one thing you would
change to beat what's already out there?
Maybe it's a product that's bigger, one
that's smaller, one that's less messy.
As long as it solves one valuable
problem no one else on the market does,
you've got a winner. Let's take soy
protein powder as an example. A quick
search of brand reviews on Reddit will
tell you that the biggest problem with
soy protein is that it clumps together.
A differentiator here could be as simple
as granulating the powder so it mixes
smoothly. That one fix could win the
market without having to reinvent the
whole category. Now, once you have your
product and the math makes sense, the
only thing that's left is deciding on
the business model itself. And there are
two options here, subscription or
category rich. A subscription model can
be highly profitable when done right,
simply because it's a consumable that
bills on a reliably predictable basis,
so the revenue stacks month after month.
That's why big brands like Pendulum and
Armra lean into it. The only catch is
that it's usually low to mid AOV. On top
of that, everybody's caught on, so there
are thousands of contract manufacturers
ready to give you a perfectly good
protein or collagen powder right off the
shelf, which means you're running into
stiff competition right off the bat.
Category rich is the opposite. It
focuses on developing lots of new
products with buy-again varieties.
Usually, building a brand like this
takes a lot of upfront capital, so there
aren't nearly as many competitors.
However, it's also something you can
grow into over time. Again, let's go
back to the soy protein example. The key
here, if you wanted to make it a
category rich business, is positioning
it as a soy brand, not a soy protein
one. So, over time you can launch soy
protein bars, a soy whey complex, soy
for gut health, and over time you have
an entire range of products that fall
under the soy umbrella. At this point,
you now have the opportunity to upsell,
cross-sell, and reactivate old customers
with something new. All things most
single product subscription brands can't
do. Either way, that brings us to our
final pillar, your acquisition and
retention machine, or how you get and
keep customers. Because most people
these days just index way too hard into
paid ads, but distribution has never
been that simple. To get it right, you
need to know how to match your product
to the channel that actually sells it.
And just as importantly, the kind of
founder you are and the type of content
your team can realistically make. Let's
say you're launching a traveling brand,
but you personally have zero interest
being on camera. Your acquisition
machine probably won't be organic
content. It'll be raising an army of Gen
Z influencers, seeding them product,
sunglasses, and bags so that they can
actually wear it on the coast of Italy
and Montenegro, letting them be the face
of the brand. But, what if you are the
founder that loves travel and doesn't
mind being on camera? Well, then you can
fly to Italy, you can shoot the content,
and do all the behind the scenes
yourself. In both of these scenarios,
it's the same product and same brand.
The only different is the temperament of
the founder and what you actually are
willing to do. And you can see a prime
example of this in a category that I
talked about earlier in the video.
Remember those Tumblr brands? Same
products, same market, but two brands in
the same category went totally different
directions. Simple Modern won on Amazon
and wholesale with tight unit economics
and barely any paid ads. On the other
hand, FrostBuddy hit over 70 million in
under 3 years, ripping TikTok organic
daily, purely because the founder Brock
was willing to be on camera and do this
kind of content every single day. So,
the honest questions you have to ask
are, do you have the funds to seed
product? Are you willing to shoot
organic content? And no matter what
distribution channel you choose, do you
have the right incentive structures in
place to make it successful? Because if
you want real natural affiliates and not
the black hat guys chasing payouts, you
have to build a product people genuinely
want to get behind. Look at a brand like
Comfort. The founder Hudson is super
involved with their affiliate marketing.
He's in Discord going live every week
talking to his affiliates directly,
hyping up a room of 18 to 24 year olds
to go make more content so they can
solve anxiety. You can't fake that
energy. So running an Amazon FBA brand
with a white label product you just
slightly improved is not going to work
the same way that Comfort does. And
that's not to say that an FBA brand
can't win. You just have to be brutally
honest about what category you're in,
what makes you special, and how are you
going to go to market. Because in the
end, there's a whole spectrum of
distribution types, product types, and
founder types that when combined in a
certain way only work when you commit to
it. Now, with that said, getting
customers is only half of the machine.
Because if the only way you ever get a
buyer is having to pay for an ad or pay
for an affiliate, you're renting every
single customer. And the day you stop is
the day they vanish, which is why the
second half is finding a cheap, reliable
way to re-engage, reactivate, and pull
customers back without paying the full
price to acquire them again. And it
really comes down to three mechanisms.
First is your welcome pop-up. This is a
form that lets you capture the details
of people who are coming on your website

But more importantly, they all followed the same three-step playbook to get there. See, after studying hundreds, if not thousands of D2C brands, I've realized [music] every single one nails these three steps, while the losers usually don't even know what they are. That's why in this video, I'm going to break down each one, because the brands that are scaling the fastest aren't necessarily just running more ads or converting more traffic. They're using a playbook that makes it almost impossible to lose. Now, the first thing they nail is the market The market you choose to play in is the single biggest determiner of how high you can peak once you succeed. You can be the best operator alive with the best product and the best ads in the game. But if you niche down too hard, you're going to hit a ceiling of who you can sell to. That ceiling is known as your TAM, or your total addressable market. Basically, the total amount of people who would ever realistically buy from you. And the reason I'm talking about this in the first place is because TAM can be pretty deceptive when you're just getting off the ground. At first, it feels great because you're converting people left and right because your content, messaging, and product are all honed in to one avatar. But once a year or two passes, and you've already reached everybody you could hit within your budget, things start to go sideways. Suddenly, you have to pay a lot more and work a lot harder to find new people to sell your core product to, which ultimately slows your growth. That's why you need to choose a market that's big enough to let you find unique pools of customers without having to create one-off products that don't truly scale. Take Hold Socks for example. While on the other hand, something like a Ninja Blender with a hundred tiny parts can become a manufacturing nightmare as you grow. More parts means more suppliers, and more suppliers means more bottlenecks. However, even though too much complexity can make your business model a lot riskier, the right amount of complexity can become your killer edge, the thing that makes your product impossible to copy. Watch exclusive interviews from the MarketingSherpa Media Center -- live from IRCE, the world's largest e-commerce event at http://MarketingSherpa.com/IRCE

Reporting live from the 10th annual IRCE in Chicago, MarketingSherpa's Allison Banko sat down with Lisa Butler, Head of Enterprise Solutions Enablement, eBay Enterprise, in the MarketingSherpa Media Center. Butler highlighted omnichannel marketing in this interview.

"Omnichannel is becoming an overrated buzzword; it's becoming meaningless. So we went to multichannel, to omnichannel, to all channels -- what it really means is just allowing customers to shop however they want," Butler said.

Butler also provided some examples of retailers that are embracing the customer experience, and how to make the experience also work for merchants.

Email Marketing for Ecommerce Subscriptions (Reduce Churn & Increase LTV)

If you're running an e-commerce brand with a subscription model (or thinking about adding one), this video is your complete playbook. I break down why relying on paid ads to grow subscriptions is so expensive—and what to do instead. You'll learn how to convert one-time buyers into subscribers using strategic email flows, how to reduce churn in the critical first three months, and how to build automated systems that grow your subscription program on autopilot. I also walk through the exact strategy we used to cut churn by 33%, triple subscriber lifetime value, and reduce ad spend by 48%.
I’ll show you how to build high-converting one-time-to-subscription flows in Klaviyo, create surprise-and-delight retention campaigns, fix payment failure churn, and nurture customers long-term so they actually use your products. If you want higher LTV, better CAC ratios, and a more profitable subscription business without scaling ad spend, this is the framework you need to implement.

Keywords
ecommerce subscription strategy, reduce subscription churn, email marketing for ecommerce, klaviyo subscription flow, increase lifetime value ecommerce, subscription retention strategy, reduce ad spend ecommerce, convert one time buyers to subscribers, subscription marketing automation, ecommerce LTV strategy, subscription email flows, klaviyo ecommerce automation, subscription churn reduction, subscription growth playbook, email marketing for ecommerce subscriptions, email marketing for ecommerce brands, klaiyo email marketing, klaviyo email marketing tutorial

segments.text: Working capital is one of the most
misunderstood parts of a business sale.
Many sellers think once they agree on
price, the number is fixed. But in real
transactions, that is often not the
case. Because even after the purchase
price is agreed, working capital
adjustments can change what the seller
actually receives at closing. So, let's
make this simple.
Working capital usually means current
assets minus current liabilities tied to
normal day-to-day operations. In other
words, it is the short-term operating
capital needed to run the business.
And in many deals, buyers expect the
business to be delivered with a
normalized level of working capital.
Why? Because the buyer wants the company
to continue operating smoothly from day
one. They do not want to buy the
business and then immediately inject
more cash just to fund payroll,
inventory, or receivables gaps. That is
where the adjustment comes in.
During the deal process, buyer and
seller usually agree on a target working
capital amount. This target is often
based on historical averages,
seasonality, and the normal operating
needs of the business. Then, at closing,
actual working capital is measured
against that target. If actual working
capital is below the agreed level, the
purchase price is typically reduced. If
it is above the target, the seller may
receive more.
This is why working capital is not a
minor accounting detail. It is a real
value issue. And sellers get into
trouble when they assume all cash stays
with them, or when they underestimate
what the business needs to operate
normally after closing.
The most common problems come from poor
preparation, unclear balance sheets,
aggressive collections timing, delayed
payables, inventory swings, or simply
not understanding what is considered
normal for the business.
The key is preparation early in the
process. Sellers should understand their
working capital trends well before going
to market. They should know what a buyer
is likely to view as normalized and
where adjustment risk may appear.
Because if you wait until late stage
diligence to understand working capital,
you are already negotiating from a
weaker position.
The core lesson is simple. Headline
price is not always final price, and
working capital adjustments are one of
the main reasons. If you understand them
early, prepare properly, and structure
the deal carefully, you protect value
and reduce surprises at closing.
EIN Business Brokers. We represent you
in business sales and acquisitions.
Confidential, structured, executed.

metadata.shortDescription: Beyond a business's cash flow and purchase price one of the biggest negotiating points in a Letter of Intent is how much working capital is to be left in a business when it is sold. In this episode we walk through what is working capital, where you find it, how its calculated and what is the appropriate amount to have in a business. If you're a Seller, knowing how much is enough allows you to remove the excess from the company before going to market. If you're a buyer, knowing how much is appropriate will protect you from buying a company and then having to write a second check just to keep it operational. Working Capital is one of the most negotiated deal points in a Letter of Intent, having a working knowledge of this concept will allow you to negotiate in good faith and protect your investment.

Shopify Inventory Management Tutorial for Beginners (2026 Step-by-Step Guide to Managing Stock)

This tutorial shows how to shopify inventory management tutorial for beginners, step by step, so you can follow along on your own screen.

Quick summary
Running out of a best seller or selling something you don't have costs you sales and trust. Shopify's inventory tools prevent both.

What you will see in this video
• In this video, we tour the inventory page.
• See where a product's stock is set and how purchase orders and transfers keep your counts right.
• Everything starts in the products section of the left menu.
• Click products and its sub page is open underneath.
• This store has no products yet, so the list is empty.
• Stock is tracked per product, so adding products comes first.
• Now click inventory just below.
• Once products exist, this page lists every variant that tracks quantity.
• At each location, with its numbers side by side.
• To find one, type a product name or a SKU in search and filter, like t-shirt.
• Here nothing is found because the store is still empty.
• Click display options to choose your columns.
• Available is what customers can buy.
• Committed is stock in unfulfilled orders, and on hand is everything physically there.
• To change many quantities at once, click export.
• You get a CSV file, edit the numbers in a spreadsheet, and bring them back with import.
• Click cancel to close it.
• Incoming stock from suppliers is handled by purchase orders, so click purchase orders in the menu.
• A purchase order records what you ordered from a supplier.
• Click create purchase order to start one.
• Choose the supplier, the destination, and the products.
• When the goods arrive, you mark them as received and Shopify adds them to your stock, so you never type those numbers by hand.
• If you sell from more than one place, like a warehouse and a shop, transfers move stock between them.
• Click create transfer to start one.
• Pick where the stock comes from, where it goes, and add the products.
• When you receive it at the destination, both locations update, so the counts stay accurate.
• Now let's see where a single product's stock is set.
• Go back to products and click add product.
• It is the same form you used to edit a product later.
• In the inventory section of the form, you enter how many units are available at each location.
• This store has one location, called mile eight.
• Type the number you have, like 25.
• You can also add a SKU and a barcode here, which makes searching and scanning much faster.
• A common mistake is turning on cell when out of stock by accident.

metadata.title: Shopify Inventory Tracking Guide: ABC Analysis, Bundles & Stock Alerts
metadata.author: Report Pundit
metadata.shortDescription:
Is your cash tied up in dead stock? In this video, we dive deep into Shopify Inventory Reports to help you track stock levels, plan reorders, and maximize your cash flow.

We move beyond the basic month-end snapshots to show you how to set up advanced tracking systems. You'll learn how to perform an ABC Analysis to identify your most profitable items, calculate accurate Reorder Points so you never go out of stock, and manage Product Bundles without the headache.

In this video, we cover:

Month-End Snapshots: Essential for accounting and seeing what you sold.
Real-Time Inventory: Tracking "Inventory on Hand" vs. "Committed Stock."
ABC Analysis: Ranking your products (A, B, or C) by revenue to know where to focus your budget.
Reorder Points: Using daily demand and lead times to automate your purchasing.
Bundle Inventory: How to prevent overselling when tracking components.

Featured Tools:

Report Pundit: Used in this video for advanced custom inventory reports. https://bit.ly/49XHYaO]

Why this matters:
Poor inventory management is the #1 reason ecommerce brands fail. Understanding your sell-through rate and inventory value is the key to scaling profitably in 2026.

👇 Do you use a spreadsheet or an app for inventory planning? Let us know in the comments!

#Shopify #InventoryManagement #EcommerceTips #StockTracking #shopifyreports #ShopifyApps #BusinessGrowth #ReportPundit #Logistics #shopifyinventory #shopifyapps #shopifyreports

metadata.title: How to Set Up Prediko: Shopify Inventory Forecasting, Purchase Orders & AI Planning (Onboarding)
metadata.author: Prediko AI Inventory Management
metadata.shortDescription:
This full onboarding webinar walks you through setting up Prediko for Shopify inventory forecasting, automated purchase orders, demand planning, and multi-location inventory management.

Hosted by Isaiah (Customer Success, US/Australia/Canada), with Revathi (UK/EMEA).

Recorded: 2 September 2026

00:00 Welcome and intro
04:24 Pia: Prediko's AI inventory assistant
05:41 Settings: suppliers, SKU mapping, lead times and unit costs
09:42 Automating purchase orders by schedule
10:32 Locations and transfers setup
12:52 Planning settings: Simple vs Smart forecasting model
15:38 Smart model: revenue targets, trend emphasis, and seasonality
17:00 Demand tab: viewing and editing your forecast plan
22:18 Creating purchase orders by order deadline
23:51 Supply tab: open to buy and stock coverage by month
25:41 Buying tab: purchase order recommendations by SKU
29:33 Buy now vs buy at order deadline explained
31:26 Creating and confirming draft purchase orders
32:16 Receiving inventory and PO status tracking
34:23 Shopify sync settings and WMS integrations
37:00 Reports and analytics dashboard
39:09 Q&A: Negative inventory syncing to Shopify when receiving a PO
40:44 Q&A: B2B and online sales across multiple locations
51:01 Q&A: Adjusting transfer quantities and recommendation policies
53:05 Wrap-up and support resources

Whether you are a fashion brand managing seasonal demand, a DTC brand with multiple warehouses, or a Shopify merchant handling B2B and online sales from the same location, this webinar covers the most common setup questions and workflows.

Questions covered: How does AI demand forecasting work in Shopify? How do I automate purchase orders in Prediko? How do I manage inventory across multiple locations? What is the difference between the Simple and Smart forecasting models? Why is my Shopify inventory showing negative numbers when receiving a PO?

metadata.title: How to Set Up Prediko: Shopify Inventory Forecasting, Purchase Orders & AI Planning (Onboarding)
metadata.author: Prediko AI Inventory Management
metadata.shortDescription:
This full onboarding webinar walks you through setting up Prediko for Shopify inventory forecasting, automated purchase orders, demand planning, bundles, and multi-location inventory management.

Hosted by Revathi, Customer Success Manager (UK/EMEA), with Isaiah (US).

Recorded: 26 August 2026

00:00 Welcome and intro
03:50 Getting started: first steps after installing Prediko
04:33 Settings: suppliers, SKU mapping, and lead times
06:44 Days of cover, safety stock, and order frequency
08:19 Planning settings: Simple vs Smart forecasting model
09:38 Smart model: revenue targets, trend emphasis, and seasonality
11:11 Manual vs auto-weekly forecast refresh
12:38 Demand tab: viewing and comparing your forecast by SKU, product, and location
15:57 Buying tab: AI-powered purchase order recommendations
19:06 Filtering by order deadline and creating draft purchase orders
20:10 MOQ scaling and location distribution
21:33 Emailing POs to suppliers as PDF or Excel
22:43 Receiving inventory and closing a purchase order
23:11 Bundles: setting up parent and child SKUs
25:56 Reports, analytics dashboard, and scheduled email reports
27:37 Pia: Prediko's AI inventory assistant
28:41 Q&A begins
29:04 Q&A: OMS integration and syncing POs from Prediko
31:12 Q&A: Multi-location purchasing, combining demand across warehouses, and using transfers
34:00 Q&A: Syncing purchase orders and transfers directly with Shopify
36:10 Wrap-up and support resources

Whether you are a fashion brand managing seasonal demand, a DTC brand selling across multiple warehouses, or a Shopify merchant looking to integrate Prediko with your OMS or WMS, this webinar covers the most common setup questions and workflows.

Questions covered: How does AI demand forecasting work in Shopify? How do I set up bundles in Prediko? How do I sync purchase orders with Shopify? Can Prediko integrate with my OMS or WMS? How do I manage inventory across multiple locations and warehouses?

segments.text: Overselling, stockouts, hours lost
updating products one by one? If you run
a Shopify store, inventory is either
your quiet superpower or your biggest
headache. In this guide, we'll walk
through every practical way to manage
Shopify inventory, what each one is good
at, and the method we think beats them
all.
First, the basics. Good inventory
management means always knowing what you
have, where it is, and when to reorder.
Give every variant a unique SKU. Set a
reorder point with a little safety
stock, so you restock before you run
out.
Sell older stock first and use ABC
analysis to focus on the products that
bring in most of your revenue. And count
regularly. Small cycle counts catch
mistakes before they turn into oversold
orders.
Method one, the Shopify admin. Go to
products, then inventory, pick a
location, and update the on-hand or
available quantity for each variant.
Shopify also keeps 180 days of
adjustment history, supports multiple
locations, and gives you reports like
sell-through rate and days of inventory
remaining. It's free and built-in, but
editing a few hundred variants this way
means a lot of clicking.
Method two, CSV import and export.
Export your inventory, edit it in a
spreadsheet, then import it back. It's
great for big one-time updates. The
catch? That file is a snapshot. The
moment an order comes in, it's out of
date, and importing an old file can
overwrite your real stock levels.
Method three, automation and dedicated
apps. Shopify Flow can alert you when
stock runs low, tag products, or hide
items that are out of stock. Inventory
apps add forecasting and purchase
orders. Powerful, but often it's another
dashboard to learn and another monthly
bill.
Which brings us to method four and our
favorite, Flexik. It turns Google Sheets
into a live control panel for your
Shopify store. The sync is two-way.
Change a price or a stock count in your
sheet and Shopify updates. Make a sale
in Shopify and your sheet updates, too.
No CSV files and no coding.
Setting it up takes a few minutes.
Install FlexSync from the Shopify app
store, click connect Google, then create
a new sheet or paste the link to an
existing one. Choose the columns you
want, add filters if you only need
certain products, and click export and
continue. Finally, paste the FlexSync
app script into your sheet under
extensions, app script. Run it once and
allow access. That switches on real-time
sync.
So, what can you manage from the sheet?
Available and on-hand stock with one
column per location, price, compare-at
price, and cost per item, SKU, barcode,
title, tags, product type, and status.
You can even set the inventory policy,
deny or continue, to decide whether a
product keeps selling when it's out of
stock.
And product and variant metafields sync
as columns, too. Bulk edits are just
spreadsheet moves. Paste a new price
list or drag a value down hundreds of
rows and FlexSync matches every row to
the right variant. Filters keep the
sheet focused. Show only one vendor, one
location, active products, or a set of
tags. Filters hide rows. They never
delete them. Then, there are formulas.
Turn on allow sheet formula and FlexSync
syncs the result of any Google Sheets
formula. Pull prices from a supplier
sheet with import range or switch
products to draft when stock hits zero.
Formula changes reach Shopify on a
5-minute schedule.
And it's not just products. Turn on
order sync and your orders and draft
orders get their own tabs. Edit a
highlighted field, like the fulfillment
status drop-down. Save the sheet, then
click push order changes to Shopify.
Draft orders work the same way.
Put it all side by side. The admin is
simple, but slow. CSV handles bulk, but
goes stale.
Apps are powerful, but complex.
FlexSync gives you bulk editing, live
two-way sync, automation, and orders in
a tool your team already knows.
Whichever method you choose, a few
habits make all the difference. Track
every SKU, set reorder points, count
regularly, and keep one source of truth.
Want to try it? Flex Sync has a free
plan for up to 500 SKUs, and paid plans
come with a 14-day free trial. Find Flex
Sync on the Shopify app store and start
managing your inventory from Google
Sheets.

10:53 Auto weekly vs manual forecast refresh

Klaviyo tutorial for beginners 2026/27: the exact setup to go from beginner to expert

Most brands install Klaviyo, turn on a couple of templates and wonder why email does nothing. Email should be doing 30–40% of your revenue. Most Shopify brands I audit sit between 10% and 18%. This video walks you through the full setup, step by step, so you're not one of them.

What you'll learn:
→ How to set up your Klaviyo account properly before you send anything 
→ How to build a signup form that actually grows your list
→ The 5 Klaviyo flows every Shopify brand needs: welcome, abandoned checkout, browse abandonment, post-purchase and win-back
→ How to segment your list and send campaigns without "annoying your customers"
→ The one number you should check every month

🌐 keptrevenue.com
📸 Instagram: @theoclough

#klaviyo #klaviyotutorial #emailmarketing #shopify #ecommerce

metadata.title: What Importers Get Wrong About US Customs (And It's Expensive) | Expert's Guide for Beginner
metadata.author: Trade Counsel
metadata.shortDescription:
What actually happens between ordering from a Chinese factory and getting the goods into your US warehouse? We follow one $10,000 order of plastic storage bins step by step: who the importer of record is, the HTS code, how the China tariffs stack up today (3.4% + 7.5% + 12.5% = 23.4% on our example), why US duty is charged on the goods and not the freight, the bond and broker, the Importer Security Filing deadline, which goods can be stopped, the 15-day and 10-working-day entry deadlines, and when the duty becomes final.

Chapters
0:00 A $10,000 order from China
0:31 Who is the importer of record?
1:00 The HTS code
1:29 The China tariff stack
2:21 Duty on the goods, not the freight
2:47 Importer number, bond and broker
3:16 The Importer Security Filing (24 hours before loading)
3:52 Can the goods come in? Agencies, origin marking, UFLPA
4:21 Entry, release and CBP Form 7501
4:50 When the duty becomes final
5:09 Four things to settle before your first order

Importing into the US (this series)
- Finding the right HTS code (next)
- Working out your duty
- Bill of lading, explained
- CBP Form 7501, box by box
- Getting overpaid duty back
On this channel: Incoterms: all 11 rules explained

Rates and rules as of 12 November 2026. The storage-bin order is an example; your own HTS code decides your rates.

Sources
- CBP CSMS #69326983 (23 Jul 2026), Section 301 forced labor import duties (China: 12.5%, HTS 9903.05.31)
- USTR, Notice of Actions in Section 301 Investigations (forced labor), 23 Jul 2026, Annex II
- HTSUS 3924.90.56.50; 9903.88.15 (Section 301, List 4A)
- Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, No. 24-1287 (U.S. Supreme Court, 20 Feb 2026)
- 19 U.S.C. § 1401a(b)(4)(A) (customs value excludes international freight and insurance shown separately)
- CBP Dec. 26-14 (FY2027 user fees: MPF 0.3464%, min $34.58, max $670.86); 19 CFR 24.24 (HMF 0.125%)
- 19 CFR Part 113 (bonds); 19 CFR Part 111 (customs brokers); 19 CFR Part 149 (Importer Security Filing)
- 19 CFR 142.2, 142.12 (entry and entry summary deadlines); CBP Form 7501
- Federal Register 2026-12669 and 2026-12670 (suspension of the de minimis exemption)
- Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, Pub. L. 117-78, § 3; 19 U.S.C. § 1304 (country-of-origin marking)
- 19 CFR 159.11 (liquidation); 19 U.S.C. § 1514 (protests); 19 U.S.C. § 1508 (records)

General information, not legal advice. Narration voice is AI-generated.

segments.text: Say you order $10,000 of plastic storage bins from a factory in China.
To bring them into the country, you'll pay U.S. Customs about $2,400 more, and
that's if every step goes right.
Miss one form before the ship even leaves China, and customs can claim another
That's because importing isn't one step.
It's a chain of them, and each one has a deadline, a name on it and a price for
getting it wrong. So let's follow that one order, from the factory to your door.
The first question comes before you pay the supplier:
whose name goes on the customs paperwork?
That company is the importer of record, and it's the one customs holds
responsible for the duty and for every detail being right.
If you buy on terms like FOB, where you arrange the shipping from the Chinese
port, that's you. If you buy DDP, Delivered Duty Paid, the seller usually takes
that role. Those terms are Incoterms, and there's a full video on them on this
channel.
As the importer, your first job is the code.
Every product has a 10-digit number in the U.S. tariff schedule, its HTS code,
and that number sets your duty rate.
Your supplier may suggest one, but customs holds you responsible for getting it
right, and if it's wrong, you can owe the difference plus penalties.
Finding the right one is the next video in this series, so subscribe if you'll
need it. For now, our storage bins are classed as household articles of plastic.
And for goods from China, the rate isn't one number.
The emergency tariffs of 2025 no longer apply, since the Supreme Court struck
them down in February 2026, but other layers remain.
First, the normal rate that applies to most countries:
for these bins, 3.4%. On top sits a China tariff under a trade law called
Section 301, in place since 2018 and 2019:
7.5% on these bins, and 25% on many other goods.
Then, since July 2026, a newer Section 301 tariff, which also hits dozens of
other countries, adds 12.5% to most goods from China.
Stack them, and these bins pay twenty-3.4%.
Goods under other tariffs, like steel or car parts, follow different rules, so
always check your own code.
That percentage is charged on the price of the goods, not the shipping.
In the U.S., ocean freight and insurance from China don't count toward the
value, as long as they're shown separately.
So on $10,000 of bins, the duty is $2,340.
Customs then adds two small fees, one for processing and, by sea, one for harbor
upkeep. That's the $2,400 from the start.
Paying it takes some setup. You need an importer number, which for most
businesses is simply their federal tax ID.
You need a customs bond, a guarantee from an insurance company that customs will
be paid what it's owed, penalties included.
Shipments worth more than $2,500 need one:
a single bond for that shipment, or a continuous bond for a year of imports,
starting at $50,000 of coverage.
And almost every importer hires a licensed customs broker to file for them.
Your broker usually also handles the form that catches first-time importers.
If your goods travel by sea, you have to send customs an Importer Security
Filing, naming the seller, the factory and that HTS code, at least 24 hours
before the goods are loaded onto the ship in China.
If it's late, wrong or missing, customs can claim $5,000 per violation against
your bond. Once the goods are on board, the carrier issues the bill of lading,
the receipt for your cargo, and that gets a video of its own.
But the filing comes first, so line up your broker before anything ships.
The goods also have to be allowed in.
Some products answer to other agencies too, like the FDA for food, and
children's products need a certificate of safety testing.
Imports generally have to show their origin:
Made in China. And one rule bites hard here.
Anything made wholly or partly in Xinjiang, or by companies on a U.S. government
list, is presumed to be made with forced labor.
Customs can detain it, and the burden of proving otherwise is on you.
Now the ship docks. You have 15 days from arrival to file the entry, the request
to release the goods, and your broker usually does it.
Within 10 working days of release, the entry summary, CBP Form 7501, is filed
and the duty is paid. We'll go through that form box by box later in this
series. And low-value shipments pay too:
the duty-free allowance for shipments worth up to $800 has been suspended since
August 2025.
Even then, the duty isn't final.
It becomes final when customs liquidates the entry, usually about 10 months
later. If you've overpaid, there are deadlines to claim it back, some before
that point and some soon after, and that's coming in this series too.
Keep your records for 5 years, because customs can ask for them.
So before your first order, settle four things:
whose name goes on the entry, the HTS code, the full tariff stack for that code,
and a broker with your bond and your security filing ready before the goods are
loaded. Get those right, and the bins arrive costing what you planned.
Get one wrong, and you find out at the port.
Most of those steps get their own video in this series, starting with the HTS
code, the number that sets everything else.
Subscribe, and you won't miss them.

videos.full_text: Say you order $10,000 of plastic storage bins from a factory in China. To bring them into the country, you'll pay U.S. Customs about $2,400 more, and that's if every step goes right. Miss one form before the ship even leaves China, and customs can claim another $5,000. That's because importing isn't one step. It's a chain of them, and each one has a deadline, a name on it and a price for getting it wrong. So let's follow that one order, from the factory to your door. The first question comes before you pay the supplier: whose name goes on the customs paperwork? That company is the importer of record, and it's the one customs holds responsible for the duty and for every detail being right. If you buy on terms like FOB, where you arrange the shipping from the Chinese port, that's you. If you buy DDP, Delivered Duty Paid, the seller usually takes that role. Those terms are Incoterms, and there's a full video on them on this channel. As the importer, your first job is the code. Every product has a 10-digit number in the U.S. tariff schedule, its HTS code, and that number sets your duty rate. Your supplier may suggest one, but customs holds you responsible for getting it right, and if it's wrong, you can owe the difference plus penalties. Finding the right one is the next video in this series, so subscribe if you'll need it. For now, our storage bins are classed as household articles of plastic. And for goods from China, the rate isn't one number. The emergency tariffs of 2025 no longer apply, since the Supreme Court struck them down in February 2026, but other layers remain. First, the normal rate that applies to most countries: for these bins, 3.4%. On top sits a China tariff under a trade law called Section 301, in place since 2018 and 2019: 7.5% on these bins, and 25% on many other goods. Then, since July 2026, a newer Section 301 tariff, which also hits dozens of other countries, adds 12.5% to most goods from China. Stack them, and these bins pay twenty-3.4%. Goods under other tariffs, like steel or car parts, follow different rules, so always check your own code. That percentage is charged on the price of the goods, not the shipping. In the U.S., ocean freight and insurance from China don't count toward the value, as long as they're shown separately. So on $10,000 of bins, the duty is $2,340. Customs then adds two small fees, one for processing and, by sea, one for harbor upkeep. That's the $2,400 from the start. Paying it takes some setup. You need an importer number, which for most businesses is simply their federal tax ID. You need a customs bond, a guarantee from an insurance company that customs will be paid what it's owed, penalties included. Shipments worth more than $2,500 need one: a single bond for that shipment, or a continuous bond for a year of imports, starting at $50,000 of coverage. And almost every importer hires a licensed customs broker to file for them. Your broker usually also handles the form that catches first-time importers. If your goods travel by sea, you have to send customs an Importer Security Filing, naming the seller, the factory and that HTS code, at least 24 hours before the goods are loaded onto the ship in China. If it's late, wrong or missing, customs can claim $5,000 per violation against your bond. Once the goods are on board, the carrier issues the bill of lading, the receipt for your cargo, and that gets a video of its own. But the filing comes first, so line up your broker before anything ships. The goods also have to be allowed in. Some products answer to other agencies too, like the FDA for food, and children's products need a certificate of safety testing. Imports generally have to show their origin: Made in China. And one rule bites hard here. Anything made wholly or partly in Xinjiang, or by companies on a U.S. government list, is presumed to be made with forced labor. Customs can detain it, and the burden of proving otherwise is on you. Now the ship docks. You have 15 days from arrival to file the entry, the request to release the goods, and your broker usually does it. Within 10 working days of release, the entry summary, CBP Form 7501, is filed and the duty is paid. We'll go through that form box by box later in this series. And low-value shipments pay too: the duty-free allowance for shipments worth up to $800 has been suspended since August 2025. Even then, the duty isn't final. It becomes final when customs liquidates the entry, usually about 10 months later. If you've overpaid, there are deadlines to claim it back, some before that point and some soon after, and that's coming in this series too. Keep your records for 5 years, because customs can ask for them. So before your first order, settle four things: whose name goes on the entry, the HTS code, the full tariff stack for that code, and a broker with your bond and your security filing ready before the goods are loaded. Get those right, and the bins arrive costing what you planned. Get one wrong, and you find out at the port. Most of those steps get their own video in this series, starting with the HTS code, the number that sets everything else. Subscribe, and you won't miss them.

metadata.title: How to Capitalize Estimated Import Duty Into Landed Cost and Reconcile Broker Bills | SKU.io
metadata.author: SKUio
metadata.shortDescription:
Capitalize estimated import duty into stock cost when goods arrive, then reconcile it with your customs broker's duty bill. In SKU.io's Landed Cost Estimates settings you choose the accrued customs duty accounts and turn on capitalization; when the broker bill arrives it clears the accrual and only the difference moves. Check every shipment's estimate against its bill in the Duty Reconciliation report.

Full written guide: https://www.sku.io/docs/guides/orders/duties-and-tariffs/capitalise-and-reconcile-duty

0:00 Open Landed Cost Estimates
0:25 The accounting entries
0:49 Choose the duty accounts
1:09 Turn on duty capitalization
1:28 When no broker bill arrives
2:09 See the booked estimate
2:20 Enter the broker's duty bill
2:39 Why the bill splits by estimated duty
2:53 Estimated vs actual duty
3:16 Open the Duty Reconciliation report
3:38 Filter, group, and export

Related guides:
• Release an estimate when no bill is coming: https://www.sku.io/docs/guides/orders/duties-and-tariffs/release-an-estimate-when-no-bill-is-coming
• Estimate duty on purchase orders and shipments: https://www.sku.io/docs/guides/orders/duties-and-tariffs/estimate-duty-on-purchase-orders
• Set up duty rates: https://www.sku.io/docs/guides/orders/duties-and-tariffs/set-up-duty-rates

AI-narrated walkthrough recorded in a SKU.io demo environment.
SKU.io is inventory, orders, and accounting for e-commerce operators: https://www.sku.io

#LandedCost #Tariffs #ImportDuty #Accounting #SKUio

segments.text: SKU.io can put the estimated import duty into stock cost the day goods arrive, not weeks later when the bill does.
To set it up, go to Settings, at the bottom of the sidebar.
Open the Purchasing group, which lists every purchasing setting.
Then choose Landed Cost Estimates, near the bottom.
The page sets out how estimated duty works, card by card.
The first card explains what happens in your books.
Step one, goods are received.
Their estimated duty goes into stock cost, and is held in an accrued customs duty account.
Step two, the broker bill arrives, and clears that account.
Step three, only the difference moves.
Stock still on hand takes its share, and sold units take theirs.
The accrued account ends at zero.
Below, the Customs duty card holds the accounts.
Accrued Customs Duty holds each estimate until its bill arrives.
Customs Duty Variance takes the difference for units already sold.
Then pick the category your broker's bills use, under Customs duty category.
Bills in it count as actual duty, and clear the estimates.
The switch stays off until a duty category and an accrued account are chosen.
Turn on Capitalise estimated customs duty.
Then click Save changes, at the top of the page.
The setting applies to every shipment you receive from today.
Shipments received earlier keep their estimate, but it stays out of stock cost.
At the bottom of the page, When no bill arrives looks after estimates that never get a bill.
It releases whatever is still waiting, a hundred and twenty days after the purchase order's last receipt.
And it flags estimates older than ninety days at month end.
Now receive a shipment.
Go to Orders in the sidebar, then choose Inbound Shipments, further down the list.
Then open a shipment that is still on its way to your warehouse.
It opens on the Overview tab.
Click Receive Items, the green button at the top.
Check the quantities in the dialog that opens.
Then click Receive 2 Items, the blue button at the bottom.
The receipt takes a moment, while the estimated duty goes into stock cost.
The Customs card now shows the estimate booked at receipt.
Its caption confirms it was added to stock cost.
The chip at the top says Awaiting bill, until the broker's bill is entered.
When the broker's bill arrives, click Enter duty bill.
The bill is already set to Customs Duty, split by estimated duty.
Choose your customs broker as the supplier, typing the first few letters of its name.
Next, type the invoice number from the broker's bill.
Then enter the duty it charged in the line's amount.
The note under the method field explains this split, by each line's booked duty estimate.
A line that carried most of the duty takes most of the bill, so each variance is fair.
When it all looks right, click Save Invoice.
The bill is saved, and the shipment's Landed Costs tab opens.
The banner compares the booked estimate with the actual duty.
Now go back to the Overview tab of the shipment.
The Customs card shows what was billed, and the variance, here about seven percent over.
The chip at the top now says Cleared.
The Items tab shows the same for each line, with its duty status.
To check every shipment at once, go to Insights, then Reports.
This page lists all your reports.
Scroll down the long list, and choose Duty Reconciliation.
The cards total the booked estimates, the actual bills, and the net variance.
Uncleared estimates are still waiting for a bill.
The line below checks them against your accrued customs duty account.
In the table, each row shows one shipment and where its bill stands.
Group by turns each row into a product, a supplier, or a month.
By product, you can see which items keep billing over their estimate.
The status tabs narrow the list, for example to big variances.
Rows past your limits are tinted, so they stand out.
And Export saves what you see as a spreadsheet.
