metadata.title: Tariff news and your landed cost
metadata.author: CFOmarketIQ
metadata.shortDescription:
This year the tariff on the same imported part could change without the rate changing at all. How tariff news actually reaches your landed cost, why 2026 has been so hard to follow, the one question to ask your customs broker, and five things to do this month.

Your first briefing is free at cfomarketiq.com: https://www.cfomarketiq.com/free-trial-report

Chapters
00:00 Same tariff, bigger bill
00:11 The math on one part
00:33 Where it was announced
00:58 What this video covers
01:16 Three tariffs in one year
01:44 Fees and the rest of landed cost
02:07 Where it hits your numbers
02:37 The question for your broker
02:55 Inside a briefing
03:27 What to do this month

Sources
White & Case, United States modifies steel, aluminum, and copper Section 232 tariffs: https://www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/united-states-modifies-steel-aluminum-and-copper-section-232-tariffs
Honigman, Supreme Court strikes down IEEPA tariffs, White House announces new 10% global tariff: https://www.honigman.com/alert-3240
Morgan Lewis, US Administration rebuilds global tariff program under Section 301: https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2026/07/us-administration-rebuilds-global-tariff-program-under-section-301
Eilan Trade, Trade alert October 2026: CBP MPF, Section 301, USMCA: https://eilantrade.com/en/trade-alert-us-mexico-trade-october-2026/
ExFreight, How to calculate landed cost: https://www.exfreight.com/how-to-calculate-landed-cost-formulas-worked-examples/
Withers, Update on IEEPA tariff refunds: https://www.withersworldwide.com/en-gb/insight/read/update-on-ieepa-tariff-refunds

Sample findings are an illustrative sample. Narration is AI-generated. Informational only. Not financial, investment or legal advice.

#CFO #Tariffs #LandedCost

segments.text: Same part, same supplier, same twenty-five percent tariff.
And since April,
two and a half times the duty.
Nobody changed the rate at all.
They changed what the rate gets charged on.
Here's the math on a hundred dollar
part that's about forty percent steel.
Before the change in April,
the twenty-five percent only hit the steel content,
so the duty came to about ten.
From April on,
it hits the full customs value.
That's twenty-five dollars of duty,
on the exact same part.
Fifteen more per unit,
and nobody on the supplier side
sent you an email about it.
And all of it was public the whole time.
A proclamation in early April,
in effect four days later,
with no exception for goods already on the water.
Keeping up with that means reading proclamations,
trade notices and law firm alerts,
and nobody on a mid-market finance team has those hours.
So a lot of CFOs found
out from the broker's invoice,
weeks later.
Or from the CEO,
asking why margin on that product line slipped.
That gap between the news and your numbers
is what CFOmarketIQ is built to close.
We'll go through how tariff news
actually reaches your landed cost,
and why this year has been so hard to follow.
And there's one question we'd ask
your customs broker before any other.
We'll get to that in a moment.
Start with the base tariffs,
because this year they changed underneath everyone.
In February the Supreme Court ruled
the emergency powers tariffs weren't authorized.
Four days later a ten percent
global tariff took their place,
and it could only last about five months.
When that ran out in July,
new tariffs of ten or twelve and a
half percent started on goods from sixty economies.
The goods on your purchase orders didn't change at all.
The legal basis for the duty changed three times.
And the duty is only one line in landed cost.
Most entries also pay a merchandise
processing fee of about a third
of a percent of value.
This month,
the cap on that fee went up again,
to a little over six hundred seventy per entry.
Anything that comes in by sea
also pays a harbor maintenance fee.
Then come freight, insurance,
the broker's fee and the truck from the port.
So where does all of this land for a CFO?
Standard costs and inventory value,
which can lag reality by a
quarter if nobody resets them.
Gross margin by product line,
because a change like the one in
April hits some lines and skips others.
Customer pricing,
and whether your contracts let you
pass any of it through.
And then there's cash,
because you pay the duty when the goods come in,
long before you sell them.
So a tariff change can squeeze
your cash a quarter before it
ever shows up in the P&L.
Now, the question we said we'd get to.
Ask your broker which of your entries are still open.
After the Supreme Court ruling,
the trade court ordered refunds of those
tariffs on entries that weren't final.
For some importers that's real cash,
and the clock matters,
because once an entry is final you
have roughly six months to protest it.
Here's how a supply cost item
shows up in a briefing,
using the illustrative sample from our website,
a company we call Acme Industrial.
Lead times on resin are up to fourteen weeks,
and Acme has six weeks on hand,
so the reorder point moves before the quarter closes.
The agent reads hundreds of articles and
checks each one against Acme's numbers,
like its twenty-two percent gross margin plan,
then ranks what it finds by what it could cost.
And every item shows where it came from and when,
so when the CEO asks how you know,
you can answer.
First,
list your top twenty imported items by spend,
with the country of origin and
the tariff code for each.
Second, flag anything with steel,
aluminum or copper in it,
and recheck the duty on the full value.
Third,
reset standard costs for the lines where the duty moved,
so your margin reports stop lagging.
Fourth,
ask your broker which of your entries are still open.
And fifth,
pull your biggest customer contracts and find out
whether any of this can be passed through.
See what it finds on your company.
Your first briefing is free.
Head to cfomarketiq.com.

segments.text: When buying or selling from foreign countries, you need to understand the true cost of your goods,
including transportation charges, insurance, tariffs, duties and taxes.
Importers can use the Shipping Solutions landed cost calculator to see tariff rates
and to compare sourcing an item from up to five different countries. Exporters can use
the landed cost calculator to determine in which markets they want to expand. Let me show you how.
I’m going to start with a Quick Quote that will show what the tariffs and duties will
be on importing 1,000 umbrellas from Canada to the US. After logging in,
I’ll choose Quick Quote under the Landed Cost tab. I’ll enter my country of Import and Export.
The country of manufacture will fill in with the same country as the country of export,
but I can change it if needed. Then I’ll enter the Harmonized
System Number. 6603203000. If you also have a subscription to the product classification
software, you can click the magnifying glass to open an HS number search window. I’ll do that
to double-check my number, but it will also be helpful if I don’t know my HS number. Here I can
see the Default Duty and other Chapter 99 codes that might apply to my item and could add more
tariffs. I have used the Product Classification software to look up these additional chapter
99 codes so I know which ones apply to my import from Canada so I’ll add them: 99030110, 99030126.
Then I’ll add my mode of transport (land) and click Next.
The Landed Cost Calculator refers to tariffs as duties so you can see the default duty is
0%. However the additional codes I entered show the special tariffs (or duties). There
is a 25% duty for the first code I entered. The description shows “in addition to” so
that is an additional duty. The second additional code I entered does not show
any additional duty as it says “use main”. I can also see the Merchandise Processing Fees
or MPF, and I can see the duties and fees if the commodity qualifies for the USMCA.
Now let’s try the Landed Cost option under the Landed Cost tab.
This time I’ll compare importing the umbrellas into the United States from
either Canada or Vietnam, so I’ll enter my country of import (United States).
Then I’ll enter the harmonized tariff schedule number: 6603203000. As I mentioned before,
if you also have a subscription to the product classification software,
you can click the magnifying glass to open an HS number search window.
Choose a date and a currency. And then you can choose if you want preferential duties and taxes,
default duties and taxes, or both. And the preferential duties and taxes are referring
to any applicable free trade agreement. So I'm going to leave it as both, and then click next.
Enter the quantity (1,000) then click add countries of export.
You can select up to five different countries so that you can compare the total landed cost from
each country. I'm just going to choose two, so I will choose Canada and Vietnam, and click okay.
Click the plus sign next to Canada to open the data entry screen. If there are any additional
HS codes that apply your item, click Add. These are needed in order to calculate the correct duty.
I know that these additional chapter 99 HS codes apply to imports from Canada:
99030110, 99030126. I also need to add the
value of the umbrellas here ($20,000). By default, the country of manufacture
will match the country of export, but I can change it if I need to. Then enter the Incoterm.
It's important to choose the correct Incoterm because it defines exactly what the seller and
buyer are paying for. I’m going to choose Cost & Freight. Enter the Incoterm value and that is
what I'm paying to the seller, which includes the cost of the umbrellas plus the freight
because I’m using the CFR incoterm ($20,349). Enter the currency in the mode of transport
(Ocean). CFR is only available for ocean shipments. Then enter the freight
charges ($349). Only the items with asterisks are required, but you can enter more charges if you
want them to be included in the calculations. Now I need to click the plus sign next to
Vietnam and enter in the information. I know this chapter 99 code applies: 99030125. I’ll
enter the value of the goods, and let’s say from Vietnam they are $15 per umbrella ($15,000).
Enter the Incoterm and the Incoterm value, which is the cost of the umbrellas plus
the freight, which is more coming from Viet Nam($16,300; freight $1300). Enter the Mode of
Transport (Sea) and freight charges. And then I click next.
The results show the default landed cost and the minimum landed cost for both countries.
Click on the plus sign to see the detail for each country.
For Canada, if my goods qualify for the USMCA, then I only pay the cost of the goods plus
freight and a small merchandise processing fee and harbor maintenance fee. If the goods don’t
qualify for the USMCA, then I also owe a special duty under 99030110 of 25%. It is noted as “In
addition to” so it adds to my cost. If I open the details for Viet Nam,
I can see that a merchandise processing fee or MPF and harbor maintenance fee or HMF have
been added. The default duty is zero, but there is a special duty of 10%.
Of course, there may be other factors besides cost that a company will use for making the final
determination of where to source the goods, such as delivery time, quality, etc, but I now have a
reliable number to add to that final equation. The results are also kept in an online audit trail.

तो आपने ये यहां पर ये जरूरी नहीं है कि 10 यूनिट्स ही होने चाहिए हर इनवॉइस के अंदर। आपने ये इनवॉइस की रिक्वायरमेंट देखनी है। जब आप प्रोडक्ट को लिस्ट करते हैं। जब आपको प्रोडक्ट अनगेट करना होता है तो तब जाके Amazon आपको वहां पर बताता है कि भाई साहब आप जिस प्रोडक्ट को सेल करने वाले हैं इसके अंदर हमें कितने यूनिट्स चाहिए। ठीक है? यानी आपके इनवॉइस के अंदर कितने यूनिट्स परचेस होने चाहिए। ठीक है? कंबाइंड कितने यूनिट्स का जो है वह हमें आपने इनवॉइस देना है। तो वहां पर यह चीज कभी 10 यूनिट की होती है तो कभी 50 यूनिट की तो कभी 100 यूनिट की तो कभी 300 यूनिट की। ठीक है? तो ये थी इनवॉइस की रिक्वायरमेंट्स। आपने इन चीजों को बिल्कुल जो है वो बारीकी से देखना है। जब भी आपको कोई ब्रांड, कोई डिस्ट्रीब्यूटर इनवॉइस सेंड करे। ठीक है? तो आपने उस इनवॉइस के अंदर अपनी इंफॉर्मेशन बहुत ही जो है वो केयरफुली आपने चीजें देखनी है क्योंकि उनकी जो इंफॉर्मेशन है जिस तरह मैंने आपसे पहले कहा तो वो ऑटोमेटिकली उसके अंदर आ जाती है वो पहले से ही करेक्ट होती हैं। लेकिन जो आपकी इंफॉर्मेशन है वो चूंकि मैनुअली डालते हैं तो इसलिए आपकी जो इंफॉर्मेशन है वो मिसमैच हो सकते हैं या फिर उसके अंदर कुछ चीजें मिसिंग हो सकती हैं। ठीक है? तो आपने अपनी इंफॉर्मेशन को बिल्कुल क्लियरली देखना है। ठीक है? तो इसके बाद इंश्लाह आपकी इनवॉइस जो है वो Amazon रिजेक्ट नहीं करेगा। क्योंकि अगर आपकी इनवॉइस जो है वो रिक्वायरमेंट्स के ऊपर पूरी है और वो जो ब्रांड है वो ऑथराइज है। वो जो है वो ऑथेंटिक ब्रांड है। ब्रांड को कैसे चेक करना है कि वो ऑथेंटिक है, स्कैमर है। तो वीडियो हमने अपलोड की है। ठीक है? डिस्क्रिप्शन के अंदर उसका लिंक भी आपको मिल जाएगा। तो उसके बाद उनकी इनवॉइसेस जो है वो Amazon एक्सेप्ट करता है। ठीक है? तो आई होप सो कि आज की ये जो वीडियो है या ये आपको अच्छी लगी होगी। आपको समझ भी आई आ गई होगी। तो अगर आपको यह वीडियो अच्छी लगी है तो वीडियो को आपने लाइक, शेयर और चैनल को भी आपने जरूर सब्सक्राइब करना है। मिलते हैं अगली वीडियो में। तब तक के लिए अल्लाह हाफिज।

Learn how to process Shopify returns and exchanges step by step inside Shopify Admin. This guide walks you through finding the order, creating the return, adding exchange items, and completing the refund process.

02:44 Outro

✍️What You'll Learn In This Video:
• How To Process Shopify Returns And Exchanges
• How To Find An Order In Shopify Admin
• How To Add Exchange Products And Variants
• How To Create A Return In Shopify
• How To Add Tracking Numbers And Carriers
• How To Complete The Refund And Exchange Process

💡Pro Tips:
• Double-check product variants before creating the exchange.
• Always verify the return tracking number and shipping carrier.
• Review any payment difference before completing the exchange.
• Keep inventory updated by processing returns promptly.
• Use clear return policies to reduce customer confusion.

metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to **Shopify Development and Dropshipping**, a practical course designed to help you build, customize, and manage Shopify stores while developing essential e-commerce operations, customer service, payment management, and business protection skills. Throughout this course, you will explore Shopify store setup, product listings, supplier sourcing, order fulfillment, shipping workflows, customer communication, marketing automation, and strategies for running a reliable online business. Whether you are a beginner, student, freelancer, entrepreneur, online seller, or aspiring Shopify developer, this course can help you understand how professional store management supports customer trust and long-term business growth.

In **Lecture 112: Professional Refund Protocols & Chargebacks Protection**, you will explore how to handle refund requests professionally and reduce the risk of payment disputes. A clear refund process helps customers understand their options, gives merchants a consistent way to review complaints, and supports fair outcomes when an order is delayed, damaged, incorrect, or otherwise fails to meet expectations.

You will learn the importance of publishing clear refund and return policies, reviewing each request against the store's terms and applicable consumer protection rules, documenting customer communications, and processing approved refunds accurately. Prompt, respectful communication can often resolve concerns before they escalate. For dropshipping stores, coordination with suppliers and fulfillment partners is especially important when investigating delivery problems, defective products, or return arrangements.

The lecture also introduces **chargebacks**, which occur when a customer disputes a payment through their bank or card issuer. Common reasons may include unrecognized transactions, items not received, products that differ from their descriptions, or dissatisfaction with how a problem was handled. Merchants can reduce avoidable disputes by providing accurate product descriptions, transparent shipping timelines, accessible support, clear billing descriptors where supported, and timely order updates. When a dispute occurs, review the reason carefully and submit relevant evidence—such as order records, tracking information, policy disclosures, and customer correspondence—within the payment provider's deadline.

No process can eliminate every chargeback, and the appropriate response depends on the circumstances, payment provider, and applicable rules. Never use misleading policies or discourage legitimate customer complaints. By establishing professional refund protocols and maintaining organized transaction records, Shopify merchants can handle disputes more consistently, protect customer relationships, and improve operational accountability.

जाएगी और यह अमाउंट आपके डिडक्शन होकर कस्टमर को वापस पे कर दी जाएगी। इसी तरह से अगर कोई ऑर्डर चार्ज बैक के अंदर जाता है तो यहां से जो पेमेंट स्टेटस है यहां पर आपको नजर आ जाएगा कि यहां से इसके ऊपर चार्ज message lands after a long shift.
>> Here it is.
Returns are not an interruption of the
business. They are a line item in the
business. Roughly one in five online
orders higher in apparel, and they cost

arrives. Know your three kinds of

Know your supplier's clocks, especially

Write a policy you can actually honor
with an overseas supplier. Prevent the
returns your pages are causing. Keep a
small reserve per order and answer fast
like it is a financial decision because
it is one.
Do that and returns become what they
should be, a routine cost you manage and
occasionally handled well, the reason a
customer trusts your store enough to buy
again.
>> One more worked example on that reserve
because percentages stay abstract until
they are dollars.
Say I ship 100 orders this month at an
average of $40.
What does the reserve actually look
like?
>> Run it with apparel planning numbers.
A 20% return rate on 100 orders is 23
returns.
Say half are supplier fault or delivery
cases where you recover some cost or

or keep it refunds where you lose most

your blended loss per return after any

10% of revenue gone, unless you planned

Spread across all 100 orders, that is $4
an order to set aside.
$4 sounds small on the day an order

That is the whole philosophy of this

>> Write the one page playbook and open the

videos.full_text: Welcome back to Dropshipping Deep Dive. I am Rocky and today we are talking about the order after the order, returns, refunds and exchanges. Not the glamorous part of this business and not the part anyone puts in a sales video, but the part that quietly decides whether a store that looked profitable in its ads manager is actually profitable in its bank account. >> And I am Alex. Let me set the scene honestly. You make a sale for $40. You celebrate. Two weeks later the customer writes in, wrong size or it arrived damaged or they just do not like it. Now you are staring at your supplier page, your own return policy and your payout balance and you realize you never actually decided what happens next. You improvise and improvising returns, one stressed message at a time is expensive. >> It is and today we are going to replace improvisation with a system. Here is the road map. First, the real return numbers for online retail right now because most sellers guess far too low. Second, what one return actually costs a drop shipper worked out in dollars and why it costs us more than it costs a store holding its own stock. Third, the three kinds of returns because a damaged item, a late item and a changed mind are three different problems with three different playbooks. Fourth, the supplier reality, specifically what CJ will and will not do and the very short clocks hiding in that policy. Fifth, how to write a return policy that is fair, legal and survivable for your margins. Sixth, prevention because the cheapest return is the one that never happens. Seventh, the handling workflow, what to say, what to ask for and order to offer options in. And finally, the Monday morning work. Building a small returns reserve and a one-page playbook the next return is a routine, not a crisis. >> Start with the numbers then. How often does this actually happen? >> More often than most new sellers budget for. The most widely cited benchmark heading into 2026 is the National Retail Federation and Happy Returns 2025 retail returns landscape. It puts returns at about 15.8% of all retail sales and about 19.3% of online sales. Say that plainly. Roughly one in five online orders comes back in some form. Brick and mortar runs far lower, somewhere in the single digits, because the customer could touch the thing before buying it. Online, your customer is buying a photograph and a promise, and some share of those promises will not match the product that arrives. >> One in five is a lot higher than the number in most sellers' heads, which I suspect is like one in 50 because it has not happened to them yet. >> Exactly. And the average hides the category spread, which is the part that matters for a store like ours. Apparel and footwear sit at the top, commonly 20 to 40% for apparel online, with footwear often in the high teens to around 30%. Fit and sizing drive about half of apparel returns. Electronics run lower, roughly 8 to 15%. Beauty runs lower still, roughly 4 to 12%. Home goods sit somewhere in the middle. So a store selling mostly clothing, like a lot of CJ stores, should not plan around the 19% average. It should plan on the apparel band and then work hard to earn its way toward the bottom of that band. >> And there is a seasonal piece too, right? We're recording this in mid-November. >> Yes. Holiday sales return at a higher rate. The Federation expected about 17% of holiday sales to come back, and January is famously the peak return month because gifts are the ultimate fit and taste gamble. Someone else guessed your size, your color, and your style. If you sell through the holidays with no returns plan, January will hand you the plan at the worst possible time all at once. >> Okay, so returns are normal. They are frequent and they are category dependent. Now the part I really want. What does one return actually cost us? Because I think most sellers answer the refund and stop there. >> The refund is only the first line. Let us work a clean example. And listeners, adjust these numbers to your own store as we go. A customer buys a $40 item. Your landed cost, product plus freight to their door, is $18. Card fees on the sale were roughly $1.46. That is 2.9% plus 30 cents on $40. The customer wants to send it back because it does not fit. Now walk the options. Option one, a traditional return. The customer ships it back. If you pay for that return shipping, a small parcel inside the United States commonly runs $8 to $12 and that money is gone whether the item is resalable or not. Then someone has to receive it, inspect it, and decide if it can be sold again. Industry estimates for processing a single return, reverse shipping, handling, inspection, and markdowns all in commonly land between $10 and $45 per return with many estimates clustering around $20 to $30. And here is the drop shipping twist. You returns to where exactly? You do not have a warehouse. Your home address is not a returns department, and we will come back to that problem. >> And even if it arrives back somewhere, can you actually resell it? >> Often not at full price. Across retail, only about half of returned items resell at full price. Tags off, packaging opened, a season passed, a faint smell of someone else's laundry detergent, any of that turns a $40 item into a discount item or a write-off. Now option two for our example, the refund and keep it route. The customer keeps or donates the item and you refund the $40. You are out the $18 landed cost, the card fee, which does not come back just because you refunded, and any add cost you paid to acquire that order. If you paid say $12 in ads to get that sale, the full swing on that order is roughly $70 against you compared with where you thought you stood. 40 refunded, 18 in product and freight, a dollar and change in fees, and $40 in ads that bought an order that no longer exists. >> Wait, let me make sure listeners heard that. The sale looked like it made maybe $10 of contribution. The return does not just erase the $10, it can put you $30 or $40 underwater on that one order. >> That is exactly right, and it is why return rate belongs in the product math from day one, not as a surprise in month two. A useful way to think about it is an expected cost per order. If one in five orders returns and an average return costs you, say $30 all in beyond the refund itself reversing the sale, then every order you ship carries about $6 of expected return cost. $6 an order. If your contribution per order was $14, returns just took a very large bite of it before you paid for a single app or a single hour of your own time. Stores do not usually die from one return. They die from pricing as if returns were zero, then discovering returns were a line item all along. >> And there is a worse version of a refund, which is the chargeback. >> There is, and every seller needs to understand the difference. A refund is you giving the money back on your terms with the relationship possibly intact. A chargeback is the customer's bank taking the money back on the bank's terms after the customer decided you were too slow, too confusing, or too hard to reach. On Shopify payments in the United States, a chargeback pulls the disputed amount out of your next payout immediately plus a $15 chargeback fee. You get a window, typically 7 to 21 days to submit evidence. The issuer can take weeks to decide and if you win, the amount and the fee come back. If you lose, they do not and the product is usually long gone as well. So on our $40 order, a lost chargeback is the $40 plus $15 in fee plus your $18 of landed cost plus the ad spend. And every chargeback, won or lost, counts toward your chargeback rate and payment providers start restricting accounts when that rate climbs toward 1% of transactions. The cheapest chargeback strategy in the world is a fast, easy refund offered before the customer ever calls their bank. $15 buys a lot of promptness. >> So a refund is a cost. A chargeback is that same cost plus a fine plus a black mark. That framing alone should change how fast people answer return emails. >> It should. Speed is a financial strategy here, not just good manners. Now, segment three. Because not all returns are the same problem and treating them the same is how sellers either over refund the wrong cases or under refund the right ones and eat chargebacks. Kind one, our fault or the supplier's fault. Damaged, defective, wrong item sent, wrong color, missing parts. The customer did everything right and the product failed them. This is the easiest decision in the business. Make it right, fast, refund or resend. Your choice guided by what the customer wants and then recover what you can from the supplier. Goodwill here is cheap, and arguing here is expensive. >> Kind two? >> Kind two is the delivery failure. The parcel never arrived. It's stalled with a label and no scan. It blew past the promised window, or it was marked delivered somewhere the customer never saw it. This one has a legal clock on it in the United States, and we will cover that in the policy segment. But the short version is a customer who paid for something that never arrived is owed a resolution, and waiting them out does not make the obligation smaller. It makes the charge back more likely. >> And kind three is the one sellers resent the most. >> Kind three is buyer preference. Wrong size ordered, changed mind, color looks different on their wall than on their screen. Bought two sizes planning to return one, which shoppers call bracketing, and which is now a normal shopping habit in apparel. Nobody broke anything. The product is fine. This is the category where your policy actually does the work. Your sizing information, your photos, your window, and your exchange options. It is also the category where you have the most legitimate choices. Offer an exchange first. Offer store credit if your policy and the situation allow it, or refund under your stated terms. What you cannot do is have no stated terms and then invent harsh ones in the moment. That is how preference returns turn into disputes. >> Let me push on bracketing for a second because apparel sellers feel personally backed by it. Is there anything to do besides accept it? >> Reduce the need for it. Bracketing is usually a sizing information failure. If a customer cannot tell whether they are a medium or a large from your page, ordering both is rational from their side of the screen. Accurate measurements in inches and centimeters, the model's size and height where you know it, fabric stretch notes, and a simple line like this style runs small. Consider sizing up. Those things cut bracketing at the source. We will go deeper on prevention later, but hold the thought. A large share of preference returns are information returns. The customer was not careless. The page was vague. >> All right, segment four, the supplier reality. This is where dropshipping returns get genuinely different from normal retail. >> This is the segment I wish someone had forced me to hear before my first return. So let us be precise about CJ since that is the supplier most of our listeners use and the pattern is similar with other overseas suppliers. First, the good news. For quality problems, damage and wrong items, CJ does offer refunds or resends and in many of those cases the customer does not have to ship the item back at all. That sounds generous and it can be, but it comes with clocks that are brutally short. Under CJ's published dispute policy, a damage dispute for an ordinary product should be opened within three days of the customer receiving it. For electronics, the window is seven days. Three days. If your customer opens their parcel on a Friday, shows you on a Tuesday and you open the dispute on a Wednesday, you may already be outside the window holding the entire cost yourself. >> Three days is not a window. That is a trap door. So the speed of your customer conversation directly determines whether the supplier shares the cost or you eat all of it. >> Exactly. And that changes your workflow. When a customer reports damage, you need photos the same day, not eventually. CJ will want evidence, clear photos of the damaged item, the packaging and the shipping label. Get all three in the first reply you send. Do not have a four-message conversation that collects one photo at a time over a week. Your first message should say, I am sorry. I will make this right. And to open your claim today, I need these three photos. Friendly and urgent. For a you do not need to burden the customer with. >> What about the other clocks? Lost parcels? >> For an order that is lost or stuck in transit, CJ's policy talks about refund or resend after the parcel has been in transit a very long time. The published figure is around 45 days for the United States and 60 days for much of the rest of the The world compare that with your customer who reasonably expects a resolution in days or a couple of weeks. And with platform rules we covered in the fulfillment episode which are far stricter. The gap between the supplier's clock and the customer's clock is your problem and financially it is your float. You will often make the customer whole first and recover from the supplier later or not at all. Price that reality in. >> And physical returns to the supplier? Can a customer just send the item back to CJ? >> Practically for preference returns, no. And sellers need to stop implying otherwise in their policies. CJ's own guidance discourages returns to its China warehouse. International return shipping is expensive. Transit can take months and items get lost. A return accepted in China may become inventory credit for future orders, not cash back to you. And the United States warehouse does not function as a returns address for your customer's preference returns. So translate that into plain English. For a low or mid-priced drop shipped item, there is usually no economical physical return path at all. The item coming back to anyone, anywhere often costs more than the item is worth. That is why the refund and keep it exchange by reship and partial solutions we will cover in the workflow segment exist. They are not generosity hacks. They are the arithmetic of reverse logistics when the product started on the other side of an ocean. >> So if your policy page says return the item to us for full refund and us is actually a warehouse in China that takes 3 months, you have written a policy you cannot honorably run. >> Correct. And customers >> can smell that, and banks deciding chargebacks can too. Your policy has to describe the process you will actually follow. We will build that policy in the next segment. One more supplier point first. Keep records per product, not just per order. If one product generates damage disputes again and again, that is not bad luck. That is product data. A product with a high damage or defect rate is a product whose true cost includes all those refunds. And at some point, the honest move is to fix the listing, change the supplier, or stop selling it, no matter how well it converts. Returns data is product selection data, arriving a little late and a little rudely. >> Segment five then. Writing the policy. What does a survivable honest return policy actually contain for a drop shipping store? >> Five elements. All in plain language, all findable before checkout, not buried after it. Element one, the window. How many days from delivery does a customer have to start a return? 30 days is a common defensible choice, and it matches what many shoppers expect. Whatever you choose, count it from delivery, not from the order date, because with overseas shipping, the difference between those two can be two weeks of the customer's window evaporating while the parcel was still on a plane. Element two, the condition. Unused, unwashed, tags on where that applies, with sensible exceptions for hygiene items that cannot be resold, stated clearly before purchase, not discovered after. Element three, who pays for what? Split by fault. If we or the supplier got it wrong, we carry the cost. If it is a preference return, say plainly what happens, whether the customer ships it to a stated address at their cost or whether you handle it another way. Element four, how the refund lands. Back to the original payment method and how long after you approve it in business days the customer should expect it. Element five, the exceptions and the process. One email address or contact route, what information to include, order number, reason, and photos for damage, and what happens next and when. >> You mentioned a legal clock earlier for delivery failures. Give listeners the short, careful version. >> Careful version. And this is general information, not legal advice for your specific store. In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission's mail, internet, or telephone order merchandise rule says a seller must have a reasonable basis for the shipping time it advertises. And if it advertises no time at all, it generally has 30 days to ship. If it cannot ship on time, it must offer the customer the choice to accept the delay or cancel for a prompt refund. And a required refund cannot be replaced with store credit or a voucher. The lesson for returns policy is simple. Your delay and cancellation language cannot promise less than that floor. A policy that says no refunds under any circumstances is not a shield. It is a liability. And payment providers and marketplaces will override it anyway, usually at the most expensive moment with a chargeback attached. >> And consistency matters too, right? The policy cannot say one thing on the store and another thing everywhere else. >> It matters a lot. Your policy page, your product pages, your shipping policy, your frequently asked questions, and any marketplace or feed listings all need to tell the same story. If one place promises a 30-day return window and another says 14 days, the customer will reasonably hold you to the more generous one. And so will a dispute reviewer. Pick one set of numbers and repeat them everywhere, word for word. And while you're at it, check the delivery promise in the same pass. A returns problem and a shipping promise problem are often the same problem wearing two coats. >> Okay. Segment six, prevention. You said the cheapest return is the one that never happens. What actually moves the rate? >> Start where the returns are born, the product page. For apparel, a real size chart with garment measurements, not just small, medium, large with no numbers behind them. State the unit, inches and centimeters both, because your customers use both. Add fit notes, runs true to size, runs small, relaxed fit, and fabric notes, stretch or no stretch, thick or thin. For everything, use the supplier's real photos and your sample photos honestly. A color that looks emerald on a heavily filtered supplier photo and arrives forest green is a return you manufactured at the listing stage. Show scale, a photo of the item in a hand or next to a common object, because size surprise is not just an apparel problem. State what is in the box and, just as important, what is not. Half of the not as described messages I have seen were really the listing let me imagine an accessory that was never included. >> What about the post-purchase side? Prevention does not end at checkout. >> No. Some of the best prevention happens after the sale. A confirmation and shipping message that restates the delivery window honestly sets the expectation that prevents the where is my order spiral. A delivery follow-up, a day or two after tracking shows delivered, that asks, did it arrive safely and how does the fit feel? Does two jobs. It catches damage inside that three-day supplier dispute window we talked about while you can still recover from CJ. And it catches a sizing problem while an exchange still feels like help instead of a fight. Silence after delivery is not neutral. It is how small problems age into refunds and chargebacks. >> And product selection itself is prevention. >> It is the deepest prevention there is. Fragile items with thin packaging will generate damage returns at a rate no policy can fix. Items with confusing sizing and no good measurements will generate fit returns forever. When you review a product to add to your store, ask the returns question up front. How will this fail? How often? And what will that failure cost me? A sample order answers a lot of that. Wear it, wash it, drop the box it came in the way a sorting facility would. The sample is not a luxury. It is returns research. >> Segment seven, the workflow. A return request lands. Walk me through the exact order of operations. >> Step one, respond fast and respond like a human. For a working seller, same day is the standard to hold and the first message has three jobs. Acknowledge the problem without arguing about it. Say what you will do and collect everything you need in that one message. Order number confirmation, the reason, and for damage, those three photos, item, packaging, and label. Every extra round trip costs days and days cost supplier dispute windows. And a practical note from hard experience. For order problems, many customers answer a text far faster than an email. If you have a legitimate order-related reason and the customer's number from their order, a short, polite text pointing them to the fix often moves in an hour what email moves in three days. Keep it about their order, keep it professional, and keep marketing out of it. >> Step two, classify it using those three kinds from earlier. >> Right. Fault, delivery, or preference. Fault and delivery get the make it right path. Refund or resend, no debate. And you open the supplier dispute the same day with your evidence. Preference gets the options ladder and the order of the ladder matters. First, can information fix it? A surprising share of preference messages are really I do not understand how to use it, assemble it, or style it. A clear answer, a short video, or a sizing tip sometimes closes the case with the product kept and the customer genuinely satisfied. Do not use that to dodge a legitimate return, but do offer help before logistics. Second, exchange. Wrong size is the classic. For a drop shipper, an exchange usually means a reship of the correct size because a physical swap across an ocean is fiction. Do the math on the reship cost versus the refund cost, and if you reship, decide plainly what happens to the wrong item. Often the customer keeps or donates it because paying to recover a low-cost item you cannot easily resell is lighting money on fire politely. Third, store credit. Where your policy allows it and the customer genuinely prefers it, some sellers add a small bonus on credit because a credit keeps the sale inside the store. Never force credit where a refund is owed, especially on fault or delivery cases. Fourth, the refund. Cleanly to the original payment method within the time your policy promises. >> There is a math decision hiding in there. When do you refund and let them keep it versus asking for the item back at all? >> Run the recovery math honestly. What is the item worth to you if it comes back realistically? Not at full retail, but at the price you can actually resell a returned unit for if you can resell it at all. What does getting it back cost? Return shipping, your time, inspection, storage in a home-based business with no returns shelf. If the recovery cost is anywhere near the recoverable value, and for most items under about $30 or $40 from an overseas supplier it is, then refund and keep it or donate it is the cheaper and kinder answer. Asking a customer to pay $14 to ship back a $25 item so you can recover almost nothing is not discipline. It is friction, and friction is what turns a preference return into a one-star review and a chargeback risk. Save physical returns for higher value items where the math genuinely works and that process clearly in your policy. >> What about the customer who is just difficult? Threatening charge backs in the first message, demanding a refund and a replacement and a discount? >> Stay boring. Be polite, be specific, put the offer in writing, and meet your own policy exactly. Do not negotiate against threats, and do not get creative under pressure. A calm written record of a fair offer made quickly is your best evidence if a dispute ever does get filed. And most angry first messages soften considerably when the reply is fast and concrete. The ones who do not soften are going to file either way, and your record is what protects you then. Also, log it. A simple note per case, date, product, kind, resolution, cost, and whether the supplier reimbursed you. 10 seconds per case, and in 90 days that log becomes the most honest product and policy review you own. >> Last segment, the Monday morning work and the reserve you mentioned at the top. >> Two builds, neither takes long. Build one is the returns reserve. Look at your last 90 days if you have them. Count orders, count returns and refunds, and work out your real return rate and your real average cost per return, including what the supplier did not cover. If you are too new to have data, start with a planning assumption from your category, say 20% for apparel, and an assumed loss per return close to your average landed cost plus fees, and refine it monthly. Then set the reserve as a per order set aside. If your expected return cost works out to $5 an order, move $5 per order into a separate pot weekly as part of your normal money routine. The point is not the exact number. The point is that when a refund lands, it comes out of a pot that exists, not out of this week's rent money or next week's ad budget. Returns stop being emergencies the day they become a budgeted cost of goods. >> And build two is >> the playbook itself. One page kept where you actually answer messages, your window in terms stated once, your three classifications, your first reply templates, one for damage asking for the three photos, one for a delivery failure with the make it right commitment, one for a preference return offering the ladder. Your supplier dispute checklist, photos, order number, deadline noted, open the same day, and your log format. 90 minutes of work once, and every return after that is faster, cheaper, and calmer. Then review it monthly against the log. If one product keeps appearing, fix or drop the product. If one reason keeps appearing, fix the page. If your reserve keeps coming up short, fix the assumption, not your mood. >> Give me the takeaway version. The thing to remember at 11:00 p.m. when a return message lands after a long shift. >> Here it is. Returns are not an interruption of the business. They are a line item in the business. Roughly one in five online orders higher in apparel, and they cost far more than the refund alone once you count product, freight, fees, ads, and the $15 chargeback fine waiting behind a slow reply. So decide everything before the message arrives. Know your three kinds of returns and the play for each. Know your supplier's clocks, especially that three-day damage window, and collect your photos in the first reply. Write a policy you can actually honor with an overseas supplier. Prevent the returns your pages are causing. Keep a small reserve per order and answer fast like it is a financial decision because it is one. Do that and returns become what they should be, a routine cost you manage and occasionally handled well, the reason a customer trusts your store enough to buy again. >> One more worked example on that reserve because percentages stay abstract until they are dollars. Say I ship 100 orders this month at an average of $40. What does the reserve actually look like? >> Run it with apparel planning numbers. A 20% return rate on 100 orders is 23 returns. Say half are supplier fault or delivery cases where you recover some cost or reship cheaply, and half are preference or keep it refunds where you lose most of the landed cost. your blended loss per return after any supplier recovery is about $20, that is $400 of return cost on $4,000 of sales. 10% of revenue gone, unless you planned for it. Spread across all 100 orders, that is $4 an order to set aside. $4 sounds small on the day an order arrives, and it sounds like genius on the day the fifth refund of the week lands and the pot simply covers it. And if your real rate comes in lower, the pot grows, and you can release the excess later with data behind you instead of releasing it early with hope behind you. That is the whole philosophy of this episode in one habit. Replace hope with a small, honest number repeated every week. >> And if listeners do one thing on Monday morning >> Write the one page playbook and open the reserve pot with whatever your math says, even if it starts small. Future you facing January returns with a system and a pot of money set aside for exactly that will be very grateful. That is it for today. Thanks for listening to Dropshipping Deep Dive, and we will see you tomorrow.

metadata.title: Google Merchant Center - Optimizing Your Feed: Custom Labels with Google Sheets & Attribute Rules
metadata.author: PPC Incubator
metadata.shortDescription:
Want granular control over your Google Shopping campaigns? In this video, I'll show you how to create and integrate Custom Labels in Google Merchant Center Next, leveraging the power of an external Google Sheet for product classification and Attribute Rules for implementation. This strategy will allow you to segment your products in unique ways, optimizing bids and boosting the performance of your Google Ads campaigns.

Attribute Rules video: https://youtu.be/ZRVSRQg_DGQ

What You'll Learn:
- What Custom Labels are and why they're essential for advanced product feed management.
- How to classify your products in an external Google Sheet using Custom Labels, with practical examples of segmentation (e.g., seasonal products, profit margins, best-sellers).
-The step-by-step process to link your Google Sheet to Google Merchant Center Next as a supplementary feed here: https://youtu.be/jR0Bb7LfCX4
- How to utilize Attribute Rules to read data from your Google Sheet and automatically assign Custom Labels to products in your main feed.
- How Custom Labels can be leveraged in Google Ads to create highly targeted ad groups and bidding strategies, improving your ROAS.

00:00 - Introduction
01:25 - Decide the Custom Label you want to use
02:16 - Set the Attribute Rules
02:28 - See the results
03:47 - Use supplemental sources
04:30 - Subdivide the campaign with the Custom Labels




By the End of This Video, You'll Be Able To:
- Create and manage Custom Labels effectively using a Google Sheet.
- Integrate your Google Sheet data into your Merchant Center feed via Attribute Rules.
-Segment your products to optimize bidding strategies and Google Ads campaign performance.
- Gain deeper, automated control over your product classification.
